activities.context: During a class lesson on “The Blue Planet,” a student looked at a picture of Earth and noticed that most of it was blue, with brown land forming a smaller part. The teacher explained that the largest water bodies are oceans, while smaller extensions are called seas, bays and gulfs. The student also learned that oceans and continents are spread unevenly between the Northern and Southern Hemispheres, and that both shape Earth’s climate and affect all life.
activities.prompt: The student asks why Earth appears mostly blue when viewed from space. Which explanation best fits the lesson?
options: The large surface area covered by water makes the planet look blue.
The blue colour represents only freshwater spread across Earth’s surface.
The brown land has been coloured blue to show where oceans are found.
The smaller water extensions cover more of Earth than the largest water bodies.

why.The blue colour represents only freshwat: The oceans are the largest water bodies.
why.The smaller water extensions cover more: Seas, bays and gulfs are smaller than oceans.

activities.explanation: Water covers almost three-fourths of Earth.

activities.context: During a class lesson on “The Blue Planet,” a student looked at a picture of Earth and noticed that most of it was blue, with brown land forming a smaller part. The teacher explained that the largest water bodies are oceans, while smaller extensions are called seas, bays and gulfs. The student also learned that oceans and continents are spread unevenly between the Northern and Southern Hemispheres, and that both shape Earth’s climate and affect all life.
activities.prompt: Why might the Northern and Southern Hemispheres look different in terms of water and land?
options: Each hemisphere contains a different balance of water and land.
Each hemisphere has exactly the same amount of water and land.
The Northern Hemisphere contains only oceans and no continents.
The Southern Hemisphere contains only land and no oceans.

why.Each hemisphere has exactly the same amo: One hemisphere has more water relative to land.
why.The Northern Hemisphere contains only oc: The other has more land relative to water.
why.The Southern Hemisphere contains only la: The picture reflects this uneven distribution.

activities.explanation: Oceans and continents are not equally distributed.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between an ocean and groundwater.
activities.answer: An ocean is a large body of water on the globe. Groundwater is water found underground. Most of the planet’s water is in oceans, but that seawater is salty and unfit for most land animals, including humans. Groundwater is one of the places where freshwater can be found.
points: An ocean is a large body of water.
Groundwater is water underground.
Ocean water is salty and unfit for humans.
Groundwater is among the sources of freshwater.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Riya’s class was studying the five oceans when the teacher drew a map for the group. It showed the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Arctic and Southern oceans, but the teacher said the dividing lines were only map conventions. Riya wondered whether seawater could move from one named ocean to another. Maya explained that the Indian Ocean lies between Asia, Africa and Australia, with the Arabian Sea near India’s west side and the Bay of Bengal to its east.
activities.prompt: Maya follows seawater moving from the Arabian Sea into the wider Indian Ocean. What should the class conclude?
options: It can continue through the Indian Ocean because the map boundary does not block seawater.
It must stop because the Arabian Sea and Indian Ocean have different names.
It can move only within the Arabian Sea because map lines mark physical walls.
It would end marine life because different ocean names prevent seawater from mixing.

why.It must stop because the Arabian Sea and: Different names do not make the oceans physically separate.
why.It can move only within the Arabian Sea: Map lines are not physical walls, and seawater flows across oceans.
why.It would end marine life because differe: Seawater flowing across oceans sustains a rich diversity of marine life.

activities.explanation: Map boundaries are only conventions, so they do not stop seawater.

activities.context: Riya’s class was studying the five oceans when the teacher drew a map for the group. It showed the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Arctic and Southern oceans, but the teacher said the dividing lines were only map conventions. Riya wondered whether seawater could move from one named ocean to another. Maya explained that the Indian Ocean lies between Asia, Africa and Australia, with the Arabian Sea near India’s west side and the Bay of Bengal to its east.
activities.prompt: Riya is placing cards for India’s two major island groups beside the correct parts of the Indian Ocean. Which arrangement is correct?
options: Andaman and Nicobar beside the Bay of Bengal; Lakshadweep beside the Arabian Sea
Andaman and Nicobar beside the Arabian Sea; Lakshadweep beside the Bay of Bengal
Both island groups beside the Arabian Sea
Both island groups beside the Bay of Bengal

why.Andaman and Nicobar beside the Arabian S: This reverses the correct locations of the two island groups.
why.Both island groups beside the Arabian Se: Lakshadweep is in the Arabian Sea, not the Bay of Bengal.
why.Both island groups beside the Bay of Ben: Andaman and Nicobar are in the Bay of Bengal, not the Arabian Sea.

activities.explanation: Andaman and Nicobar are in the Bay of Bengal, while Lakshadweep is in the Arabian Sea.

activities.prompt: Explain how the map lines and the movement of seawater give different ideas about whether the oceans are separate.
activities.answer: The lines make it look as though the oceans are separate areas, but they are only conventions. Seawater constantly flows across the oceans, so the named oceans are not really separate. Their connected waters also sustain a rich diversity of marine life.
points: Map lines are conventions.
Seawater flows across the oceans.
The oceans are not really separate.
Connected ocean waters support rich marine life.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Following a strong earthquake in Indonesia on 26 December 2004, a huge wave travelled across the Indian Ocean and struck India and 13 other countries. In India, the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and the coasts of Tamil Nadu and Kerala were severely affected. More than two lakh people lost their lives. The disaster was handled under disaster management, and countries, including India, contribute to an early warning system for Indian Ocean tsunamis.
activities.prompt: What benefit could the Indian Ocean Tsunami Warning System provide if another tsunami were detected before reaching the coast?
options: It could help warn coastal communities before the tsunami hit.
It could make the tsunami stop travelling across the ocean.
It could change the strong earthquake into a cyclone.
It could prevent all damage in coastal areas.

why.It could make the tsunami stop travellin: Detection does not stop a tsunami.
why.It could change the strong earthquake in: A warning system does not change an earthquake.
why.It could prevent all damage in coastal a: It cannot guarantee that every kind of damage will be prevented.

activities.explanation: A warning system can provide warning before impact.

activities.context: Following a strong earthquake in Indonesia on 26 December 2004, a huge wave travelled across the Indian Ocean and struck India and 13 other countries. In India, the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and the coasts of Tamil Nadu and Kerala were severely affected. More than two lakh people lost their lives. The disaster was handled under disaster management, and countries, including India, contribute to an early warning system for Indian Ocean tsunamis.
activities.prompt: What could happen if a tsunami were not detected before it reached a coast?
options: Coastal areas could be submerged, and lives and property could be lost.
The monsoon rains could stop bringing rain to the continents.
The clouds seen from space could disappear.
The strong earthquake could be prevented from causing a huge wave.

why.The monsoon rains could stop bringing ra: Lack of detection does not stop the ocean’s monsoon rains.
why.The clouds seen from space could disappe: Warning systems do not affect clouds.
why.The strong earthquake could be prevented: Not detecting a tsunami does not prevent its formation.

activities.explanation: Tsunamis can submerge coastal areas and cause widespread destruction.

activities.prompt: Explain why rain is important for life and why monsoon rain from the ocean is important for agriculture.
activities.answer: Rain is essential because agriculture and all life would suffer without it. Since India’s monsoon rains originate in the ocean, rain brought by clouds supports farming and life on the continents. Thus, the ocean’s clouds and the monsoon rains they produce help sustain agriculture and living things.
points: Rain is necessary for agriculture and all life.
India’s monsoon rains originate in the ocean.
Clouds bring rain to the continents.
Without these rains, agriculture and life would suffer.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student is preparing a classroom display about how continents are counted. The display uses the seven-continent list because it is the one most widely adopted and used. It shows North America and South America as separate continents, while Europe and Asia are shown as one landmass. The size diagram shows relative sizes rather than actual shapes. A caption asks visitors to compare land in the two hemispheres, and another explains the meaning of the Olympic rings.
activities.prompt: To explain the Olympic rings accurately, which set should the student put on the display?
options: Africa, America, Asia, Australia and Europe
Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia and Europe
Africa, America, Antarctica, Europe and Australia
Africa, America, Asia, Europe and South America

why.Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia and: This includes Antarctica and leaves out one of the five named continents.
why.Africa, America, Antarctica, Europe and: This includes Antarctica and leaves out Asia.
why.Africa, America, Asia, Europe and South: This leaves out Australia and replaces Asia with South America.

activities.explanation: This exactly matches the five inhabited continents represented by the rings.

activities.context: A student is preparing a classroom display about how continents are counted. The display uses the seven-continent list because it is the one most widely adopted and used. It shows North America and South America as separate continents, while Europe and Asia are shown as one landmass. The size diagram shows relative sizes rather than actual shapes. A caption asks visitors to compare land in the two hemispheres, and another explains the meaning of the Olympic rings.
activities.prompt: If the student adds one caption about the hemispheres, which statement is accurate?
options: The Northern Hemisphere has more land than the Southern Hemisphere.
The Southern Hemisphere has more land than the Northern Hemisphere.
The Northern Hemisphere and Southern Hemisphere have equal amounts of land.
The Southern Hemisphere has no land, while the Northern Hemisphere has all of it.

why.The Northern Hemisphere and Southern Hem: The fact does not say that the two hemispheres have equal land.
why.The Southern Hemisphere has no land, whi: The fact says the Southern Hemisphere has less land, not none.

activities.explanation: This agrees with the stated difference in land between the hemispheres.

activities.prompt: Why can the same world be described using different numbers of continents?
activities.answer: Different groups can treat connected landmasses differently. North America and South America may be counted separately or together. Europe and Asia may also be separated, even though they form one landmass. Because these choices are allowed, continents can be counted in several ways, from four to seven.
points: North America and South America may be counted separately or together.
Europe and Asia may be separated despite forming one landmass.
The number of continents can range from four to seven.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: While studying a map, Ananya sees that some small pieces of land have water on every side, while larger land areas do too. Her teacher says there are lakhs of islands of different sizes, and Greenland is the largest. India has more than 1,300 small islands: Andaman and Nicobar lie in the Bay of Bengal, while Lakshadweep lies in the Arabian Sea. Another display shows Indian scientists working in Antarctica, a very cold continent with a harsh environment.
activities.prompt: Ananya asks whether Antarctica should be entered in the same list as Greenland. What should the teacher explain?
options: It should be left off the island list because Antarctica is a continent, even though it is mostly ice.
It should be added because water surrounds every part of it.
It should be added because ice cover makes a continent an island.
It should be added because Indian scientists have a base station there.

why.It should be added because water surroun: Being surrounded by water alone is not enough, because large continents are also surrounded by water.
why.It should be added because ice cover mak: Ice cover does not decide whether a landmass is an island.
why.It should be added because Indian scient: Having a scientific base does not turn a continent into an island.

activities.explanation: Antarctica is a continent, so it is not classified as an island.

activities.context: While studying a map, Ananya sees that some small pieces of land have water on every side, while larger land areas do too. Her teacher says there are lakhs of islands of different sizes, and Greenland is the largest. India has more than 1,300 small islands: Andaman and Nicobar lie in the Bay of Bengal, while Lakshadweep lies in the Arabian Sea. Another display shows Indian scientists working in Antarctica, a very cold continent with a harsh environment.
activities.prompt: A map maker accidentally swaps the sea labels for India's two island groups. What correction should Ananya make?
options: Put Andaman and Nicobar beside the Bay of Bengal, and keep Lakshadweep beside the Arabian Sea.
Put Andaman and Nicobar beside the Arabian Sea, and keep Lakshadweep beside the Bay of Bengal.
Put both groups beside Antarctica because scientists work there.
Put both groups beside Greenland because it is the largest island.

why.Put Andaman and Nicobar beside the Arabi: This reverses the locations shown in the case.
why.Put both groups beside Antarctica becaus: Antarctica is where Indian scientists work, not where India's island groups are located.
why.Put both groups beside Greenland because: Greenland's position as the largest island does not connect it to India's island groups.

activities.explanation: Andaman and Nicobar are in the Bay of Bengal, while Lakshadweep is in the Arabian Sea.

activities.prompt: Explain why Antarctica is not an island even though it is surrounded by water.
activities.answer: An island is a smaller piece of land surrounded by water on all sides. A continent is also surrounded by water, but it is so large that it is not an island. Antarctica is a continent, so its icy surface does not make it an island.
points: An island is smaller and has water on every side.
Continents are also surrounded by water but are very large.
Antarctica is classified as a continent.
Its ice cover does not change its classification.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A coastal community depends on the sea for food and trade. After large amounts of plastic enter the water, fish begin to struggle, and fishing yields fall as more boats cast their nets. At a World Oceans Day event, residents argue that the sea should be protected, not used without limits. A student asks why an ocean can support life while also facing such dangers.
activities.prompt: What should the community do next to protect the sea?
options: Reduce plastic waste and excessive fishing to protect marine life.
Increase plastic use and add more fishing trips to obtain more food.
Keep waste and fishing practices unchanged because the sea has always supplied food.
Stop all fishing and trade because every use of the sea causes harm.

why.Increase plastic use and add more fishin: More plastic and fishing would increase the damage to marine life.
why.Keep waste and fishing practices unchang: Unchanged harmful practices would not protect the ocean.
why.Stop all fishing and trade because every: Avoiding all use would ignore the community's dependence on the sea.

activities.explanation: Reducing waste and excessive fishing directly addresses the threats described.

activities.context: A coastal community depends on the sea for food and trade. After large amounts of plastic enter the water, fish begin to struggle, and fishing yields fall as more boats cast their nets. At a World Oceans Day event, residents argue that the sea should be protected, not used without limits. A student asks why an ocean can support life while also facing such dangers.
activities.prompt: If the oceans had much more flourishing flora than they do now, what would be the most likely effect?
options: More oxygen would be produced, helping sustain life on Earth.
Less oxygen would be produced, weakening support for life on Earth.
Oceans would no longer play any role in regulating climate.
Rainfall to continents would stop, and Earth would become a desert.

why.Less oxygen would be produced, weakening: More flourishing flora would mean more oxygen production, not less.
why.Oceans would no longer play any role in: Oceans regulate climate, and more flora would not remove that role.
why.Rainfall to continents would stop, and E: The water cycle carries ocean water to the continents as rain.

activities.explanation: Ocean flora produce more than half of the world's oxygen.

activities.prompt: Explain why oceans are called the planet's lungs and why they matter for life on Earth.
activities.answer: Oceans are called the planet's lungs because more than half of the world's oxygen is produced by their flora. They also send rain to the continents through the water cycle, regulate climate, and sustain life on Earth. Without oceans, there would be no rainfall and Earth would be a desert.
points: More than half of the world's oxygen comes from ocean flora.
Oceans send rain to the continents through the water cycle.
Oceans regulate climate and sustain life.
Without oceans, there would be no rainfall.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

chapters.title: Landforms and Life
chapters.summary: In this chapter: landforms: three main types; mountains: their shapes and world locations; mountain environment and life; plateaus: raised land with broad surfaces.

lessons.title: Landforms: Three Main Types

activities.prompt: What makes Earth’s land look so different from place to place?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Touring Three Main Landforms
activities.body:
Imagine beginning a journey across land that looks different in every region. You might see many changing shapes along the way. You learn that a landform is a physical feature on Earth’s surface. Landforms can take millions of years to form.

Your tour begins with mountains. They are much higher than the surrounding landscape. You can recognise them by a broad base, steep slopes and a narrow summit. Some mountains are covered with snow because of their height.

At very high altitudes, snow may never melt. This can leave a mountain permanently snowcapped.

Next, you reach a plateau, one of the three main types. A plain completes the trio. Together, these three landforms show how greatly land can vary.

Landforms can have different climates. They also support varied plants and animals. People have adapted to all three main types. You may notice that different numbers of people live on them around the world.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: What are landforms?
activities.body: Land looks very different in different places. A landform is a natural shape on Earth's surface. Landforms take millions of years to form. The three main types are mountains, plateaus and plains. A plateau is high, flat land. Each type has its own climate (usual weather), plants and animals. People have learned to live in all three.
keyPoints: A landform is a natural shape on Earth's surface.
The three main types are mountains, plateaus and plains.
Each landform has its own climate, plants and animals.
activities.explanation: Landforms shape the land around us. They take a very long time to form.

activities.prompt: A family sees two snowy mountains. One is very high. Why might it keep snow on its summit?
steps: One mountain reaches a very high altitude.
At very high altitudes, snow may never melt.
Because the snow remains, the summit stays covered.
Therefore, the higher mountain may be permanently snowcapped.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: A landform is a physical feature on Earth's surface.
activities.explanation: This is the plain meaning of a landform.

activities.prompt: There are three main types of landforms: ______, plateaus and plains.
activities.hint: Choose the type that can be much higher than the land around it.
activities.explanation: Mountains are much higher than the land around them.

activities.prompt: Match each clue to its landform word.
pairs: A physical feature on Earth's surface
Much higher than the surrounding landscape
Different climates and varied plants and animals
activities.explanation: The clues describe a landform, mountains, and landforms in general.

activities.prompt: Which set of features recognises a mountain?
options: A broad base, steep slopes and a narrow summit
A narrow base, flat slopes and a broad summit
A broad base, gentle slopes and a wide summit
A narrow base, gentle slopes and a wide summit
activities.explanation: Mountains can be recognised by a broad base, steep slopes and a narrow summit.

activities.prompt: Put a mountain's features in order, from bottom to top.
activities.explanation: The wide base comes first. Then the slopes. The narrow summit is at the top.

activities.prompt: Which sentence is true about people and landforms?
options: The same number of people live on every landform.
The number of people on each landform is different around the world.
People can live only on mountains.
Every landform has the same number of people.
activities.explanation: The number of people on each landform is different around the world.

activities.prompt: Two mountains rise above nearby land. One reaches a very high altitude. Which one may stay snowcapped?
options: The higher one, because its snow may never melt.
The lower one, because its snow may never melt.
The wider one, because its broad base traps snow.
The smaller one, because less snow reaches its summit.

why.The lower one, because its snow may neve: This wrongly assumes that the lower mountain is at the very high altitude.
why.The wider one, because its broad base tr: This confuses the broad base with what causes lasting summit snow.
why.The smaller one, because less snow reach: This wrongly thinks a smaller summit means the mountain is lower.

activities.explanation: At very high altitudes, snow may never melt, leaving a permanent snowcap.

activities.prompt: A plain and a nearby plateau support different plants and animals. What difference is likely between their climates?
options: They are likely to have different climates.
They are likely to have formed much faster.
They are likely to have identical plant life.
They are likely to have equal populations.

why.They are likely to have formed much fast: This wrongly assumes different landforms must have formed at different speeds.
why.They are likely to have identical plant: This wrongly assumes the same landforms support exactly the same plants and animals.
why.They are likely to have equal population: This wrongly uses equal population as the main difference between climates.

activities.explanation: Different landforms have different climates, which support varied plants and animals.

activities.prompt: A traveller sees a broad base and steep slopes. The landform also has a narrow summit. What can we conclude about its height?
options: It rises much higher than the surrounding landscape.
It lies almost level with the surrounding landscape.
It has the same height as the surrounding plateau.
It stands below every nearby mountain slope.

why.It lies almost level with the surroundin: This wrongly treats a mountain as almost level with nearby land.
why.It has the same height as the surroundin: This wrongly assumes a mountain has the same height as a plateau.
why.It stands below every nearby mountain sl: This wrongly assumes the mountain is lower than nearby land.

activities.explanation: Mountains are much higher than the surrounding landscape.

activities.prompt: Three homes stand on a mountain, a plateau, and a plain. What does this show about people?
options: People have adapted to all three main landforms.
People can adapt only to the plain.
People cannot live on the plateau.
People avoid mountains because of their slopes.

This wrongly limits human adaptation to plains.
This wrongly says people cannot live on plateaus.
why.People avoid mountains because of their: This wrongly assumes people cannot adapt to mountain slopes.

activities.explanation: Humans have adapted to all three main landforms.

lessons.title: Mountains: Their Shapes and World Locations

activities.prompt: Ready to discover what makes mountains look so different from one another?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour Through Mountain Shapes
activities.body:
Imagine a mountain tour through the Himalayas, the Alps and the Andes. These mountain ranges show you that mountains often gather in lines. Some ranges stretch for thousands of kilometres.

Meet Mount Everest and Kanchenjunga, the two highest peaks of the Himalayan range. Visit Mount Aconcagua, the highest peak of the Andes. In the Alps, Mont Blanc stands highest. You reach south India, where Anamudi, also called Anai Peak, is the highest mountain.

Not every high mountain belongs to a range. Kilimanjaro stands alone as an isolated mountain. You now compare a lone mountain with peaks gathered in ranges. Your guide shows you how hills are lower, less steep and more rounded than mountains.

Your tour next reaches the Aravalli Range, where the hills are much older. Here, erosion has rounded the hills over time. The Himalayas offer a different picture because they are relatively young mountains.

Mountains do not always keep the same shape. Upliftment and erosion continue to affect some mountains today. By comparing ranges, lone peaks and rounded hills, you learn to read their shapes.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Meet Some Famous Mountains
activities.body: Hills are lower, less steep and more rounded than mountains. The Himalayas, Alps and Andes are mountain ranges. Mount Everest and Kanchenjunga are the highest Himalayan peaks. Mount Aconcagua is highest in the Andes, while Mont Blanc is highest in the Alps. Mount Kilimanjaro is isolated. The Himalayas are relatively young. The Aravalli hills are older and rounded by erosion. Upliftment and erosion continue today.
keyPoints: Hills are lower, less steep and more rounded than mountains.
Mountain ranges contain famous peaks.
Some mountains are young, while others are older and changing.
activities.explanation: Mountains can be grouped by their shapes, ages and locations.

activities.prompt: Meera sees a high place that is lower, less steep, and more rounded. Is it a hill or a mountain?
steps: The high place is lower and less steep than a mountain.
These features match hills, which are gentler and more rounded.
So Meera should call it a hill, not a mountain.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Hills or Mountains?
activities.prompt: Which sentence describes hills?
options: Lower, less steep and rounder than mountains
Higher, steeper and less round than mountains
Low, flat land far from mountains
Sharp tops with very steep sides
activities.explanation: Hills are highlands. They are lower, less steep and rounder than mountains.

activities.title: Very Long Ranges
activities.prompt: Some mountain ranges stretch for thousands of kilometres.
activities.explanation: Some mountain ranges are very long. They stretch for thousands of kilometres.

activities.title: Match Mountains and Places
activities.prompt: Match each place with its mountain.
activities.explanation: These pairs show famous peaks and where they are. Anamudi is also called Anai Peak.

activities.title: The Isolated Mountain
activities.prompt: Which mountain is isolated? Isolated means alone. It is not part of a mountain range.
options: Mount Kilimanjaro
Mount Everest
Mount Aconcagua
Mont Blanc
activities.explanation: Mount Kilimanjaro is an isolated mountain. It is not part of a range.

activities.title: Young and Older Mountains
activities.prompt: The Himalayas are fairly young mountains.
activities.explanation: The Himalayas are fairly young. The Aravalli Range hills are much older.

activities.title: Range Before Peak
activities.prompt: Put each mountain range before its highest peak.
activities.explanation: Mount Everest is a highest peak of the Himalayas. Mount Aconcagua is the highest peak of the Andes.

activities.prompt: Upliftment and erosion still affect some mountains today. What may happen to their height and shape?
options: Their height and shape may keep changing.
Their height and shape will stay exactly the same.
They will soon become part of a mountain range.
They will quickly stop being mountains.

why.Their height and shape will stay exactly: This mistake assumes that mountains never change after they appear.
why.They will soon become part of a mountain: This wrongly assumes that changing mountains become mountain ranges.
This wrongly assumes that every change quickly removes mountain status.

activities.explanation: Upliftment and erosion continue to affect some mountains today.

activities.prompt: A hiker sees rounded hills and young mountains. Which group is older?
options: The Aravalli Range hills are older.
The Himalayas are much older.
Both groups have the same age.
Neither group has rounded hills.

This reverses the fact that the Himalayas are relatively young.
This overlooks the clear age difference between the two groups.
The Aravalli hills are rounded, so this claim is false.

activities.explanation: The Aravalli hills are older and rounded by erosion.

activities.prompt: A map shows one mountain alone. No range joins it. Which peak is on the map?
options: Mount Everest
Mount Aconcagua
Mount Kilimanjaro
Mont Blanc

why.Mount Everest: Kilimanjaro is isolated and belongs to no mountain range.
why.Mount Aconcagua: Everest belongs to the Himalayan range, so it is not alone.
why.Mont Blanc: Mont Blanc is the highest mountain of the Alps range.

activities.explanation: Aconcagua is the highest peak of the Andes range.

activities.prompt: A walker wants a gentle, rounded highland. Which place should they choose?
options: The Aravalli Range hills
The relatively young Himalayas
The Andes mountain range
The isolated Mount Kilimanjaro

why.The relatively young Himalayas: Being relatively young does not identify the rounded hill group.
why.The Andes mountain range: The Andes are a mountain range, not the named rounded hill group.
why.The isolated Mount Kilimanjaro: Kilimanjaro is an isolated mountain, not a group of rounded hills.

activities.explanation: The Aravalli hills are rounded by erosion, so they match the wish.

activities.prompt: A walker follows one mountain range for many days. Why might the walk stay inside it?
options: The range may stretch for thousands of kilometres.
The range may move once every day.
Every peak may have the same height.
The range may contain only one hill.

This mistake imagines that the whole range travels each day.
A long range does not mean all its peaks share one height.
Stretching for thousands of kilometres does not mean only one hill.

activities.explanation: Some ranges stretch for thousands of kilometres, so the walk can continue.

lessons.title: Mountain Environment and Life

activities.prompt: What can you discover while travelling through a mountain environment?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Journey Through Mountain Life
activities.body:
You begin your journey among rugged mountain terrain, where steep slopes shape the land ahead. Soon, you enter montane forests, forests that often cover mountain slopes. Tall conifer trees rise around you, their thin, pointed leaves and cone-shaped forms reaching skyward.

Climb higher, and the trees gradually give way to grasses, mosses and lichen. This change in plant life feels like a new chapter on your journey. Nearby, mountain forests, rivers, lakes, grasslands and caves shelter diverse fauna.

Follow the Ganga, the largest river that originates in the Himalayas. Many tributaries join it, each bringing another river into the shared flow. Regular farming can be practised only in some mountain valleys. Terrace farming is done by cutting steps into mountain slopes.

Some communities prefer herding to agriculture in mountainous regions. Tourism often provides important income for some mountain communities. However, too many visitors can put pressure on the fragile mountain environment. Your tour ends among mountains with diverse fauna. You have passed forests, rivers, lakes, grasslands and caves.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Life in the Mountains
activities.body: Mountain slopes often have montane forests. Conifers are tall, cone-shaped and have thin, pointed leaves. Higher up, trees give way to grasses, mosses and lichen. Mountain forests, rivers, lakes, grasslands and caves have diverse fauna. Diverse fauna means many animals live there. Only some valleys allow regular farming. Terrace farming cuts steps into mountain slopes. Herding is often preferred to agriculture. Tourism often provides mountain communities with income.
keyPoints: Montane forests often cover mountain slopes.
Higher slopes have grasses, mosses and lichen.
Farming, herding and tourism shape mountain life.
activities.explanation: These ideas show how mountains shape forests, farming and daily life.

activities.prompt: A family on a steep mountain slope wants to grow crops. What can they do?
steps: The ground is rugged and steep, so regular farming there is difficult.
Some mountain valleys allow regular farming, but this family is on a slope.
To grow crops on their slope, they can cut steps into it.
These steps are terrace farming, so it is a clear farming choice.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Forests on Mountain Slopes
activities.prompt: What are the forests on a mountain slope called?
options: Montane forests
Grasslands
Caves
Tributaries
activities.explanation: Montane forests often grow on mountain slopes.

activities.title: Life at Higher Altitudes
activities.prompt: At higher altitudes, grasses, mosses and ______ grow instead of trees.
activities.hint: It grows high up, where there are no trees.
activities.explanation: At higher altitudes, grasses, mosses and lichen grow instead of trees.

activities.title: Match Mountain Terms
activities.prompt: Match each word with its meaning.
pairs: Forests often found on mountain slopes
Tall and cone-shaped, with thin, pointed leaves
activities.explanation: Each pair uses a fact about forests, trees, farming or rivers.

activities.title: Life on a Mountain
activities.prompt: Put these in order by altitude (how high up). Start low.
activities.explanation: Higher up, there are fewer trees. Grasses, mosses and lichen grow there.

activities.title: The Ganga
activities.prompt: Which sentence about the Ganga is true?
options: It is the largest river that starts in the Himalayas.
It is a small river in the Himalayas.
It is a tributary of the Himalayas.
It is a river without tributaries.
activities.explanation: The Ganga is the biggest river that starts in the Himalayas. It also has many tributaries.

activities.prompt: A village sits on a steep mountain slope. How can farmers grow crops there?
options: Cut farming steps into the slope.
Plant regular crops on the steep slope.
Plant regular crops at the slope's top.
Use the slope only for animal herding.

This assumes regular crops suit every steep mountain slope.
This assumes the mountaintop is flat and easy for farming.
Herding does not grow the crops that the family wants.

activities.explanation: Terrace farming cuts steps into slopes, so it suits this steep land.

activities.prompt: A map shows smaller rivers joining the Ganga. What does this show?
options: The Ganga has several tributaries.
The Ganga is the largest Himalayan river.
These smaller rivers all rise in the Himalayas.
The Ganga is the only river on the map.

why.The Ganga is the largest Himalayan river: The map does not show which river is largest.
why.These smaller rivers all rise in the Him: Joining the Ganga does not show where those rivers rise.
Other rivers may appear, so this conclusion is too strong.

activities.explanation: Rivers joining the Ganga are its tributaries, so this is right.

activities.prompt: A family lives on rugged ground with steep slopes. What work often suits them?
options: Herding animals rather than farming crops.
Farming crops on the steepest slope.
Farming crops in every mountain valley.
Herding animals beside every mountain river.

Steep, rugged ground makes regular crop farming difficult.
This assumes every mountain valley allows regular farming.
why.Herding animals beside every mountain ri: This wrongly assumes river water makes steep ground easy for herding.

activities.explanation: Herding is often preferred in mountainous regions, so it fits their land.

lessons.title: Plateaus: Raised Land with Broad Surfaces

activities.prompt: What can you discover while touring a plateau?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Plateaus
activities.body:
Imagine standing on a vast table of land. Its surface is more or less flat. You can look across its broad surface. You may wonder how such land formed.

During your journey, you meet plateaus of different ages. Some are young, while others are old in Earth’s history. You see heights from a few hundred metres to several thousand metres. Each view adds another chapter to your journey.

Now, you arrive at the Tibetan Plateau. It is the largest and highest plateau in the world. Its average altitude is 4,500 metres. Next, you visit the Deccan Plateau. It formed through volcanic activity millions of years ago.

Here, you look below your feet and notice the soil. Many plateaus have rocky soil. Lava plateaus often have rich black soil. Plateaus are rich in mineral deposits. Mining is therefore a major activity on plateaus. Finally, you hear rushing water. Many spectacular waterfalls are found on plateaus.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: What is a plateau?
activities.body:
A **plateau** is raised land. Its top is mostly flat. Its height can be a few hundred metres. It can also be several thousand metres.

Plateaus can be young or old. They have many mineral deposits. So mining is important.

Many have rocky soil. Lava plateaus often have rich black soil. Many waterfalls are found on them.
keyPoints: A plateau has a mostly flat surface.
Plateau heights are very different.
Plateaus can be young or old.
activities.explanation: Plateaus are high, flat lands with many important features.

activities.prompt: A child sees two broad, flat lands on a map. One is a few hundred metres high, and one is the Tibetan Plateau. Why can both be plateaus?
steps: A plateau has a more or less flat surface, so both flat lands fit.
The first land is a few hundred metres high, which is within the plateau height range.
The Tibetan Plateau is also a plateau, even though it is much higher.
Therefore, different heights do not stop either flat land from being a plateau.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which plateau is the biggest and highest in the world?
options: Deccan Plateau
Tibetan Plateau
Lava Plateau
Rocky Plateau
activities.explanation: The Tibetan Plateau is the biggest and highest plateau in the world.

activities.prompt: The top of a plateau is mostly flat.
activities.explanation: Yes. A plateau has a wide top that is mostly flat.

activities.prompt: The Tibetan Plateau has an average altitude (height above sea level) of ______ metres.
activities.hint: Look at the altitude given for the Tibetan Plateau.
activities.explanation: The Tibetan Plateau has an average altitude of 4,500 metres.

activities.prompt: Match each plateau with its right fact.
pairs: biggest and highest plateau in the world
activities.explanation: Each pair joins a plateau with a fact from the lesson.

activities.prompt: Why is mining a big job on plateaus?
options: Because every plateau has rich black soil.
Because plateaus have many waterfalls.
Because plateaus have many mineral deposits.
Because plateaus are always young.
activities.explanation: Mining is a big job on plateaus because they have many mineral deposits.

activities.prompt: Which sentence about plateaus is right?
options: Many plateaus have black soil. Lava plateaus have rocky soil.
Many plateaus have rocky soil. Lava plateaus have black soil.
The Tibetan Plateau formed by volcanoes. The Deccan Plateau has black soil.
The Deccan Plateau is the highest. The Tibetan Plateau has rocky soil.
activities.explanation: This sentence matches many plateaus with rocky soil. It matches lava plateaus with black soil.

activities.prompt: Plateaus are rich in mineral deposits. Ravi wants work. Why might mining suit a plateau?
options: Rich mineral deposits make mining a major activity here.
The flat surface is the main reason mining happens here.
Many waterfalls are the main reason mining happens here.
Rich black soil is the main reason mining happens here.

why.The flat surface is the main reason mini: This mistakes the plateau’s shape for the cause of mining.
why.Many waterfalls are the main reason mini: Waterfalls may attract visitors, but they do not explain mining.
why.Rich black soil is the main reason minin: Black soil can fit lava plateaus, but it does not explain mining here.

activities.explanation: Minerals give a clear reason for mining on plateaus.

activities.prompt: Two sources describe the Tibetan Plateau and the Deccan Plateau. Which comparison is supported?
options: The Tibetan Plateau is larger and higher than the Deccan Plateau.
The Deccan Plateau is larger and higher than the Tibetan Plateau.
The Tibetan Plateau formed through volcanic activity, while Deccan did not.
Both plateaus have the same average altitude of 4,500 metres.

why.The Deccan Plateau is larger and higher: This reverses the size and height facts about the Tibetan Plateau.
why.The Tibetan Plateau formed through volca: The facts only say that the Deccan formed through volcanic activity.
why.Both plateaus have the same average alti: Only the Tibetan Plateau has the stated average altitude.

activities.explanation: The Tibetan Plateau is the largest and highest in the world.

activities.prompt: Two plateaus look alike from above. Can one be young and the other old?
options: Yes, because plateaus can be young or old in Earth’s history.
No, because every plateau formed in the same period.
No, because a flat surface must be very old.
No, because young plateaus cannot have flat surfaces.

why.No, because every plateau formed in the: This wrongly assumes that all plateaus formed at the same time.
why.No, because a flat surface must be very: This wrongly treats a flat surface as proof of great age.
why.No, because young plateaus cannot have f: This wrongly assumes that young plateaus cannot be flat.

activities.explanation: A plateau’s age can differ, even when the surface looks flat.

activities.prompt: Two maps show plateaus. One is a few hundred metres high. Can this be true?
options: Yes, because plateau heights can start at a few hundred metres.
No, because every plateau is several thousand metres high.
No, because only the Tibetan Plateau can be this low.
No, because plateaus must all have the same height.

why.No, because every plateau is several tho: This ignores the wide range in plateau heights.
why.No, because only the Tibetan Plateau can: The height range includes plateaus other than the Tibetan.
why.No, because plateaus must all have the s: This wrongly assumes that all plateaus have one height.

activities.explanation: Plateau heights can range from a few hundred metres upward.

activities.prompt: A visitor wants a broad, flat surface and a spectacular waterfall. Why can a plateau suit this trip?
options: Plateaus have broad surfaces, and many have spectacular waterfalls.
Plateaus have broad surfaces, but waterfalls are never found there.
Waterfalls cover every flat surface in the world.
Rich minerals make every flat surface hold a waterfall.

why.Plateaus have broad surfaces, but waterf: This wrongly says that waterfalls do not occur on plateaus.
why.Waterfalls cover every flat surface in t: This turns “many plateaus” into a claim about every flat surface.
why.Rich minerals make every flat surface ho: This wrongly links mineral deposits with the presence of waterfalls.

activities.explanation: A plateau is more or less flat, and many have spectacular waterfalls.

lessons.title: Plains and River Life

activities.prompt: What makes river plains special for people, farms and communities?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Plains and River Life
activities.body:
Imagine yourself walking across a vast plain. The land stretches far, with gentle rises and dips. Plains generally rise no more than 300 metres above sea level. As you travel, rivers slowly carry sediment and spread it across the land. Their deposits create very fertile soil.

From your journey, you learn why the first civilisations grew near rivers in fertile plains. You discover rich soil beside the water. You also learn that many people live on plains around the world.

Now you enter the Ganga plain. About 40 crore people live here. This is over one-fourth of India’s population. You see people fish in rivers and farm fertile land. These are important occupations in the plain.

You can travel easily by boat because plains rivers have a gentle slope. Irrigation helps farmers grow more food. However, it also reduces groundwater.

Later, you visit a sacred river location. Here, many communities hold festivals, ceremonies and rituals. As you return, you understand why plains and rivers support life together. You remember the flat land, fertile soil and easy river travel.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Life on the Plains
activities.body: Plains are big, flat lands. Some plains are gently rolling. They are usually no more than 300 metres above sea level. Rivers leave **sediments** (mud and soil) on them. This makes the soil **fertile**, good for growing crops. The first civilisations grew up near rivers on these plains. Many people live there. Farming, river fishing, easy river travel and holy festivals are important parts of river life.
keyPoints: Plains are flat or gently rolling.
Plains are usually no more than 300 metres above sea level.
River sediments make plains fertile.
activities.explanation: Plains have rich soil, calm rivers and lively communities.

activities.prompt: A family lives on a flat plain beside a gentle river. Why do many people settle, work, and gather there?
steps: Rivers leave fertile soil, so farming can support communities.
The gentle slope makes navigation easy, so river travel is simple.
Sacred river places hold festivals, so communities gather and celebrate together.
Therefore, plains are important places for living, working, travelling, and celebrating together.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Good Things and Problems
activities.body: Irrigation means bringing water to farms. It helps farms grow more food. But irrigation also lowers groundwater. Groundwater is water under the ground. River life includes farming and fishing. Rivers on plains are easy to travel on. The land slopes down gently. Many communities hold festivals and ceremonies at holy river places. These facts show how river plains help work, travel and community life.
keyPoints: Irrigation helps farms grow more food.
Irrigation also lowers groundwater.
Holy river places are used for community events.
activities.explanation: This shows the good and bad of irrigation.

activities.title: Which Land is a Plain?
activities.prompt: Which sentence describes plains?
options: Flat or gently rolling land
Steep slopes everywhere
Always more than 300 metres high
Dry land with no rivers
activities.explanation: Great choice! Plains are large, flat or gently rolling land.

activities.prompt: Plains are always more than 300 metres above sea level.
activities.explanation: Plains are usually not more than 300 metres above sea level. The word 'always' makes this wrong.

activities.title: Match the River Fact
activities.prompt: Match each plains fact with its right ending.
pairs: Important jobs in the Ganga plain
activities.explanation: Good job! These facts show why plains are good for river life.

activities.title: Easy River Travel
activities.prompt: Why is river navigation (travelling by boat) easy on plains?
options: Rivers have a steep slope
Rivers have no slope
Rivers have a gentle slope
Rivers have rocky banks
activities.explanation: Well done! Rivers have a gentle slope. So navigation is easy on plains.

activities.title: The Crowded Ganga Plain
activities.prompt: About 40 crore people live in the ______ plain.
activities.hint: Use the river name from the lesson.
activities.explanation: Correct! About 40 crore people live in the Ganga plain.

activities.title: Build a Fertile Plain
activities.prompt: Put these steps in order. Each step makes the next one happen.
items: Rivers leave sediment (mud and sand) on plains
The soil becomes very fertile (good for crops)
The first civilisations grow up near rivers, on fertile plains
activities.explanation: Great order! Rivers leave sediment (mud and sand) on plains. This makes fertile soil. Early villages grow up near rivers.

activities.prompt: A river carries sediment onto nearby plains. Why does this help farming there?
options: River sediment makes the soil more fertile.
River sediment makes the soil very salty.
River sediment makes the soil very dry.
River sediment makes the soil less fertile.

why.River sediment makes the soil very salty: This mistake thinks river sediment makes soil salty.
This mistake thinks river sediment dries the soil.
why.River sediment makes the soil less ferti: This mistake thinks rivers remove goodness from the soil.

activities.explanation: This is right because river sediment makes the soil fertile.

activities.prompt: Before irrigation, farm production was lower. After irrigation began, what changed?
options: Farm production rose, but groundwater levels fell.
Farm production fell, and groundwater levels rose.
Farm production and groundwater levels both rose.
Farm production and groundwater levels both fell.

why.Farm production fell, and groundwater le: This mistake thinks irrigation lowers farm production instead of increasing it.
why.Farm production and groundwater levels b: This mistake thinks irrigation restores groundwater instead of reducing it.
This mistake reverses both effects of irrigation on farms and groundwater.

activities.explanation: This is right because irrigation raises farm production but reduces groundwater.

activities.prompt: A map shows a wide plain below 300 metres above sea level. Its surface is gently sloping. What does this suggest about river travel there?
options: River navigation is likely easy because the slope is gentle.
River navigation is likely hard because the slope is steep.
River navigation is likely easy because the plain is very high.
River navigation is likely hard because the plain is very flat.

why.River navigation is likely hard because: This mistake confuses a gentle river slope with a steep one.
why.River navigation is likely easy because: This mistake treats under 300 metres as very high ground.
why.River navigation is likely hard because: This mistake thinks a flat plain makes a river slope steep.

activities.explanation: This is right because gentle slopes make river navigation easy.

activities.prompt: Some families live beside rivers in fertile plains. Why did the first civilisations begin there?
options: Fertile river soil helped people settle and farm there.
Fertile river soil made people avoid farming there.
Rivers gave early people no way to grow food.
Rivers made fertile plains difficult to reach.

why.Fertile river soil made people avoid far: This mistake thinks fertile soil discourages farming instead of helping it.
why.Rivers gave early people no way to grow: This mistake thinks rivers prevent people from growing food.
why.Rivers made fertile plains difficult to: This mistake thinks rivers block people from reaching fertile plains.

activities.explanation: This is right because fertile river plains helped farming and early settlement.

activities.prompt: About 40 crore people live in the Ganga plain. Which jobs might you expect to see there?
options: People doing agriculture and river fishing in the plains.
People doing agriculture and avoiding all river work.
People doing river fishing and avoiding all farming work.
People attending festivals but no farming or fishing.

why.People doing agriculture and avoiding al: This mistake thinks people in the Ganga plain avoid all river work.
why.People doing river fishing and avoiding: This mistake thinks people in the Ganga plain avoid all farming work.
why.People attending festivals but no farmin: This mistake confuses festivals with the important everyday occupations.

activities.explanation: This is right because agriculture and river fishing are important occupations there.

activities.prompt: At a sacred river place, people gather for a festival. What does this show about the river's importance to the community?
options: They value this place for its sacred meaning.
They choose it because river navigation is easy.
They choose it because river soil is fertile.
They choose it because many people live there.

why.They choose it because river navigation: This mistake confuses easy navigation with sacred meaning.
why.They choose it because river soil is fer: This mistake confuses fertile soil with sacred meaning.
why.They choose it because many people live: This mistake confuses a large population with sacred meaning.

activities.explanation: This is right because sacred river places are used for festivals and rituals.

lessons.title: Deserts and the Bigger Picture

activities.prompt: How do people and animals find a way in deserts?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Deserts and the Bigger Picture
activities.body:
You begin your journey among deserts. You meet unique plants and animals in each one.

First, you visit the Sahara in Africa and the Thar in India. Both are hot deserts. Next, you travel to the Gobi Desert in Asia. Here, you find a cold desert.

As you continue, you meet people who live in most deserts. Despite harsh living conditions, humans have adapted to these places. You see how people can live in difficult surroundings.

Then, your guide opens a book of ancient Tamil Sangam poetry. It describes five landscapes called tiṇais. You notice that their classification differs from the three main types.

This wider view helps you understand the bigger picture. Landforms form an important part of culture around the world. Every landform offers both challenges and opportunities.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Deserts, Landforms and Culture
activities.body: Deserts have unique plants and animals. The Sahara and Thar are hot deserts. The Gobi is cold. Humans have adapted to most deserts despite harsh conditions. Ancient Tamil Sangam poetry describes five landscape types called tiṇais. A tiṇai is one type in this classification. They use a different landform classification from the three main types. Landforms matter to culture around the world. Every landform offers both challenges and opportunities.
keyPoints: Hot deserts include the Sahara and Thar.
The Gobi is a cold desert.
Five tiṇais use a different classification from the three main types.
activities.explanation: Deserts show how living things adapt and how landforms connect with culture.

activities.prompt: Why can’t the tiṇai hall and main-types hall share one list?
steps: Ancient Sangam poetry describes five tiṇais, so culture included five named landscapes.
The tiṇais differ from the three types, so their labels cannot match.
Every landform offers challenges and opportunities, so each hall should show both.
Landforms matter in culture, so both halls should explain their role in life.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Hot Desert Pairs
activities.prompt: Which pair has only hot deserts?
options: Sahara and Gobi
Thar and Gobi
Sahara and Thar
Sahara, Thar and Gobi
activities.explanation: The Sahara and Thar are hot deserts. The Gobi is a cold desert.

activities.title: A Hot Desert in Africa
activities.prompt: The ______ is a hot desert in Africa. The Thar is a hot desert in India.
activities.hint: This hot desert is in Africa.
activities.explanation: The Sahara is a hot desert in Africa. The Thar is also hot.

activities.title: What Do Tiṇais Describe?
activities.prompt: What do the five tiṇais describe?
options: Three main landform types
Only desert climates
Five different landscapes
Hot and cold deserts
activities.explanation: A Sangam poem describes five landscapes. These landscapes are called tiṇais.

activities.title: Deserts and Their Places
activities.prompt: Match each desert with its place.
activities.explanation: The Sahara is in Africa. The Thar is in India. The Gobi is in Asia.

activities.title: A Trip Across Deserts
activities.prompt: A path goes from Africa to India to Asia. Put the deserts in that order.
activities.explanation: The path goes to Africa, then India, then Asia. The deserts follow this same order.

activities.title: Correcting Two Claims
activities.prompt: A friend says all deserts are hot. She says all deserts have the same landforms. Which answer shows she is wrong?
options: The Sahara and Thar are hot. Deserts have their own plants and animals.
People live in most deserts. Every landform gives people something.
Tiṇais describe five landscapes. Landforms matter to culture.
The Gobi is cold. Tiṇais group land in a different way.
activities.explanation: The Gobi is cold. So not all deserts are hot. Tiṇais group land in a different way.

activities.prompt: A map shows three deserts. The Sahara is in Africa. The Thar is in India. The Gobi is in Asia. The Sahara and Thar are hot. The Gobi is cold. Which desert fits a cold-desert study trip?
options: Gobi Desert in Asia.
Sahara Desert in Africa.
Thar Desert in India.
No desert shown on this map.

This mistake treats a hot desert as cold.
This mistake also treats a hot desert as cold.
This mistake ignores the map’s desert clues.

activities.explanation: This matches the map and the cold-desert clue.

activities.prompt: A child visits a desert. What should the child notice about its plants and animals?
options: They have kinds found only in deserts.
They are the same everywhere.
They are all missing from deserts.
They include only three animal kinds.

This wrongly assumes deserts lack special plants and animals.
This wrongly assumes desert life matches life everywhere.
This wrongly turns unique kinds into a fixed number.

activities.explanation: Deserts have their own unique plants and animals.

activities.prompt: An ancient Tamil Sangam poem names five landscapes called tiṇais. What does this source show about ancient Tamil culture?
options: It included ideas about five named landscapes.
It ignored every idea about the land.
It used the three main landform types.
It described only one kind of landscape.

This wrongly assumes the source ignored the land.
This wrongly swaps tiṇais for the three main types.
This wrongly reduces five landscapes to one.

activities.explanation: The poem names five landscapes, so the source shows five landscape ideas.

activities.prompt: A student has a chart of five tiṇais. Another chart has three main landform types. Should the student treat both charts as the same list?
options: No, their landform classifications differ.
Yes, both charts classify land the same way.
Yes, five types must be more complete.
No, three types cannot show landforms.

why.Yes, both charts classify land the same: This wrongly assumes both classifications work the same way.
This wrongly treats a larger number as a better match.
This wrongly thinks three main types are not landforms.

activities.explanation: This is right because the two classifications are different.

activities.prompt: People celebrate a nearby landform. They also plan around its difficulties and chances. What broad idea does this show?
options: Landforms shape culture and bring both kinds of effects.
Culture ignores landforms and their difficulties.
Culture shows landforms but never their difficulties.
Culture shows landforms but never their chances.

why.Culture ignores landforms and their diff: This wrongly separates culture from landform problems.
why.Culture shows landforms but never their: This wrongly thinks culture avoids landform challenges.
This wrongly thinks culture avoids landform opportunities.

activities.explanation: This is right because landforms matter in culture and offer both.

lessons.title: Test practice
lessons.sceneAlt: Snow-covered Himalayan peaks surround a rocky mountain lake in Chola Valley, Nepal.
lessons.sceneCaption: Snowy Himalayan peaks rise above a mountain lake in Chola Valley, Nepal.

activities.context: A family lives on a mountain in one region. The mountain rises steeply from a broad base and has a narrow summit. Snow stays on the summit because it is at a very high altitude. The family has adapted to life there. In another region, people live on a plain, where the number of people may be different.
activities.prompt: If the mountain were at a lower altitude, what would most likely happen to the snow on its summit?
options: The snow could melt, so the summit might no longer remain permanently snowcapped.
The snow would certainly remain, and the summit would stay narrow.
The broad base would become steep slopes because the snow melted.
The mountain would change into one of the other two main landform types.

why.The snow would certainly remain, and the: A permanent snowcap depends on very high altitude.
why.The broad base would become steep slopes: Melting snow does not change the mountain’s slopes.
why.The mountain would change into one of th: Melting snow does not change a mountain into another landform type.

activities.explanation: Lower height can allow snow to melt.

activities.context: A family lives on a mountain in one region. The mountain rises steeply from a broad base and has a narrow summit. Snow stays on the summit because it is at a very high altitude. The family has adapted to life there. In another region, people live on a plain, where the number of people may be different.
activities.prompt: If the family moved to the plain, what should they expect?
options: They would need to adapt to the plain, and the number of people there could be different.
They would need to adapt to the plain, and exactly the same number of people would live there.
They would not need to adapt because all landforms have identical conditions.
They would need to adapt, and the plain would soon become a mountain.

why.They would need to adapt to the plain, a: The population on another landform is not guaranteed to be identical.
why.They would not need to adapt because all: Different landforms can have different climates, plants and animals.
why.They would need to adapt, and the plain: Living on a plain does not turn it into a mountain.

activities.explanation: Humans adapt to each main landform, and populations vary between them.

activities.prompt: Explain why land can look very different from one region to another.
activities.answer: Land has many physical forms, and each landform is a feature of Earth’s surface. Different landforms can have different climates and support different plants and animals. These differences help make the appearance of land vary greatly between regions.
points: Land has many forms.
Landforms are physical features on Earth’s surface.
Different landforms can have different climates.
Different landforms support varied plants and animals.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a geography lesson, a class is preparing a map display about mountains. One card labels the Himalayas as relatively young, while another explains that the Aravalli Range hills have become rounded through erosion. A student places Mount Kilimanjaro with the Himalayas and a card for Mount Aconcagua with the Andes. The teacher asks the class to check each choice before finishing the display.
activities.prompt: How should the class correct the placement of Mount Kilimanjaro on the display?
options: Leave it outside every range because it stands alone.
Place it with the Himalayas because Everest and Kanchenjunga are in that range.
Place it with the Alps because Mont Blanc is the highest mountain there.
Place it with the Andes because Aconcagua is the highest peak there.

why.Place it with the Himalayas because Ever: Wrong: Being in the Himalayas does not make Kilimanjaro part of that range.
why.Place it with the Alps because Mont Blan: Wrong: Mont Blanc belongs to the Alps, not Kilimanjaro.
why.Place it with the Andes because Aconcagu: Wrong: Aconcagua belongs to the Andes, not Kilimanjaro.

activities.explanation: Correct: Kilimanjaro is an isolated mountain.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between hills and mountains.
activities.answer: Hills are highlands that are lower, less steep, and more rounded than mountains. Mountains are higher and steeper, while hills have rounded shapes. A rounded hill and a steep mountain may both be highlands, but they differ in height, steepness, and shape.
points: Hills are highlands.
Hills are lower than mountains.
Hills are less steep than mountains.
Hills are more rounded than mountains.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Geeta and her family live in a Himalayan valley. Their village lies among conifer-covered slopes, with a lake and cave nearby. Tourism provides income for the community, and the family helps visitors. The family also herds animals and grows crops on terraced land cut into a steep slope. Recently, visitor numbers have increased, and the family is unsure whether to encourage more tourists or protect the area.
activities.prompt: What is likely to happen if even more visitors come to the valley?
options: The fragile mountain environment may begin to suffer.
The conifer-covered slopes will change into a lake.
Regular farming will become possible on every slope.
The Ganga will lose all its tributaries.

why.The conifer-covered slopes will change i: The conifer-covered slopes will not turn into a lake because of visitors.
why.Regular farming will become possible on: Regular farming is possible only in some mountain valleys.
Visitors will not cause the Ganga to lose all its tributaries.

activities.explanation: Too many visitors can place pressure on a fragile mountain environment.

activities.context: Geeta and her family live in a Himalayan valley. Their village lies among conifer-covered slopes, with a lake and cave nearby. Tourism provides income for the community, and the family helps visitors. The family also herds animals and grows crops on terraced land cut into a steep slope. Recently, visitor numbers have increased, and the family is unsure whether to encourage more tourists or protect the area.
activities.prompt: Why might the community prefer herding to farming on the rugged mountain land?
options: Mountain terrain is rugged and steep, so herding is often a practical choice.
Herding removes the need to protect animals from rugged terrain.
Regular crops grow easily on every mountain slope.
Herding makes it easier to build farming terraces.

why.Herding removes the need to protect anim: Herding is often preferred to agriculture in mountainous regions.
why.Regular crops grow easily on every mount: Regular farming is not possible on every mountain slope.
why.Herding makes it easier to build farming: Herding and terrace farming are different activities.

activities.explanation: Mountain terrain is usually rugged and has steep slopes.

activities.prompt: Explain why mining is a major activity on plateaus.
activities.answer: Plateaus are rich in mineral deposits, and mining is a major activity on plateaus. This explains why mining is closely linked with plateau land. Of the activities mentioned, it is mining that directly makes use of the mineral deposits; measuring height, comparing soils, and locating waterfalls concern other plateau facts.
points: Plateaus contain rich mineral deposits.
Mining is a major activity on plateaus.
Mining directly uses the mineral deposits.
Height, soil, and waterfalls are other plateau facts.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A family in the Ganga Plain grows crops, catches fish, and travels along the river. Its gentle slope makes movement by boat easy. The family also joins other community members at a sacred river place for a festival, ceremony, and ritual. The family has increased irrigation to its fields. Crop production has risen, but the underground water supply has fallen. The family is considering what this means for farming, river travel, and community life.
activities.prompt: If the family increases irrigation further, what change should they expect?
options: The underground water supply will become smaller.
The soil on the plains will lose its fertility.
The river will develop a steeper slope.
River navigation will become more difficult.

why.The soil on the plains will lose its fer: River sediments make plain soil fertile; irrigation does not make it less fertile.
Nothing in the case connects irrigation with a change in the river’s slope.
why.River navigation will become more diffic: Easy navigation results from the river’s gentle slope, not from irrigation.

activities.explanation: The lesson states that increased irrigation reduces groundwater.

activities.context: A family in the Ganga Plain grows crops, catches fish, and travels along the river. Its gentle slope makes movement by boat easy. The family also joins other community members at a sacred river place for a festival, ceremony, and ritual. The family has increased irrigation to its fields. Crop production has risen, but the underground water supply has fallen. The family is considering what this means for farming, river travel, and community life.
activities.prompt: Why does the family travel to the sacred river place?
options: To take part in community traditions.
To carry crops to the market more quickly.
To catch fish for their occupation.
To irrigate their fields.

why.To carry crops to the market more quickl: The visit described is for community traditions, not for transporting crops.
Fishing is an occupation in the Ganga Plain, but it is not the reason for this visit.
Irrigation takes place in fields, not at sacred gatherings.

activities.explanation: Sacred river locations are used for festivals, ceremonies, and rituals.

activities.context: A family in the Ganga Plain grows crops, catches fish, and travels along the river. Its gentle slope makes movement by boat easy. The family also joins other community members at a sacred river place for a festival, ceremony, and ritual. The family has increased irrigation to its fields. Crop production has risen, but the underground water supply has fallen. The family is considering what this means for farming, river travel, and community life.
activities.prompt: Why is travelling by boat easy along rivers on the plains?
options: The water flows down only a slight incline.
The river leaves fertile soil on the plains.
A large population lives in the Ganga Plain.
Sacred ceremonies are held at the river.

why.The river leaves fertile soil on the pla: Fertile soil supports farming but does not explain easy navigation.
why.A large population lives in the Ganga Pl: Population growth shows the importance of plains but does not explain boat travel.
Sacred ceremonies show community life but do not explain the ease of navigation.

activities.explanation: The rivers on plains have a gentle slope, which makes navigation easy.

activities.prompt: Explain how the physical features of plains make river-based life easier.
activities.answer: Plains have an extensive flat or gently undulating surface and are generally not more than 300 metres above sea level. This form allows rivers to have a gentle slope, making river navigation easy. Rivers also deposit sediments that make the soil fertile, supporting farming, river fishing, and the first civilisations.
points: Plains have a broad, flat or gently undulating surface.
They are generally not more than 300 metres above sea level.
A gentle river slope makes navigation easy.
River sediments make soil fertile and support river-based life.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A school student chooses a topic for a geography display about deserts. The display explains that deserts contain their own unique plants and animals, even though harsh living conditions make them difficult places to live. The student also learns that the Sahara and Thar are hot deserts, while the Gobi is cold. To explain how deserts fit into a wider picture of landforms and culture, the student plans to introduce the five tiṇais from ancient Tamil Sangam poetry.
activities.prompt: Why should the student include the five tiṇais in a display about deserts and the bigger picture of landforms?
options: They show that landforms can be classified in more than one way.
They show that every landform must be classified in exactly the same way.
They show that landforms have no connection with culture.
They show that only one way of dividing land exists.

why.They show that every landform must be cl: This wrongly claims that all classifications must be identical.
why.They show that landforms have no connect: This contradicts the connection between landforms and culture.
why.They show that only one way of dividing: This ignores the use of different landform classifications.

activities.explanation: The tiṇais use a classification different from the three main types.

activities.context: A school student chooses a topic for a geography display about deserts. The display explains that deserts contain their own unique plants and animals, even though harsh living conditions make them difficult places to live. The student also learns that the Sahara and Thar are hot deserts, while the Gobi is cold. To explain how deserts fit into a wider picture of landforms and culture, the student plans to introduce the five tiṇais from ancient Tamil Sangam poetry.
activities.prompt: Which statement best explains how the display should present deserts as part of the bigger picture of landforms?
options: Desert study offers chances to learn about unique life, while harsh living conditions also create difficulties.
Desert study offers only chances to learn about unique life, because deserts have no difficulties.
Life in every hot desert is easier than life in every cold desert.
Deserts have unique life, but all landforms offer difficulties without opportunities.

why.Desert study offers only chances to lear: It wrongly presents deserts as having no challenges.
why.Life in every hot desert is easier than: It makes an unsupported comparison between hot and cold deserts.
why.Deserts have unique life, but all landfo: It wrongly claims that landforms never offer opportunities.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between the deserts mentioned in the lesson.
activities.answer: The Sahara in Africa and the Thar in India are hot deserts. The Gobi Desert in Asia is a cold desert. The difference is therefore their hot or cold desert category and their location: Africa, India, and Asia respectively.
points: Sahara is a hot desert.
Thar is a hot desert.
Gobi is a cold desert.
Their locations are Africa, India, and Asia.
