chapters.title: Timeline and Sources of History
chapters.summary: In this chapter: how we learn about the past; how time is measured in history; timelines, centuries and millenniums; what are the sources of history?.

lessons.title: How We Learn About the Past

activities.prompt: What can we discover by looking back?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Learning Earth's Past
activities.body:
Imagine beginning a journey through the Earth's very, very long history. You find that humans occupy only a tiny and recent part of this story. The journey begins with people who study the history of the Earth.

First, you meet geologists. They study features of the Earth, such as soil, stones, hills, mountains and rivers. Some are trained to uncover secrets beneath the Earth's surface. You watch them examine these features to understand the past.

Next, you meet palaeontologists. They study fossils of plants, animals and humans from millions of years ago. Some fossils show impressions of footprints. Others preserve parts of plants and animals.

Then, you meet archaeologists. They study the past by digging up remains left by people, plants and animals. You see them dig up these remains.

Finally, you meet anthropologists. They study human societies and cultures from the oldest times to the present. Together, these people show you many ways to study the Earth's past.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Researchers of Earth's Past
activities.body: Earth has a very long history. Humans are only a tiny, recent part of it. Many people study this history. Geologists study soil, stones, hills, mountains and rivers. Palaeontologists study fossils. A fossil can be a footprint. It can also be a part of a plant or animal, kept for a long time. Anthropologists study how people live in groups, and their cultures. Archaeologists dig up remains from the past.
keyPoints: Earth's history is very long. Humans are only a tiny, recent part.
Researchers study Earth's features, fossils, cultures and remains.
A fossil can be a footprint or a saved part of a plant or animal.
activities.explanation: Different researchers help us learn about Earth's long history.

activities.prompt: A child finds a footprint in stone. What can it show?
steps: A footprint can be a fossil because fossils may preserve impressions.
A palaeontologist should study it because palaeontologists study fossils.
It matters because such fossils can give clues about ancient life.
Studying it helps us learn about Earth's long past.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Who studies fossils of plants, animals and people from millions of years ago?
options: Geologists
Anthropologists
Palaeontologists
Archaeologists
activities.explanation: Palaeontologists study fossils of plants, animals and people from millions of years ago.

activities.prompt: Archaeologists study the past by digging up things left by people, plants and animals.
activities.explanation: Archaeologists study the past by digging up things left by people, plants and animals.

activities.prompt: ______ study the Earth. They study soil, stones, hills, mountains and rivers.
activities.hint: Think about the scientist who studies soil and stones.
activities.explanation: Geologists study the Earth. They study soil, stones, hills, mountains and rivers.

activities.prompt: Match each researcher with the work they do.
pairs: Study soil, stones, hills, mountains and rivers
Study fossils from millions of years ago
Study groups of people and their ways of life
Dig up things left behind by people, plants and animals
activities.explanation: Each pair matches a researcher with their work.

activities.prompt: A person digs up old things from people, plants and animals. Who is this?
options: Geologists
Palaeontologists
Anthropologists
Archaeologists
activities.explanation: Archaeologists dig up old things from people, plants and animals. They study the past.

activities.prompt: Fossils show only parts of old plants and animals. They never show footprints.
activities.explanation: Fossils can show footprints. They can also show parts of old plants and animals.

activities.prompt: Which researcher studies human societies and cultures from the oldest times to the present?
options: Geologists
Anthropologists
Archaeologists
Palaeontologists
activities.explanation: Anthropologists study human societies and cultures from the oldest times to the present.

activities.prompt: Put these ideas in the right order.
items: The Earth has a very long history.
Humans are a tiny, new part of that history.
Many people study the history of the Earth.
Some are trained to find secrets under the Earth's surface.
Geologists study features of the Earth.
activities.explanation: This order goes from the Earth's long history to scientists who study it.

activities.prompt: Earth's history is very long. Humans occupy a tiny recent part. Where on a timeline?
options: Very near the beginning, when Earth was still very young.
Near the end, because humans arrived quite recently.
In the middle, because humans lived for millions of years.
Across the whole timeline, because humans lived with Earth.

why.Very near the beginning, when Earth was: Humans occupy only a tiny and recent part of Earth's history.
why.In the middle, because humans lived for: Humans did not live for millions of years.
why.Across the whole timeline, because human: Humans occupy only a small part, not Earth's whole history.

activities.explanation: Humans are recent compared with Earth's very long history.

lessons.title: How Time Is Measured in History

activities.prompt: How do people count years before and after today?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour Through Time
activities.body:
Imagine you are a time traveller visiting different societies. Each society and culture has developed its own way of measuring time. So your journey begins with many calendars.

Important events, like a ruler's reign beginning, can mark a new era. One calendar uses the conventional year of Jesus Christ's birth as its starting point. You count years forward from that chosen point.

The Gregorian calendar has twelve months, adding up to 365 days. Among 1800, 1900 and 2000, only 2000 was a leap year. Careful checking helps you understand such differences.

You also meet Hindu, Muslim, Jewish and Chinese calendars, plus others. These calendars are also used across different societies and cultures. Each system measures time in its own cultural way.

After the starting point, the period is called the Common Era, or CE. Before it, the period is called Before Common Era, or BCE. The Gregorian calendar has no year zero. For a BCE date and a CE date, add them and subtract one. For example, 2 BCE to 2 CE spans three years.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Ways of Measuring Time
activities.body: Different societies and cultures have measured time in their own ways. Important events, such as a ruler’s reign beginning, have marked new eras. The Gregorian calendar has twelve months and 365 days. Jesus Christ’s conventional birth year became the starting point. Time before it is BCE, and time after it is CE. Between BCE and CE dates, add the dates and subtract one. The Gregorian calendar has no year zero.
keyPoints: Different cultures have their own ways of measuring time.
Important events can mark new eras.
BCE and CE count years around Jesus Christ’s birth year.
activities.explanation: These ideas explain how calendars divide time and count years.

activities.title: Walk from BCE into CE

tasks.then: In BCE, years count down towards the starting point.
From 2 BCE to 2 CE is three years, because there is no year zero.

activities.takeaway: BCE years count down and CE years count up.
activities.explanation: BCE years count down and CE years count up.

activities.prompt: How have people in different places measured time?
options: Each group used its own ways
All groups used only the Gregorian calendar
Every group used the same way
Their ways never changed
activities.explanation: Each group of people has had its own ways to measure time.

activities.prompt: The Gregorian calendar has twelve months that add up to 365 days.
activities.explanation: Its twelve months add up to 365 days.

activities.prompt: Years after the starting point are counted ______.
activities.hint: Think about which way we count years.
activities.explanation: Years after the starting point are counted forward.

activities.prompt: Which of these years is a leap year?
activities.explanation: Only 2000 was a leap year among 1800, 1900 and 2000.

activities.prompt: Match each calendar word with its meaning.
pairs: the time after the starting point
the time before the starting point
twelve months that add up to 365 days
the starting point of the calendar
activities.explanation: Each word shows a time period or the calendar’s starting point.

activities.prompt: Put these parts of calendar time in order.
items: the time before the starting point
the time after the starting point
activities.explanation: The starting point comes after BCE and before CE.

activities.prompt: How do you find the years between a BCE date and a CE date?
options: Add the dates, then take away one
Take one date away from the other
Add the dates only
Count backwards from the CE date
activities.explanation: For example, from 2 BCE to 2 CE is three years.

activities.prompt: The time before the starting point is called CE.
activities.explanation: It is called BCE. CE is the time after the starting point.

activities.prompt: A museum places 3 BCE and 3 CE on one timeline. Which order is correct?
options: 3 BCE comes before 3 CE.
3 CE comes before 3 BCE.
Both dates belong after the starting point.
Both dates belong before the starting point.

This reverses the order of the Before and After periods.
why.Both dates belong after the starting poi: This wrongly places the BCE date after the starting point.
why.Both dates belong before the starting po: This wrongly places the CE date before the starting point.

activities.explanation: This is right because BCE comes before CE on the timeline.

lessons.title: Timelines, Centuries and Millenniums

activities.prompt: How can one line guide you through centuries and millennia?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Walk Through Time
activities.body:
Imagine you enter a room where history stretches along one long line. A timeline is a useful tool for marking historical events. It shows a sequence of dates and events within a period.

As you walk, notice how the line keeps events in order. This helps you understand the order in which historical events happened. Sometimes, a dotted part shows that a period has been skipped.

Now look at two markers on the line. The timeline shows that the Buddha was born before Jesus. A decade is a period of ten years. A century is any period of 100 years.

Next, you reach a new part of your journey. The 21st century CE runs from 2001 to 2100. A millennium is any period of 1,000 years. The 3rd millennium CE began in 2001 and will end in 3000.

Step back, and you see the whole tour. Timelines do more than place events. They help you understand the order in which historical events happened.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Understanding time periods
activities.body: Timelines place historical events in date order. A dotted part shows a period that has been skipped. A decade lasts ten years. A century lasts 100 years. A millennium lasts 1,000 years. The 21st century CE runs from 2001 to 2100. The 3rd millennium CE began in 2001 and will end in 3000.
keyPoints: Timelines show the order of historical events.
A decade has ten years, a century has 100 years, and a millennium has 1,000 years.
The 21st century CE runs from 2001 to 2100.
activities.explanation: Timelines help you see when events happened and how long periods lasted.

activities.prompt: A class wants to show that the Buddha was born before Jesus. How should it show this?
steps: A timeline is useful because it shows dates and events in sequence.
Both births can be marked because a timeline marks historical events.
Place the Buddha's birth first, because it happened before Jesus's birth.
The ordered timeline will clearly show that the Buddha was born before Jesus.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: A useful history tool
activities.prompt: What is a timeline good for?
options: Marking past events
Drawing old maps
Writing speeches about history
Making models of history
activities.explanation: A timeline marks past events. It helps us put each event in order.

activities.title: Match each time period
activities.prompt: Match each time to its number of years.
activities.explanation: Good job! A decade is shorter than a century. A century is shorter than a millennium.

activities.title: How long is a century?
activities.prompt: A century is a period of ______ years.
activities.hint: Think of one hundred.
activities.explanation: Yes! A century covers 100 years.

activities.title: The dotted part
activities.prompt: What does a dotted part on a timeline show?
options: A time that was skipped
An event that happens twice
The end of the timeline
The first event on the timeline
activities.explanation: The dotted part shows skipped time. It helps you see that some time is left out.

activities.title: Shortest to longest
activities.prompt: Put these time periods from shortest to longest.
activities.explanation: Well done! A decade has ten years. A century has 100 years. A millennium has 1,000 years.

activities.title: The third millennium
activities.prompt: Which sentence about the 3rd millennium CE is true?
options: It began in 2001 and will end in 3000.
It began in 2001 and will end in 2100.
It began in 2100 and will end in 3000.
It began in 1000 and will end in 2000.
activities.explanation: The 3rd millennium CE began in 2001. It will end in 3000. Remember: a millennium covers 1,000 years.

activities.prompt: A class must show dated events in order. Which tool fits best?
options: a timeline with dates and events
a dotted line with no events
a single date with no events
a list of events with no dates

why.a dotted line with no events: This mistake thinks a dotted line alone can show events.
why.a single date with no events: This mistake thinks one date can show an event sequence.
why.a list of events with no dates: This mistake leaves out the dates needed for order.

activities.explanation: This tool shows dates and events in their sequence.

activities.prompt: From 2001 to 2100 is 100 years. Which rule fits this period?
options: a century
a decade
a millennium
a dotted section

why.a decade: This mistake applies the ten-year rule to 100 years.
why.a millennium: This mistake applies the 1,000-year rule to 100 years.
why.a dotted section: This mistake treats a display mark as a period length.

activities.explanation: A century is a period of 100 years.

activities.prompt: Centuries have 100 years; decades have ten years. Which is longer?
options: a century, because 100 is more than ten
a decade, because ten is more than 100
a century, because ten is more than 100
a decade, because 100 is less than ten

why.a decade, because ten is more than 100: This mistake reverses the sizes of the two periods.
why.a century, because ten is more than 100: This mistake combines the century name with the wrong sizes.
why.a decade, because 100 is less than ten: This mistake reverses which number is larger.

activities.explanation: 100 years is longer than ten years.

activities.prompt: A timeline shows Jesus's birth before the Buddha's. What must you fix?
options: the order of the two births
the dotted section between the births
the dates shown beside the births
the century and millennium names

why.the dotted section between the births: This mistake thinks the dotted section causes the wrong order.
why.the dates shown beside the births: This mistake thinks the dates beside events, not order, need fixing.
why.the century and millennium names: This mistake thinks century and millennium names set birth order.

activities.explanation: The Buddha was born before Jesus, so the order must change.

lessons.title: What Are the Sources of History?

activities.prompt: What secrets might the past reveal when we look for clues together?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Following History's Clues
activities.body:
Imagine you are beginning a journey into the past. Your guide is a source: a place, person, text or object. Each can give you information about what happened.

You visit a place and inspect its objects and structures. Every object or structure can tell a story about the past. At home, family histories can be learnt from photographs and diaries. Identity cards and family memories can add more clues.

You then follow clues through literature, a key group of historical sources. Archaeological and oral sources can also provide information about history. Historians work with archaeologists, epigraphists, anthropologists and other experts. Together, these sources help put historical events together.

You collect as many sources as you can find. Sometimes, different sources confirm the same information. Other times, they disagree, so you decide which source you trust more. You may still have missing pieces in your historical puzzle.

You can also study ancient climates and excavated materials. These studies give fresh insights into the past. Finally, you build a careful account from the strongest clues available.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Clues About the Past
activities.body: History has many sources. A source is a place, person, text or object. It tells us about the past. Every object or structure can tell a story about the past. We can learn family history from photos, diaries, ID cards and memories. Historians collect many sources. They check where the sources agree. Some pieces of history may still be missing.
keyPoints: Sources can be places, people, texts or objects.
Objects and structures can tell stories about the past.
Historians collect and check many sources.
activities.explanation: Historians use different clues to learn about the past.

activities.prompt: Two family sources tell different stories about a celebration. Which one should I trust?
steps: I start with photographs and diaries because both give family history.
I compare them because different sources can confirm the same information.
Disagreements matter, so I compare sources and choose the more trusted one.
I use many sources and accept that some pieces may remain missing.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Every object or building can tell us about the past.
activities.explanation: Objects and buildings can tell us how people lived.

activities.title: A Family Clue
activities.prompt: You can learn family history from photos, diaries, ______ and memories.
activities.hint: Think of a card that shows who a person is.
activities.explanation: Identity cards can help historians learn about families.

activities.title: Checking Sources
activities.prompt: What can happen when different sources give the same information?
options: The information can be confirmed
All sources become useless
The sources must disappear
The puzzle always stays complete
activities.explanation: Different sources may confirm the same information.

activities.prompt: When two sources disagree, historians choose the one they trust more.
activities.explanation: When sources disagree, historians pick the one they trust.

activities.title: New Ideas About the Past
activities.prompt: Why do studies of old weather and dug-up things help?
options: They take the place of all old records
They show that nothing is missing
They help us understand the past better
They stop historians from looking for more clues
activities.explanation: These studies help historians understand the past better.

activities.title: How Historians Work
activities.prompt: Put these steps in order.
items: When sources disagree, decide which one you trust more.
Put the events together, using many kinds of sources.
activities.explanation: Historians gather, check and judge sources. Then they put events together.

activities.prompt: A child wants to know about a family celebration. A photograph and a diary both tell about it. What should the child do?
options: Use both sources and compare what they say about the celebration.
Use only the photograph because pictures give every detail.
Use only the diary because written words cannot be wrong.
Use neither source because one old event is not important.

why.Use only the photograph because pictures: This overtrusts pictures and ignores other useful family evidence.
why.Use only the diary because written words: This treats written words as always correct, even when sources disagree.
why.Use neither source because one old event: This discards useful evidence that could help learn about the past.

activities.explanation: This uses both sources and compares their information.

activities.prompt: Two old sources give different details about one historical event. What should the historian do?
options: Check both sources and decide which one is more trusted.
Choose the first source because it was found first.
Choose the last source because it was read last.
Combine all details even when they do not fit.

why.Choose the first source because it was f: Finding a source first does not show that it is more reliable.
why.Choose the last source because it was re: Reading a source last does not show that it is more reliable.
why.Combine all details even when they do no: This ignores source reliability and may create a wrong account.

activities.explanation: Historians compare sources and choose the one they trust more.

activities.prompt: A historian visits a dug-up place and listens to an older person's memory. What can these visits provide?
options: They can provide archaeological and oral information about history.
They can provide information from only one written source.
They can provide every detail with no missing pieces.
They can provide information about only recent events.

why.They can provide information from only o: This wrongly treats both visits as one written source.
why.They can provide every detail with no mi: This assumes history is complete, although some pieces may remain missing.
why.They can provide information about only: This wrongly limits these sources to recent events, while they give past information.

activities.explanation: Dug-up places and spoken memories can provide archaeological and oral information.

activities.prompt: A historian has an old object and a written record. The historian needs more help. What should the historian do?
options: Ask archaeologists and other experts to study the evidence.
Stop looking because the object already gives every answer.
Keep all findings to avoid confusing other experts.
Choose one source so the story becomes simpler.

why.Stop looking because the object already: This assumes one object can explain every part of the past.
why.Keep all findings to avoid confusing oth: This avoids expert help that could provide useful knowledge.
why.Choose one source so the story becomes s: This ignores the value of gathering and comparing many sources.

activities.explanation: Historians work with archaeologists and other experts to understand sources.

activities.prompt: Several sources agree about most of an old event. One detail has no source. What should the historian conclude?
options: Some pieces of the historical puzzle may remain missing.
The missing piece can always be found with certainty.
The missing piece does not matter to understanding history.
All pieces must agree before history can be learned.

why.The missing piece can always be found wi: This assumes missing evidence can always be found, but it may not.
why.The missing piece does not matter to und: This ignores that missing evidence can limit our understanding.
why.All pieces must agree before history can: This treats agreement as a requirement, but sources can disagree.

activities.explanation: Some parts of history can stay missing even when several sources agree.

lessons.title: The Beginnings of Human History

activities.prompt: How did our earliest ancestors find food, shelter, and one another?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Journey into Early Life
activities.body:
Imagine beginning your journey through human history. You will discover that modern humans have walked the Earth for about 300,000 years. Yet this journey is only a tiny part of the Earth's history.

Your early ancestors lived in bands and groups, so they could help one another. You follow them as they searched for shelter and food. They were mainly hunters and gatherers.

Sometimes, you stop at temporary camps, rock shelters or caves. You rely on hunting and gathering edible plants and fruits to survive. You use fire and make tools for easier lives.

You watch them make stone axes, blades, arrowheads and other tools. They communicate through languages that are now lost. You also learn about their beliefs about nature and possible ideas about life after death.

You can read life in rock paintings found in hundreds of caves. You make ornaments, such as beads and pendants, and sometimes exchange them. These discoveries connect your small group to a much longer human story.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: How Early Humans Lived
activities.body: Modern humans have walked the Earth for about 300,000 years. Human history is only a tiny part of Earth's history. Early humans lived in bands to help each other. They searched for shelter and food, mainly through hunting and gathering. They used fire, made stone tools, and wore ornaments. They had beliefs about nature and perhaps life after death. Their languages are now lost, but their lives appear in rock paintings.
keyPoints: Human history is a tiny part of Earth's history.
Early humans lived in groups and helped each other.
Their lives can be seen in rock paintings.
activities.explanation: These clues show how early humans survived and left traces.

activities.prompt: A small group needs food, shelter, and useful tools. What should they do together?
steps: Stay together as a band because members can help each other.
Hunt and gather because the group needs food to survive.
Use a temporary camp, rock shelter, or cave because it gives shelter.
Make tools and use fire because these make survival easier.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Early humans lived in bands (small groups). They did this to help each other.
activities.explanation: Living in groups helped early humans. They could help each other.

activities.title: Finding Food
activities.prompt: Early humans gathered ______ plants and fruits to stay alive.
activities.hint: This word tells us that the plants and fruits were safe to eat.
activities.explanation: They gathered plants and fruits that were safe to eat.

activities.title: Early Life Connections
activities.prompt: Match each part of early life with its related fact.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a place, activity, tool, or decoration from early life.

activities.title: Traces of Early Life
activities.prompt: Which answer gives two traces of early human life?
options: Lost languages and modern cities
Rock paintings and ornaments
Farm tools and books
Camps and roads
activities.explanation: Rock paintings show their lives. Ornaments included beads and pendants.

activities.prompt: Languages used by early humans are still spoken today.
activities.explanation: The languages early humans used are now lost.

activities.title: Evidence in Caves
activities.prompt: We can see early human life in ______ paintings. Hundreds of caves have them.
activities.hint: These paintings were made on cave walls.
activities.explanation: Rock paintings in hundreds of caves show early human life.

activities.prompt: One person gathers fruits while another hunts. Why was life safer for early humans in a band?
options: They could help each other find food and survive.
They had to find food without helping one another.
They could share food without hunting or gathering.
They needed one person to do every kind of work.

why.They had to find food without helping on: This wrongly assumes that early people worked alone.
why.They could share food without hunting or: This wrongly treats sharing as a reason not to find food.
why.They needed one person to do every kind: This wrongly assumes cooperation meant one person did all work.

activities.explanation: This is right because bands helped members support one another.

activities.prompt: Cave paintings show people, animals, and nature. What can they help us understand?
options: The exact words used by every early human group.
The exact number of caves where early humans lived.
Paintings can identify the first human group on Earth.
Early human life, including beliefs about nature.

why.The exact words used by every early huma: This wrongly claims the paintings give exact lost words.
why.The exact number of caves where early hu: This wrongly treats hundreds as an exact cave number.
why.Paintings can identify the first human g: This wrongly treats paintings as proof of the first humans.

activities.explanation: This is right because paintings show life and beliefs about nature.

lessons.title: First Crops and Growing Communities

activities.prompt: What made people settle down and grow together?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: First Crops and Growing Communities
activities.body:
Before your tour, you learn about a very cold period. An Ice Age was a time when much of the Earth was covered with ice. The last Ice Age lasted from over 100,000 years ago to around 12,000 years ago.

You watch people settle down. They grow cereals and grains. They domesticate animals such as cattle and goats. You see living conditions improving for people in many parts of the world.

You walk towards a river, where many communities often settle. The land is worked collectively. There is no sense of individual ownership.

As more food becomes available, you see communities grow in size and number. You watch people exchange goods in villages. You see food, clothing and tools passing between them.

Finally, you see a chieftain caring for the community's well-being. New technologies include pottery and the use of metals such as copper and iron.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: How communities grew
activities.body: Life got better for humans in many parts of the world. People settled down. They grew cereals and grains. They domesticated cattle and goats, which means they tamed them. More food helped communities grow in size and number. Communities often settled near rivers. Chieftains were in charge of community well-being, meaning health and happiness. The land was worked collectively. This means people worked together. Villages traded food, clothes and tools. New inventions included pottery and metals like copper and iron.
keyPoints: People settled down and grew cereals and grains.
More food helped communities grow.
People worked together and traded goods.
activities.explanation: These ideas show how farming and working together helped communities grow.

activities.prompt: A family used to move often. What helped them settle and join a larger community?
steps: Growing cereals and grains gave them more food.
Domesticating cattle and goats helped them raise animals in one place.
More food allowed their community to grow in size and number.
So growing food and raising animals helped them settle together.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: First Farming
activities.prompt: What did people start to grow when they lived in one place?
options: Cereals and grains
Pottery and copper
Food, clothing and tools
Cattle and goats
activities.explanation: People began to live in one place and grow cereals and grains.

activities.title: Living in One Place
activities.prompt: People grew cereals and grains after they began to live in one place.
activities.explanation: Living in one place and growing cereals and grains happened together.

activities.title: A useful place to settle
activities.prompt: Communities often settled near ______.
activities.hint: Look at where communities settled.
activities.explanation: The lesson says communities often settled near rivers.

activities.title: Why did communities grow?
activities.prompt: Why did communities get bigger and increase in number?
options: They had more food
They made pottery
They lived near rivers
They traded tools
activities.explanation: More food helped communities grow bigger and increase in number.

activities.title: Village life
activities.prompt: Match each thing with its part in village life.
pairs: People who look after the village
activities.explanation: Each pair shows an animal, a person, technology or trade in village life.

activities.title: The community leader
activities.prompt: Who took care of the whole community?
options: The chieftain
Animals like cows and goats
Villages that traded things
New inventions like pottery
activities.explanation: A chieftain took care of the whole community.

activities.prompt: People grow cereals and grains. More food is available. What is likely to happen next?
options: The community can grow in size and number.
The community must have less food each year.
The community will stop sharing its work.
The community will use fewer farm animals.

why.The community must have less food each y: This reverses the link between more food and community growth.
why.The community will stop sharing its work: This wrongly assumes that more food ends collective work.
why.The community will use fewer farm animal: This wrongly assumes that more food means fewer domesticated animals.

activities.explanation: This is right because more food allowed communities to grow.

activities.prompt: Village A is beside a river. Village B is far from one. Which comparison fits the fact?
options: Village A fits a common pattern, but not every village.
Village B fits a common pattern because it is far from rivers.
Both villages fit because every village sat near a river.
Neither fits because the fact says nothing about villages.

why.Village B fits a common pattern because: This mistakes a place far from rivers for the common pattern.
why.Both villages fit because every village: This changes often into every, which the fact does not say.
why.Neither fits because the fact says nothi: This ignores the fact that communities often settled near rivers.

activities.explanation: This is right because communities often settled near rivers.

activities.prompt: Village A gives food. Village B gives clothing and tools. What does this show about them?
options: They exchanged goods with each other.
They kept every good inside each village.
They shared one piece of land together.
They made no pottery or metal tools.

why.They kept every good inside each village: This mistakes exchange for communities keeping all goods.
This confuses exchanging goods with collective land ownership.
This mistakes received tools for a lack of pottery or metals.

activities.explanation: This is right because villages exchanged goods with each other.

activities.prompt: Two families work land that the whole community works. What fits collective ownership?
options: They work it together, because no one owned the land alone.
One family owns it, because growing food needs private land.
Both families own it, because they both help work it.
The chieftain owns it, because the chieftain guides the community.

why.One family owns it, because growing food: This wrongly treats collective farming as private ownership.
why.Both families own it, because they both: This wrongly thinks that working together creates individual ownership.
why.The chieftain owns it, because the chief: This wrongly thinks that responsibility means the chieftain owns the land.

activities.explanation: This is right because the land was worked collectively.

activities.prompt: A village display shows pottery, copper tools and iron tools. What can we learn from it?
options: It shows new technologies used by the community.
It shows domesticated animals kept by the community.
It shows exchanged goods that were never made.
It shows community rules about shared land work.

why.It shows domesticated animals kept by th: This mistakes tools and pottery for domesticated animals.
why.It shows exchanged goods that were never: This confuses exchanged goods with technologies that people made.
why.It shows community rules about shared la: This mistakes objects for rules about collective ownership.

activities.explanation: This is right because pottery and metals were new technologies.

activities.context: At a riverbank near hills, a student notices an impression in a stone. The student wonders whether it is a fossil and asks a geologist about it. The geologist studies soil, stones, hills, mountains and rivers. The geologist explains that palaeontologists study fossils of plants, animals and humans from millions of years ago. An archaeologist is digging up remains left by people, plants and animals. The student sees that learning about Earth's long past can require several kinds of experts.
activities.prompt: What should the student do next to find out whether the impression is a fossil?
options: Ask a palaeontologist to examine the possible fossil.
Ask an anthropologist to study the impression as evidence of a human society.
Ask an archaeologist to dig up every remain near the stone.
Ask the geologist only to identify what kind of stone it is.
activities.explanation: Palaeontologists study fossils.

activities.context: At a riverbank near hills, a student notices an impression in a stone. The student wonders whether it is a fossil and asks a geologist about it. The geologist studies soil, stones, hills, mountains and rivers. The geologist explains that palaeontologists study fossils of plants, animals and humans from millions of years ago. An archaeologist is digging up remains left by people, plants and animals. The student sees that learning about Earth's long past can require several kinds of experts.
activities.prompt: Which explanation best shows why the student may need several kinds of experts?
options: Each specialist has a different focus: Earth features, fossils, or remains of past life.
They all examine the same kinds of evidence, so one expert is always enough.
Only archaeologists can investigate evidence beneath the Earth's surface.
Anthropologists examine fossils, while geologists study how people lived together.

why.They all examine the same kinds of evide: Their areas of study are not identical.
why.Only archaeologists can investigate evid: Archaeologists are not the only relevant specialists.

activities.explanation: The specialists study different evidence.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between BCE and CE.
activities.answer: BCE means Before Common Era and marks years before the calendar’s chosen starting point. CE means Common Era and marks years after that point. The conventional year of Jesus Christ’s birth was chosen as the starting point, and the Gregorian calendar has no year zero.
points: BCE stands for Before Common Era.
BCE years come before the chosen starting point.
CE stands for Common Era.
CE years are counted forward from the starting point.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: While preparing a class timeline, a student notices that one stretch is drawn with dots. She wonders whether those missing years mean the timeline is wrong. Her timeline also places the birth of the Buddha before the birth of Jesus, helping her compare their order. She wants to explain clearly how her timeline works so classmates can read it correctly.
activities.prompt: A classmate says the dotted stretch means the timeline has an error. What should the student explain?
options: The dotted part marks a period that the timeline skips.
It shows that no events occurred during that period.
It shows that the events in that period happened at the same time.
It shows that the period is being included in full.

why.It shows that no events occurred during: Skipping a period does not mean that no events occurred.
why.It shows that the events in that period: A dotted part does not mean that events happened together.
why.It shows that the period is being includ: A dotted part marks a gap rather than a complete period.

activities.explanation: The dotted part indicates a skipped period.

activities.context: While preparing a class timeline, a student notices that one stretch is drawn with dots. She wonders whether those missing years mean the timeline is wrong. Her timeline also places the birth of the Buddha before the birth of Jesus, helping her compare their order. She wants to explain clearly how her timeline works so classmates can read it correctly.
activities.prompt: The student wants to label the exact period 2001–2100 on the timeline. Which label belongs beside it?
options: 21st century CE
3rd millennium CE
A decade
A millennium

why.3rd millennium CE: The 3rd millennium CE runs from 2001 to 3000.

activities.explanation: The 21st century CE runs from 2001 to 2100.

activities.prompt: Explain how a timeline helps us understand historical events.
activities.answer: A timeline places dates and events in the order in which they happened. This lets a student compare when events occurred. For example, it can show that the Buddha was born before Jesus. A dotted part also makes a skipped period clear.
points: Timeline arranges dates and events in sequence
Order of events can be compared
Buddha was born before Jesus
Dotted part marks a skipped period
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student is studying how a community’s past can be reconstructed. The student finds family photographs, a diary and an identity card, and asks a relative to share memories. Nearby, excavated materials and oral accounts give further clues about ancient life. One written source and one oral account do not agree, while another written source supports the oral account. The student gathers all these sources and consults experts before deciding which information is most trustworthy.
activities.prompt: What should the student do when the written source and the oral account disagree?
options: Trust the written source automatically because it is written.
Trust the oral account automatically because it comes from a person.
Compare the sources and decide which one can be trusted more.
Keep only one source so that the account is simpler.

why.Trust the written source automatically b: A written source is not automatically more trustworthy.
why.Trust the oral account automatically bec: Being a person does not make an oral account automatically reliable.
why.Keep only one source so that the account: Disagreement is a reason to compare sources, not remove them.

activities.explanation: Comparing sources helps the student judge which one is more trustworthy.

activities.context: A student is studying how a community’s past can be reconstructed. The student finds family photographs, a diary and an identity card, and asks a relative to share memories. Nearby, excavated materials and oral accounts give further clues about ancient life. One written source and one oral account do not agree, while another written source supports the oral account. The student gathers all these sources and consults experts before deciding which information is most trustworthy.
activities.prompt: If another source about the community is discovered, what should the student do next?
options: Discard the earlier sources because the new one is better.
Use only the new source because it provides the newest information.
Add it to the other sources and continue comparing all of them.
Stop searching because one complete account has already been found.

why.Discard the earlier sources because the: New information does not make earlier sources useless.
why.Use only the new source because it provi: Gathering many sources helps historians understand the past better.
why.Stop searching because one complete acco: Some parts may remain missing, so more sources are valuable.

activities.explanation: Comparing sources can confirm information or reveal disagreement.

activities.prompt: Explain why historians need to use more than one kind of source.
activities.answer: Historians use many kinds of sources because each gives information about the past. Photographs, diaries, identity cards, memories, literature, oral accounts and excavated materials can be combined. Comparing them can confirm the same information, reveal disagreement and help show which source is more trustworthy, although some parts may remain missing.
points: Uses several kinds of sources
Explains that sources can be combined
Mentions confirmation and disagreement
Notes that some parts may remain missing
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Consider an early human group travelling together in search of food and shelter. The group stays in a temporary camp beside a rock shelter. They hunt animals and gather edible plants and fruits, use fire, and shape stone axes, blades and arrowheads. The group uses a language that is now lost, makes beads and pendants, and sometimes exchanges them with another group. Rock paintings in a cave show parts of their life.
activities.prompt: If a stone blade breaks while the group is preparing food, what should they do next?
options: Make another stone blade.
Use a pendant in place of the blade.
Stop making tools and rely only on hunting and gathering.
Exchange a bead for a new blade instead of making one themselves.

Beads and pendants were ornaments, not cutting tools.
why.Stop making tools and rely only on hunti: Tools made their lives easier, so they should not abandon them.
why.Exchange a bead for a new blade instead: They sometimes exchanged ornaments, but they could also make their own tools.

activities.explanation: Stone blades were among the tools early humans made.

activities.context: Consider an early human group travelling together in search of food and shelter. The group stays in a temporary camp beside a rock shelter. They hunt animals and gather edible plants and fruits, use fire, and shape stone axes, blades and arrowheads. The group uses a language that is now lost, makes beads and pendants, and sometimes exchanges them with another group. Rock paintings in a cave show parts of their life.
activities.prompt: Why is it difficult for us to know exactly how this group communicated?
options: Their spoken language has disappeared, so its words and rules cannot be learned today.
They wrote their language on cave walls, so complete messages survive.
They used beads and pendants to record every word they spoke.
They all spoke a language that people still use today.

why.They wrote their language on cave walls,: Cave paintings show parts of life, not complete written messages about their language.
why.They used beads and pendants to record e: Ornaments were made and exchanged, but they did not record speech.
why.They all spoke a language that people st: The language they used is now lost rather than still being known today.

activities.explanation: The group used a language that is now lost.

activities.context: Consider an early human group travelling together in search of food and shelter. The group stays in a temporary camp beside a rock shelter. They hunt animals and gather edible plants and fruits, use fire, and shape stone axes, blades and arrowheads. The group uses a language that is now lost, makes beads and pendants, and sometimes exchanges them with another group. Rock paintings in a cave show parts of their life.
activities.prompt: The group meets another band that can help them find food. What should they do?
options: Talk with the other band and keep working together.
Stay silent because their language is now lost.
Exchange a bead for all the food and shelter they need.
Separate from their own group and travel alone.

why.Stay silent because their language is no: A language being lost to us today does not mean the people could not speak it.
why.Exchange a bead for all the food and she: Ornaments were sometimes exchanged, but they did not replace food or shelter.
why.Separate from their own group and travel: Early humans lived in groups so that they could help each other.

activities.explanation: Living in groups helped early humans help one another, and language enabled communication.

activities.prompt: Explain how human history compares with the Earth's history.
activities.answer: Human history is only a tiny part of the Earth's history. Modern humans have walked the Earth for about 300,000 years, which is very short compared with the Earth's much longer history. Therefore, human history covers only a small part of the Earth's story.
points: Human history is a tiny part of Earth's history.
Modern humans have walked the Earth for about 300,000 years.
Human history is much shorter than the Earth's history.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Following the last Ice Age, villagers settled beside a river and grew cereals and grains while raising cattle and goats. When more food became available, more families joined the settlement. The chieftain was responsible for everyone’s well-being, although no family owned the land separately; it was worked collectively. Villagers exchanged food, clothing, and tools, and villagers began producing pottery and items made from copper and iron.
activities.prompt: The settlement produces more food than before. What is the most likely result according to the case?
options: The community may become larger as more families can be fed.
The community may become smaller because people will leave the river.
The community may stay the same because settled villages cannot grow.
The community may become larger only if collective land use ends.

why.The community may become smaller because: This reverses the connection between more food and community growth.
why.The community may stay the same because: It contradicts the case’s explanation of why communities expanded.
why.The community may become larger only if: Collective land use does not prevent growth; the two can continue together.

activities.explanation: More food supports more people, allowing the community to grow.

activities.context: Following the last Ice Age, villagers settled beside a river and grew cereals and grains while raising cattle and goats. When more food became available, more families joined the settlement. The chieftain was responsible for everyone’s well-being, although no family owned the land separately; it was worked collectively. Villagers exchanged food, clothing, and tools, and villagers began producing pottery and items made from copper and iron.
activities.prompt: If villagers adopt pottery and metalworking while continuing to trade, what most likely follows?
options: The settlement gains new ways of making goods while keeping its exchange links.
The settlement must end collective farming before using the new technologies.
The settlement must stop keeping cattle and goats before making metal goods.
The settlement can ignore the chieftain’s responsibility because production becomes more varied.

why.The settlement must end collective farmi: The case gives no reason to end collective farming before adopting them.
why.The settlement must stop keeping cattle: Raising cattle and goats could continue alongside pottery and metalworking.
why.The settlement can ignore the chieftain’: The chieftain remained responsible for the community despite new technologies.

activities.explanation: Pottery and metalworking are new technologies that can be combined with existing trade.

activities.prompt: Explain why having more food could lead to a larger and more numerous community.
activities.answer: More food allowed the settlement to support additional people. As families joined, the community could grow in both size and number. This helped settled life develop around farming and herding. The case clearly connects a larger food supply with the growth of the village.
points: More food can support more people.
Joining families increase the community’s population.
Greater food supply helps the village expand.
Farming and herding supported settled life.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: Which sentence about human history is true?
options: Human history is a tiny part of Earth's long history.
Humans take up most of Earth's history.
Humans have lived on Earth since Earth began.
Earth has a short history.
activities.explanation: Earth's history is very long. Humans take up only a tiny, recent part.

activities.prompt: Match each expert with what they study.
pairs: soil, stones, hills, mountains and rivers
fossils from millions of years ago
human groups and their ways of life
old things left by people, plants and animals
activities.explanation: Each expert studies a different part of Earth's past.

activities.prompt: A dotted part of a timeline shows a period that was skipped.
activities.explanation: The dotted part marks a period left out of the timeline.

activities.prompt: A millennium is a period of ______ years.
activities.hint: This is a very long period.
activities.explanation: A millennium has one thousand years.

activities.prompt: Put these dates in the right order.
activities.explanation: BCE dates come before the birth of Jesus. CE dates come after it.

activities.prompt: The time from 2 BCE to 2 CE is four years.
activities.explanation: Add the two dates. Then take away one. The time is three years.

activities.prompt: When sources disagree, historians choose the source they can trust ______.
activities.hint: Pick the source with bigger trust.
activities.explanation: Different sources can disagree. Historians decide which source they trust more.

activities.prompt: Match each clue with its description.
pairs: Temporary camps, rock shelters or caves
Rock paintings in hundreds of caves
activities.explanation: These clues show where people lived, what they made and what they kept.

chapters.title: India, That Is Bharat
chapters.summary: In this chapter: india in the past and the first indian names; regional names in the mahābhārata; two names for the whole indian subcontinent; aśhoka, bhārata and india's ancient geography.

lessons.title: India in the Past and the First Indian Names

activities.prompt: What stories might help us understand India’s past?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Names Across Time
activities.body:
Begin your journey with modern India. It has defined borders and states. Its population is also known.

Now imagine looking back 500, 2,000 or even 5,000 years. You would find a very different India. Across this journey, you will meet many names for the Indian Subcontinent. Its boundaries have also changed.

Next, you visit the evidence used to trace these names. Old texts, travellers’ accounts and pilgrims’ accounts all offer clues. Inscriptions offer more clues too.

Your tour then reaches the Ṛig Veda, India’s oldest text. It is several thousand years old. Here, you discover that the Ṛig Veda calls the north-western region Sapta Sindhava. This means the land of the seven rivers. The name Sindhava comes from Sindhu. This word can mean the Indus River or a river in general.

Finally, you return to the modern map. You find defined borders, defined states and a known population. Remember how the Subcontinent’s names and boundaries have changed.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Looking at India's Past
activities.body: Today, India has clear borders, clear states and a known population. Long ago, it looked very different. The subcontinent means the land of India. It had many names. Its borders changed. We learn about India's past from old texts. We also use travellers' accounts, pilgrims' accounts and inscriptions. Inscriptions are written marks from the past. The Ṛig Veda is India's oldest text. It is several thousand years old.
keyPoints: Long ago, India looked very different.
Old sources help us learn about India's past.
The Ṛig Veda is India's oldest text.
activities.explanation: This lesson shows the sources we use to study India's past.

activities.prompt: A child sees Sapta Sindhava and wonders why it names rivers.
steps: The Ṛig Veda is India's oldest text, so it helps us learn.
It calls the north-west Sapta Sindhava, so we learn an old name.
It means the land of seven rivers, so the name describes rivers.
Sindhava comes from Sindhu, so the old name is linked to rivers.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: The Ṛig Veda is India’s ______ text.
activities.hint: Think about how old the text is.
activities.explanation: People say the Ṛig Veda is India’s oldest text.

activities.prompt: What does Sapta Sindhava mean?
options: A country in general
The land of one river
The land of the seven rivers
The oldest Indian text
activities.explanation: The Ṛig Veda calls the north-west part of India Sapta Sindhava.

activities.prompt: Match each name with its correct meaning.
pairs: The land of the seven rivers
The Indus River or a river in general
activities.explanation: Each match comes from the Ṛig Veda or its name for Sindhu.

activities.prompt: Put these clues in order. Start with the text's status. End with its meaning.
items: The Ṛig Veda is India's oldest text.
It is several thousand years old.
It calls the north-western region Sapta Sindhava.
Sapta Sindhava means the land of the seven rivers.
activities.explanation: Start with the text's status. Then give its age, name and meaning.

activities.prompt: Modern India has defined borders, states and a known population. The subcontinent had many names and changing boundaries. What should we remember about India's past?
options: India's borders and names did not always stay the same.
India's borders and names always stayed exactly the same.
India's population and borders always stayed exactly the same.
India's many names prove it always had defined borders.

why.India's borders and names always stayed: This mistake assumes that the past was exactly like modern India.
why.India's population and borders always st: This mistake assumes that population and boundaries never changed.
why.India's many names prove it always had d: This mistake thinks many names prove that borders were always fixed.

activities.explanation: This is right because the facts say that names and boundaries changed.

activities.prompt: The Ṛig Veda is India's oldest text, several thousand years old. A student wants this text's name and another source to check it. Which plan fits?
options: Use the Ṛig Veda, then compare it with one other source.
Use a traveller's account, then compare it with another account.
Use a pilgrim's account, then compare it with one inscription.
Use an inscription, then compare it with the same inscription.

why.Use a traveller's account, then compare: This mistake ignores the required oldest text and checks one source twice.

why.Ignore every old source, because modern: This mistake ignores old clues and trusts only modern India.
why.Choose the shortest source, because a sh: This mistake believes length shows quality instead of comparing sources.

activities.explanation: This is right because many different sources can teach us about the past.

activities.title: A Tour of Regional Names
activities.body:
Imagine opening an old Indian book and beginning a journey through its regional names. The Mahābhārata is one of India’s most famous texts. As time went on, names for different parts of India appeared in old writings. You can travel through these names as a special tour.

You meet Kāshmīra, one of the many regions listed in the Mahābhārata. This name refers roughly to today’s Kashmir. Kurukṣhetra appears, referring to parts of today’s Haryana. Here, you begin to see how old names connect with places you know.

Moving onward, you find Vanga, which refers to parts of Bengal. You also meet Prāgjyotiṣha, roughly referring to today’s Assam. Kaccha greets you as another name for today’s Kutch. Each stop helps you recognise an older way of naming places.

Your tour brings you to Kerala in the Mahābhārata. The name was used there for roughly today’s Kerala. You wonder why these names matter to a social science lesson. They show how regional names were recorded in a famous text. Scholars think the Mahābhārata was written from a few centuries BCE onward.

Kurukṣhetra is in today's Haryana. Vanga is in Bengal. Prāgjyotiṣha is about today's Assam. Kaccha is today's Kutch. The name Kerala was used for about today's Kerala.

lessons.title: Two Names for the Whole Indian Subcontinent

activities.prompt: What if one place had two ancient names?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Two Names for One Land
activities.body:
Imagine you are reading the Mahābhārata. You meet two names for one vast land.

First comes Bhāratavarṣa. The text clearly uses it for the entire Indian Subcontinent. Under this wider name, you find many rivers and peoples. The name means “the country of the Bharatas”.

Then you meet Jambudvīpa. It means “the island of the fruit of the jamun tree”. The jamun is a common tree native to India. Later, Jambudvīpa came to mean the Indian Subcontinent.

Your tour reaches an older name: Bharata. This name first appears in the Ṛig Veda. Here, Bharata refers to one of the main Vedic groups of people. You discover how a name can grow from a people to a whole land.

As you continue, you hear of several kings named Bharata. Your final thought is simple: two names can describe one whole land.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Two Names for India
activities.body: The Mahābhārata uses two names for the whole Indian Subcontinent: Bhāratavarṣa and Jambudvīpa. Bhāratavarṣa clearly refers to the entire Indian Subcontinent. It means “the country of the Bharatas”. Jambudvīpa means “the island of the fruit of the jamun tree”. The jamun is a common tree native to India. Later, Jambudvīpa came to mean the Indian Subcontinent.
keyPoints: The Mahābhārata uses Bhāratavarṣa and Jambudvīpa.
Bhāratavarṣa means the country of the Bharatas.
Jambudvīpa later came to mean the Indian Subcontinent.
activities.explanation: These two names help us understand how the Mahābhārata describes the Indian Subcontinent.

activities.prompt: Two old books give different names to the same large region. Why can both names be right?

Bhāratavarṣha fits because it means the country of the Bharatas.
Jambudvīpa fits because it means the island of the jamun fruit.
Later, Jambudvīpa meant the Indian Subcontinent, so both names fit one region.

activities.title: How the Name Bharata Changed
activities.body: The name Bharata first appears in the Ṛig Veda. There, Bharata is the name of one main Vedic group. Later writings mention some kings named Bharata. In the Mahābhārata, Bhāratavarṣa is a wider name. It is the name for the whole Indian Subcontinent. The book names many rivers and groups of people under this wider name.
keyPoints: Bharata first appears in the Ṛig Veda.
At first, it names a main Vedic group of people.
Bhāratavarṣa has a wider meaning in the Mahābhārata.
activities.explanation: The word Bharata has different meanings in different writings.

options: It changed from a people to a country name.

lessons.title: Aśhoka, Bhārata and India's Ancient Geography

activities.prompt: What might you discover about an ancient name?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Ancient India
activities.body:
You begin a journey through ancient India with Aśhoka. He lived around 250 BCE. The India under him included Bangladesh and Pakistan, and parts of Afghanistan.

Along the way, you find many inscriptions left by Aśhoka. These written marks help you imagine his presence. Then, a few centuries later, Bhārata becomes the general name for the Indian Subcontinent.

You open the Viṣhṇu Purāṇa, an ancient text describing Bhārata. The text describes Bhārata as the country north of the ocean. It also describes Bhārata as the country south of the snowy mountains.

Today, you still meet the name Bhārata. In northern India, the name is generally written as Bharat. In southern India, the name is often written as Bharatam. Different spellings now point back to the same name.

In another corner of your journey, you hear about an ancient Tamil poem. It came from about 2,000 years ago. It praised a king. Your tour now links Aśhoka's inscriptions with Bhārata's many meanings.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Aśhoka and Bhārata
activities.body: Aśhoka was an emperor of India. He lived around 250 BCE. He left many inscriptions. His India had today's Bangladesh, Pakistan and parts of Afghanistan. A few centuries later, Bhārata became the common name for the Indian Subcontinent. The Viṣhṇu Purāṇa says Bhārata is north of the ocean. It is south of snowy mountains. Today, people write the name Bharat in northern India. In southern India, they write it Bharatam.
keyPoints: Aśhoka lived around 250 BCE and left many inscriptions.
Aśhoka's India included today's Bangladesh, Pakistan and parts of Afghanistan.
Bhārata became the common name for the Indian Subcontinent.
activities.explanation: This lesson links Aśhoka's empire with the ancient geography of Bhārata.

lessons.title: How Persians and Greeks Named India

activities.prompt: Why do we call this place India?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How India Got Its Name
activities.body:
You begin your journey in Iran, where the ancient Persians lived. The Persians were the first foreign people to mention India.

During your visit, you hear about a military campaign. In the sixth century BCE, a Persian emperor launched it. The Persians gained control of the Indus River region. This area had earlier been called Sindhu.

As you look through Persian records and inscriptions, you find names for this region. They called India Hind, Hidu or Hindu. These Persian names were adaptations of the word Sindhu.

You learn that the ancient Persian word Hindu was only a geographical name. You also learn that it did not refer to the Hindu religion.

Next, you meet the ancient Greeks, who called the region Indoi or Indike. The Greeks dropped the letter h from Hindu. They dropped h because that letter was not in their language.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Ancient Names for India
activities.body: The ancient Persians were the first foreign people to mention India. The Indus River region was earlier called Sindhu. Persian records called India Hind, Hidu or Hindu. These names were changed forms of Sindhu. In ancient Persian, Hindu was only a name for the place. It did not refer to the Hindu religion. Greeks called the region Indoi or Indike. Greeks dropped h, which their language did not contain.

Persian names came from the earlier name Sindhu.
Hindu was a place name, not a religion, in ancient Persian.
Greeks used Indoi and Indike after dropping h.

lessons.title: Chinese Names, Travellers and Hindustān

activities.prompt: What might an ancient traveller’s name for India tell us?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Names on the Journey
activities.body:
Imagine setting out from ancient China, curious to learn what lay beyond its borders. Centuries ago, Chinese people and India knew of one another. Would this journey change what people called a place?

In the 7th century CE, you could follow Xuanzang from China to India. He travelled through many parts of India and met scholars. He collected Buddhist texts and later carried them home. His journey took him away for 17 years. Then you return with him to China.

There, Xuanzang translated the Sanskrit manuscripts he had taken home. Several other Chinese scholars also visited India over the centuries. Now you meet Tianzhu, another Chinese name derived from Sindhu. Foreign visitors mostly took their names for India from the Sindhu or Indus River. You might also understand Tianzhu as heavenly master.

Your tour ends with Hindustān, a name first seen in a Persian inscription. That inscription appeared about 1,800 years ago. Most invaders later used Hindustān for the Indian Subcontinent. So, as you travel through names, you uncover old routes of contact.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Journeys and names
activities.body: Ancient Chinese people had contact with India. Xuanzang travelled there in the 7th century CE. He visited many places. He met scholars. He collected Buddhist texts. After 17 years, he went back to China. He translated Sanskrit manuscripts. Other Chinese scholars also visited India over many centuries. Tianzhu came from Sindhu. It could mean heavenly master. Hindustān first appeared in a Persian inscription about 1,800 years ago. Later, most invaders used this name for the Subcontinent.
keyPoints: Xuanzang travelled to India and collected Buddhist texts.
Tianzhu came from Sindhu and could mean heavenly master.
Hindustān first appeared in a Persian inscription.
activities.explanation: These facts join Xuanzang's journey with the names Tianzhu and Hindustān.

activities.prompt: Two maps show different names for India. Why are both names connected?
steps: Foreign visitors mostly took India's names from the Sindhu or Indus River.
Hindustān fits this river-based naming pattern.
Tianzhu was a Chinese name derived from Sindhu.
So both names lead back to the same river name, though from different peoples.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: How India got new names
activities.body: Most foreign visitors took their names for India from Sindhu. Sindhu is also called the Indus River. A Chinese name, Tianzhu, came from Sindhu. It may also mean heavenly master. Hindustān first appeared in a Persian inscription (words carved in stone) about 1,800 years ago. Most invaders (people who came to conquer) later used Hindustān for the Indian Subcontinent.
keyPoints: Most foreign names for India came from Sindhu (Indus River).
Tianzhu was a Chinese name that came from Sindhu.
Most later invaders used the name Hindustān for the Indian Subcontinent.
activities.explanation: The names Tianzhu and Hindustān came through links with Sindhu.

activities.prompt: Xuanzang went back to China. After how many years?
options: 7 years
17 years
17 months
1,800 years
activities.explanation: Xuanzang went back to China after 17 years.

activities.prompt: Most foreign visitors got their names for India from the Sindhu or Indus River.
activities.explanation: The lesson says most foreign visitors used these river names.

activities.prompt: Match each name with its correct fact.
pairs: First appeared in a Persian inscription
Sources for foreign visitors' names for India
activities.explanation: Each pair links a traveller or name with its supported fact.

activities.prompt: Which meaning of Tianzhu is given in the lesson?
options: Heavenly master
The Indus River
A Persian inscription
Buddhist texts
activities.explanation: Tianzhu could also be understood as heavenly master.

activities.prompt: A student says Hindustān first appeared about 1,800 years ago. Which fact supports this?
options: Most invaders later used it for the Indian Subcontinent.
It came from the Chinese name Tianzhu.
Foreign visitors took India's names only from this Persian word.
It first appeared in a Persian inscription.
activities.explanation: the lesson directly links Hindustān's first appearance with a Persian inscription.

activities.prompt: Put Xuanzang's journey in the correct order.
items: Met scholars and collected Buddhist texts
Translated the Sanskrit manuscripts he took to China
activities.explanation: This order follows his journey, return and translation work.

activities.prompt: Xuanzang brought Sanskrit manuscripts to China. Why did he translate them?
options: He wanted Chinese readers to know Buddhist texts.
He wanted to take the texts back to India.
He wanted to change what the Buddhist texts said.
He wanted to hide the Buddhist ideas from readers.

why.He wanted to take the texts back to Indi: This reverses the journey because he brought the texts from India.
why.He wanted to change what the Buddhist te: This mistakes translation for changing the text's meaning.
why.He wanted to hide the Buddhist ideas fro: This mistakes sharing knowledge for hiding it.

activities.explanation: Translating let Chinese readers understand the Buddhist texts.

activities.prompt: A Persian visitor uses the Indus River rule. Which name fits best?
options: Hindustān is the likely name.
Tianzhu is the likely name.
Sanskrit is the likely name.
Buddhist is the likely name.

Tianzhu was a Chinese name, not the Persian name here.
Sanskrit is the text's language, not a river-based country name.
Buddhist describes the texts, not the country's name.

activities.explanation: Persian use and the river rule point to Hindustān.

activities.prompt: Xuanzang visited India, then returned after 17 years. What does this show?
options: He made a long journey between China and India.
He stayed in China during all 17 years.
He visited only one scholar in all of India.
He returned before collecting any Buddhist texts.

This reverses where he stayed during those years.
why.He visited only one scholar in all of In: This mistakes meeting many scholars for meeting only one.
why.He returned before collecting any Buddhi: This puts collecting the texts after his return, not before.

activities.explanation: He travelled to India and returned only after 17 years.

activities.prompt: Most invaders used “Hindustān” for the Indian Subcontinent. What does this suggest?
options: They followed the usual river-based naming rule.
They copied the name from Buddhist manuscripts.
They chose a name meaning heavenly master.
They avoided names connected with the Indus.

why.They copied the name from Buddhist manus: This confuses Buddhist texts with the source of place-names.
why.They chose a name meaning heavenly maste: This mixes up Tianzhu's possible meaning with Hindustān's use.
why.They avoided names connected with the In: This is opposite to the river-based naming pattern.

activities.explanation: Their use matches the foreign naming rule based on the Indus.
