activities.context: Reena is preparing a poster about India's past. She sees that modern India has defined borders, defined states and a known population, but an old book describes a region called Sapta Sindhava. The teacher explains that the Indian Subcontinent has had many names and changing boundaries. The class reads the Ṛig Veda, India's oldest text, and compares old texts, travellers' accounts, pilgrims' accounts and inscriptions. Reena wonders what the name Sindhu reveals about the region.
activities.prompt: What should Reena do to explore how the region was named in the past?
options: Compare the accounts and look for repeated references to Sindhu, Sapta Sindhava and the region.
Use only modern place-names because older names cannot provide information about the past.
Choose one old name and use it for every period without checking the other accounts.
Ignore differences between accounts because different names make the sources unreliable.

why.Use only modern place-names because olde: Only modern names would hide how the Subcontinent's names changed.
why.Choose one old name and use it for every: Choosing one name without checking would miss evidence from other sources.
why.Ignore differences between accounts beca: Differences can reflect many names and changing boundaries rather than unreliable sources.

activities.explanation: Comparing several sources can reveal repeated names and descriptions.

activities.context: Reena is preparing a poster about India's past. She sees that modern India has defined borders, defined states and a known population, but an old book describes a region called Sapta Sindhava. The teacher explains that the Indian Subcontinent has had many names and changing boundaries. The class reads the Ṛig Veda, India's oldest text, and compares old texts, travellers' accounts, pilgrims' accounts and inscriptions. Reena wonders what the name Sindhu reveals about the region.
activities.prompt: If two old accounts use different names for the same region, what is the best response?
options: Compare their contexts and allow for the possibility that the Subcontinent had many names and changing boundaries.
Assume the account with the unfamiliar name must be wrong because all regions had one fixed name.
Conclude that modern borders and states never existed at any time.
Choose whichever name appears more often and treat it as the only correct name.

why.Assume the account with the unfamiliar n: The Subcontinent has had many names, so unfamiliar names are not automatically wrong.
why.Conclude that modern borders and states: Modern India's defined borders and states do not prove that they never existed earlier.
why.Choose whichever name appears more often: Repeated use may be useful, but frequency alone cannot settle every difference.

activities.explanation: Different names can result from changing names and boundaries.

activities.prompt: Explain how the Mahābhārata helps us learn about old regional names in India.
activities.answer: Names for different parts of India began appearing in old writings as time went on. The Mahābhārata is one of India's most famous texts and lists many regions, including Kāshmīra. This lets us connect old regional names with parts of present-day India, although some matches are rough.
points: Names for Indian regions appeared in old writings over time.
The Mahābhārata is a famous text that lists many regions.
Kāshmīra is one listed regional name.
Old names can be matched roughly with present-day areas.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between Bhāratavarṣa and Jambudvīpa as names for the Indian Subcontinent, and explain how Bharata appears in the Ṛig Veda.
activities.answer: In the Mahābhārata, Bhāratavarṣa names the country of the Bharatas and refers to the entire Indian Subcontinent. Jambudvīpa also names that region, but means “the island of the fruit of the jamun tree.” Bharata in the Ṛig Veda referred to one of the main Vedic groups, not the whole region.
points: Bhāratavarṣa refers to the entire Indian Subcontinent.
Bhāratavarṣa means the country of the Bharatas.
Jambudvīpa means the island of the jamun fruit.
In the Ṛig Veda, Bharata refers to a main Vedic group.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student is preparing a short exhibit about ancient India. The display places Aśhoka around 250 BCE and includes examples of his inscriptions. A map shows that his territory reached beyond modern northern India into present-day Bangladesh, Pakistan, and part of Afghanistan. A timeline places Bhārata a few centuries after Aśhoka. The student must also explain how the name is written in different parts of India today.
activities.prompt: The student is completing a map of Aśhoka’s India. Which areas should be added to show the full extent of his territory?
options: Bangladesh, Pakistan, and part of Afghanistan
Bangladesh only, leaving out Pakistan and Afghanistan
Pakistan and Afghanistan only, leaving out Bangladesh
Bangladesh and Pakistan only, leaving out Afghanistan

why.Bangladesh only, leaving out Pakistan an: This incorrectly leaves Pakistan and Afghanistan outside the map.
why.Pakistan and Afghanistan only, leaving o: This incorrectly leaves Bangladesh outside the map.
why.Bangladesh and Pakistan only, leaving ou: This correctly includes two areas but leaves Afghanistan out.

activities.explanation: This option correctly includes all the areas named in the facts.

activities.context: A student is preparing a short exhibit about ancient India. The display places Aśhoka around 250 BCE and includes examples of his inscriptions. A map shows that his territory reached beyond modern northern India into present-day Bangladesh, Pakistan, and part of Afghanistan. A timeline places Bhārata a few centuries after Aśhoka. The student must also explain how the name is written in different parts of India today.
activities.prompt: The student is making two labels for displays about northern and southern India. Which spellings should be used?
options: Bharat for northern India and Bharatam for southern India
Bharatam for northern India and Bharat for southern India
Bharat for both displays
Bharatam for both displays

why.Bharatam for northern India and Bharat f: This reverses the usual regional spellings.
why.Bharat for both displays: This overlooks the spelling commonly used in southern India.
why.Bharatam for both displays: This overlooks the spelling generally used in northern India.

activities.explanation: These are the spellings generally used in northern and southern India respectively.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between Aśhoka’s India and the later name Bhārata.
activities.answer: Aśhoka’s India was the emperor’s realm around 250 BCE. It included today’s Bangladesh and Pakistan, and part of Afghanistan. A few centuries later, Bhārata became the general name for the Indian Subcontinent. The first term refers to Aśhoka’s territory; the second refers to the later name for the wider region.
points: Aśhoka lived around 250 BCE.
His India included Bangladesh, Pakistan, and part of Afghanistan.
Bhārata became the general name a few centuries later.
Bhārata referred to the wider Indian Subcontinent.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Asha prepares a “Names of India” display. She learns that Persians were the first foreign people to mention India and that the ancient Persians lived in Iran. She studies a Persian emperor’s campaign in the 6th century BCE. She learns that the Persians gained control of the Indus region, earlier called Sindhu. Persian records and inscriptions used Hind, Hidu, or Hindu. Asha must explain how ancient Greeks came to use Indoi or Indike and keep geography separate from religion.
activities.prompt: If the Greek language had included the letter h, what change would best fit how the Greek names were formed?
options: They could keep h, making the Greek form closer to Sindhu.
They would still leave it out because Persian records had several spellings.
They would change the word’s meaning from a region to a religion.
They would use Iran because that was where the Persians lived.

why.They would still leave it out because Pe: Different Persian spellings do not explain the removal of h.
why.They would change the word’s meaning fro: The Greek names still referred to a geographical region.
why.They would use Iran because that was whe: Iran was where the Persians lived, not the earlier name of the Indus region.

activities.explanation: The absence of h explains why the Greeks removed it.

activities.context: Asha prepares a “Names of India” display. She learns that Persians were the first foreign people to mention India and that the ancient Persians lived in Iran. She studies a Persian emperor’s campaign in the 6th century BCE. She learns that the Persians gained control of the Indus region, earlier called Sindhu. Persian records and inscriptions used Hind, Hidu, or Hindu. Asha must explain how ancient Greeks came to use Indoi or Indike and keep geography separate from religion.
activities.prompt: If Asha adds one sentence explaining why the Greek names differ from the Persian forms, which sentence is most accurate?
options: The Greeks left out h because their language did not contain that letter.
The Greeks added h because it was common in their language.
The Greeks used separate names because Sindhu had no Persian form.
The Greeks changed the word to give it a religious meaning.

why.The Greeks added h because it was common: The Greeks dropped h rather than adding it.
why.The Greeks used separate names because S: Sindhu was adapted into the Persian forms Hind, Hidu, and Hindu.
why.The Greeks changed the word to give it a: The Greek names were geographical, not religious.

activities.explanation: This gives the stated reason for dropping h.

activities.prompt: Explain why the Persian names Hind, Hidu, and Hindu came to be used for the Indus region.
activities.answer: Persian records and inscriptions called the Indus region Hind, Hidu, or Hindu. These were adaptations of Sindhu, the region’s earlier name. In ancient Persian, Hindu was only a geographical name; it did not refer to the Hindu religion. Thus, the Persian words named a place.
points: Persian records and inscriptions used these names.
The names were adapted from Sindhu.
Hindu was a geographical name.
It did not refer to the Hindu religion.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: Explain how Xuanzang's journey helped Chinese scholars learn about India.
activities.answer: Xuanzang travelled from China to India in the 7th century CE. During his 17 years there, he visited many parts of India, met scholars and collected Buddhist texts. He then returned to China and translated the Sanskrit manuscripts he had taken back. His journey therefore supported learning about India and the translation of Buddhist works.
points: He travelled from China to India in the 7th century CE.
He visited many parts of India and met scholars.
He collected Buddhist texts during his stay.
He returned after 17 years and translated the Sanskrit manuscripts.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

chapters.title: The Beginnings of Indian Civilisation
chapters.summary: In this chapter: what is a civilisation?; from village to city; town-planning; water management.

lessons.title: What Is a Civilisation?

activities.prompt: What helps people build a busy, well-run society together?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of a Civilisation
activities.body:
You begin your journey by wondering what a civilisation is. You find that it means an advanced stage of human society. Such a society needs some form of government and administration. These help manage society and its many activities.

Next, you explore how cities grow. Urbanism includes town planning, the growth of cities and their management. Town planning often includes water management and a drainage system.

After this, you visit people practising many crafts. You see goods made from stone or metal. Then you watch a trade exchange. Trade includes exchanges within a city or region, and with distant places. It can reach other parts of the world too.

Your tour now turns towards culture. You find it expressed through art, architecture, literature, oral traditions or social customs. You might notice it in a building design, a written story, or a shared custom.

Finally, you see productive agriculture at work. It provides enough food for both villages and cities. Your journey shows how government, towns, crafts, trade, culture and food production work together.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: What Makes a Civilisation?
activities.body: A civilisation is an advanced stage of human society. It needs government and administration to manage society. Urbanism includes town planning, city growth and city management. Town planning often includes water management and drainage. People make crafts from stone or metal. Trade happens within a city or region, and with distant places. Culture appears in art, architecture, literature, oral traditions and social customs. Productive agriculture gives enough food for villages and cities.
keyPoints: Civilisation needs government and administration to manage society.
Urbanism covers town planning, city growth and city management.
Culture uses art, architecture, literature, oral traditions and social customs.
activities.explanation: These parts help a civilisation manage society, make goods, trade, share culture and feed its people.

activities.prompt: A growing town needs water, trade, crafts, culture and enough food. How can its people manage it as a civilisation?
steps: Government and administration are needed because they manage society and its activities.
Urbanism helps because it includes town planning, city growth and city management.
Water management and drainage should be planned because towns often need both.
Together, these show why civilisation is an advanced stage of human society.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which answer gives the meaning of civilisation?
options: An advanced stage of human society
A way to manage water in a city
A type of food grown by people
Buying and selling between regions
activities.explanation: Civilisation means an advanced stage of human society. The other answers name parts of it.

activities.prompt: A civilisation needs some form of ______ and administration.
activities.hint: It helps manage society and its activities.
activities.explanation: Government and administration help manage society and its activities.

activities.prompt: Match each part of civilisation with its meaning.
pairs: An advanced stage of human society
Planning, growing and running towns and cities
Buying and selling in a city, a region, or far away
Art, buildings, books, spoken stories, or social customs
Farming that makes enough food for villages and cities
activities.explanation: Each match is one part of civilisation with its meaning. Together, they help a society work well.

activities.prompt: A maker sends stone goods to a buyer far away. Which activity is this?
options: Culture
Urbanism
Trade
Town planning
activities.explanation: Trade can be with faraway places. Sending stone goods to a buyer is trade.

activities.prompt: Put these parts in order. They make one true sentence about a civilisation.
items: needs a government and people to run things.
help to run the society and all its work.
activities.explanation: A civilisation needs a government and people to run things. They help to run the society and all its work.

activities.prompt: Why are town planning, water management and government important to a civilisation?
options: They help manage society, cities and their activities.
They show culture through art, literature and customs.
They make crafts from stone or metal.
They give food to villages and cities.
activities.explanation: Town planning often includes water management and drainage. These help manage society and cities.

activities.prompt: A city has trade, crafts, culture and many daily activities. How can it manage itself as a civilisation?
options: A government and administration that organise all the activities.
A drainage system that manages water inside the town.
A food supply that feeds people in villages and cities.
A culture that expresses art, architecture and social customs.

why.A drainage system that manages water ins: This manages water, but it does not manage every city activity.
why.A food supply that feeds people in villa: Food supports the city, but it does not organise every activity.
why.A culture that expresses art, architectu: Culture shows how people live, but it does not manage activities.

activities.explanation: This is right because government and administration manage society's activities.

activities.prompt: A town first grew without planning. Later, it planned water and drainage. What changed?
options: Its town planning and management became more organised.
Its culture disappeared when the town began planning.
Its trade ended when drainage was added.
Its food supply became less important after planning.

why.Its culture disappeared when the town be: Planning water does not remove art, traditions or customs.
Adding drainage does not stop exchanges within or beyond the town.
why.Its food supply became less important af: Planning does not reduce the need for food in villages and cities.

activities.explanation: This is right because urbanism includes town planning and management.

activities.prompt: Builders add water management and drainage as a town grows. Why do they do this?
options: Because town planning includes managing the town's growth.
Because culture requires every town to remove all water.
Because trade can happen only after drainage systems are built.
Because agriculture needs towns to grow without any planning.

why.Because culture requires every town to r: This wrongly connects culture with water management.
why.Because trade can happen only after drai: This wrongly makes drainage a condition for all trade.
why.Because agriculture needs towns to grow: This wrongly treats town growth and planning as opposite ideas.

activities.explanation: This is right because town planning includes water management and drainage.

lessons.title: From Village to City

activities.prompt: What might you discover on a journey beside India’s ancient rivers?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Along the Harappan Rivers
activities.body:
Imagine beginning your journey beside the Indus River, where ancient settlements rose near its water. You follow the river and its five main tributaries. Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, and many other sites spread along these waterways. Life gathered near the rivers, and the settlements grew into important cities.

Sindh greets you on the next part of your journey. Harappa was the first city of this civilisation to be excavated. The Harappan civilisation was one of the oldest civilisations in the world. The people who lived there were called Harappans. The civilisation is also known by several names. These include Harappan, Indus, and Indus-Sarasvatī Civilisation.

Now, you turn towards the Sarasvatī River. Many sites stood along its course. This river is now called Ghaggar in India and Helmand in Afghanistan. The Sarasvatī River is first mentioned in the Rigveda.

As your tour ends, you see a special pattern. Rivers helped shape where people settled and cities flourished. Many Harappan sites stood beside these rivers. Your journey shows how closely rivers and cities were linked.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: The Harappan Civilisation
activities.body: The Harappan civilisation was India's earliest civilisation. It has several names. Some are Harappan, Indus and Indus-Sarasvatī Civilisation. Its people were called Harappans. Harappa, in Sindh, was the first city excavated (dug up). Important cities grew along rivers, including Mohenjo-daro and Harappa.
keyPoints: The Harappan civilisation was India's earliest civilisation.
Its people were called Harappans.
Harappa was the first city excavated (dug up).
activities.explanation: Now you know its names, its people and its important cities.

activities.prompt: A child sees Ghaggar on one map and Helmand on another. Why might both maps show the same river?
steps: The Rigveda first mentions the Sarasvatī River.
In India, that river is now called Ghaggar.
In Afghanistan, that river is now called Helmand.
So two modern maps can show one river with different names.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which name is for India's oldest civilisation?
options: Mohenjo-daro
Ghaggar
Harappan
Rigveda
activities.explanation: Harappan is one name for India's oldest civilisation.

activities.prompt: Match each place or river with the correct fact.
activities.explanation: These pairs connect the important cities and rivers of the Harappan civilisation.

activities.prompt: In India, the Sarasvatī River is called the Ghaggar. What is its name in Afghanistan?
options: Helmand
Harappa
Indus
Rigveda
activities.explanation: Now, the Sarasvatī River is called the Helmand in Afghanistan.

activities.prompt: What does the lesson say about Harappa and Mohenjo-daro?
options: They were the first two cities dug up.
They both grew along rivers.
They stood only on the Sarasvatī River.
They are names for the people who lived there.
activities.explanation: Harappa and Mohenjo-daro were important cities. Both grew along rivers.

activities.prompt: The Rigveda mentions a river. Many Harappan sites stood along it. Which river fits both facts?
options: The Sarasvatī River fits both facts.
The Indus River fits both facts.
The Ghaggar River fits both facts.
The Helmand River fits both facts.

This confuses the Indus name with the river having many sites.
This is its modern name in India, not the name in the Rigveda.
This is its modern name in Afghanistan, not the name in the Rigveda.

activities.explanation: The Rigveda mentions Sarasvatī, and many sites stood along it.

activities.prompt: A museum guide says the first excavated city lay in Sindh. It belonged to the Harappan civilisation. Which place should the guide show?
options: The city of Mohenjo-daro
The city of Harappa
The river called Indus
The river called Sarasvatī

why.The city of Mohenjo-daro: Mohenjo-daro was important, but Harappa was excavated first.
why.The river called Indus: The Indus is a river name, not the excavated city in Sindh.
why.The river called Sarasvatī: The Sarasvatī is a river name, not the excavated city in Sindh.

activities.explanation: Harappa in Sindh was the first city of this civilisation to be excavated.

activities.prompt: The Indus River has five main tributaries. A map draws one of them. What is still missing?
options: Four more main branches of the Indus River.
Five more main branches of the Indus River.
The first city of the Harappan civilisation.
The river first mentioned in the Rigveda.

why.Five more main branches of the Indus Riv: This counts all five again and forgets the one already drawn.
why.The first city of the Harappan civilisat: This confuses a city with the tributaries of a river.
why.The river first mentioned in the Rigveda: This confuses one river with the tributaries of another.

activities.explanation: One of the five tributaries is shown, so four remain.

activities.prompt: A map in India labels the river Ghaggar. A map in Afghanistan labels it Helmand. What can we conclude?
options: They name the same Sarasvatī River.
They name two different rivers.
They show the Indus River under two names.
They show two old Harappan cities.

This mistake treats two names for one river as two rivers.
why.They show the Indus River under two name: This mistake mixes the Indus name with the Sarasvatī River.
This mistake treats river names as names of cities.

activities.explanation: The facts give two modern names for one river.

lessons.title: Town-Planning

activities.prompt: How were early towns organised, and how were their streets planned?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Towns of the Indus Valley
activities.body:
Imagine joining a tour of Harappa and Mohenjo-daro. You first visit Harappa and then Mohenjo-daro. These were the first two Harappan cities discovered. These cities were also the first of the civilisation to be discovered.

Your guide explains that many more sites were later found in the Indus plains. At first, this civilisation was called the Indus Valley civilisation. Other major cities included Dholavira, Rakhigarhi and Banawali.

Now, you walk through a city built to a precise plan. Many streets point towards the cardinal directions. Most cities had fortification walls. Each had two distinct parts, an upper town and a lower town.

In the upper town, the local elite probably lived. Common people lived in the lower town. You pass large buildings used for collective purposes. Most of these buildings were generally made of bricks.

As your tour ends, you look across the walls and straight streets. You remember the city's precise plan. You also notice the large brick buildings used by many people.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: How Harappan cities were planned
activities.body: Big Harappan cities were built with careful plans. Many streets faced the cardinal directions (north, south, east and west). Most cities had walls for defence and two separate parts. Rich, powerful people probably lived in the upper town. Common people lived in the lower town. Some big buildings were for the whole community. Most of these buildings were made of bricks.
keyPoints: Streets often faced the cardinal directions.
Most cities had walls and two separate parts.
Rich, powerful people probably lived in the upper town.
activities.explanation: These clues show how Harappan people planned their cities.

activities.prompt: Imagine drawing a Harappan town map for the local elite and common people. Where should each group live?
steps: Put the local elite in the upper town, because elites probably lived there.
Put common people in the lower town, because they probably lived there.
Keep the two parts distinct, because most cities had separate areas.
This map shows careful planning, because large cities followed precise plans.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The first cities found
activities.prompt: Which two Harappan cities were found first?
options: Dholavira and Banawali
Rakhigarhi and Dholavira
Harappa and Mohenjo-daro
Banawali and Rakhigarhi
activities.explanation: Harappa and Mohenjo-daro were the first two Harappan cities found.

activities.title: The first name
activities.prompt: At first, people called this civilisation the Indus Valley civilisation.
activities.explanation: People first gave the civilisation this name.

activities.title: More sites are found
activities.prompt: Many more sites were found later in the ______ plains.
activities.hint: The first name of the civilisation has this word.
activities.explanation: Later, many more sites were found in the Indus plains.

activities.title: Match each clue
activities.prompt: Match each clue to its fact.
activities.explanation: Each clue matches the fact next to it.

activities.title: Where did people live?
activities.prompt: Where did common people live in Harappan cities?
options: Upper town
Lower town
A large collective building
The Indus plains
activities.explanation: Common people lived in the lower town.

activities.title: A guide looks at a town
activities.prompt: A guide sees streets that go north, south, east and west. What can the guide say?
options: Common people probably lived in the upper town.
Its big buildings were all made of bricks.
This town was planned, like big Harappan cities.
The town had no strong walls around it.
activities.explanation: Big Harappan cities had careful plans. Many streets went north, south, east and west.

activities.prompt: A map shows streets, walls, and two parts. What does it suggest?
options: The city was planned and divided into areas.
The city grew randomly and had one shared area.
The city was planned, but its streets were random.
The city had parts, but its streets lacked careful planning.

why.The city grew randomly and had one share: This mistakes a planned city for a random, shared space.
why.The city was planned, but its streets we: This treats the shown streets as evidence of unplanned growth.
why.The city had parts, but its streets lack: This ignores the careful planning shown by the city's layout.

activities.explanation: It connects careful planning with the city's two areas.

activities.prompt: Harappa and Mohenjo-daro came before Indus plains finds. What does this show?
options: They were first discovered, not the only Harappan cities.
They were the only Harappan cities ever built.
They were discovered after every other Indus site.
They had more sites than all later discoveries.

why.They were the only Harappan cities ever: This confuses first discovered with the only cities built.
why.They were discovered after every other I: This reverses the order in which sites were discovered.
why.They had more sites than all later disco: This mistakes later sites for the first two discovered cities.

activities.explanation: It joins early discoveries with many sites found later.

activities.prompt: A child makes a town model. Which model follows Harappan planning rules?
options: Cardinal streets, fortification walls, and two town parts.
Random curved streets, fortification walls, and one town part.
Cardinal streets, no fortification walls, and two town parts.
Random curved streets, no fortification walls, and one town part.

why.Random curved streets, fortification wal: Random streets and one part do not follow the known plan.
why.Cardinal streets, no fortification walls: It remembers cardinal streets but forgets the walls.
why.Random curved streets, no fortification: It forgets both the cardinal streets and the city's two parts.

activities.explanation: It follows precise planning, cardinal streets, walls, and two parts.

activities.prompt: The civilisation's first name was Indus Valley civilisation. What explains it?
options: Many more sites were found in the Indus plains.
Only Harappa and Mohenjo-daro were ever found anywhere.
Most large buildings were made of bricks there.
Many streets faced the cardinal directions there.

why.Only Harappa and Mohenjo-daro were ever: This confuses the first two cities with all sites ever found.
why.Most large buildings were made of bricks: Building materials do not explain the civilisation's early name.
why.Many streets faced the cardinal directio: Street directions do not explain the civilisation's early name.

activities.explanation: Many sites in the Indus plains explain the civilisation's early name.

lessons.sceneCaption: The citadel mound at Mohenjo-daro contains ruins of ancient administrative buildings built on a massive mud-brick platform.

lessons.title: Water Management

activities.prompt: How did ancient people manage water and keep their homes clean?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Following the Water
activities.body:
You meet Harappans who gave great importance to water management and cleanliness. Their homes often had separate bathing areas. These areas connected to larger drains beneath the streets. The drains generally ran below streets and carried away waste water. You follow this network as you explore.

As you walk through Mohenjo-daro, you see hundreds of brick wells. People drew water from these wells. These wells were built from bricks. You can imagine drawing water during your journey.

In other regions, you might see people taking water from ponds, streams or reservoirs. At Dholavira, you find at least six large reservoirs. Most of these reservoirs were linked by underground drains. This network supported water harvesting and distribution.

Your tour ends beside the drains. You now understand why water management mattered greatly to the Harappans.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: How Harappans Managed Water
activities.body: Harappans cared a lot about **water management**. This means caring for water and using it properly. They also cared about cleanliness. Many homes had their own bathing areas. These joined bigger drains under the streets. The drains carried waste water away. Mohenjo-daro had hundreds of wells made of bricks. In other places, people may have taken water from ponds, streams or **reservoirs** (large water tanks). Dholavira had at least six large reservoirs. Most were joined by underground drains.
keyPoints: Harappans cared about water management and cleanliness.
Home bathing areas joined bigger drains.
Mohenjo-daro had hundreds of wells made of bricks.
Most reservoirs at Dholavira were joined by underground drains.
activities.explanation: These facts show how well Harappans looked after water.

activities.prompt: Imagine a Harappan child finishes bathing at home. Where does the used water go next?
steps: Families washed in separate bathing areas because this helped keep their homes clean.
The bathing areas sent waste water into larger drains because homes were connected to them.
These drains ran below streets, so they carried waste water away from the homes.
This shows why Harappans gave great importance to water management and cleanliness.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Separate Bathing Areas
activities.prompt: Where were the Harappans' separate bathing areas?
options: Inside their homes
Under the streets
Inside reservoirs
At brick wells
activities.explanation: Harappans often had separate bathing areas within their homes.

activities.title: Caring for Water
activities.prompt: The Harappans thought water ______ and cleanliness were very important.
activities.hint: This word means caring for water and using it well.
activities.explanation: Water management was very important to the Harappans.

activities.title: Match Water Details
activities.prompt: Match each Harappan water thing with its detail.
pairs: Connected to a larger drain system
activities.explanation: Each pair matches a water thing with its detail from the lesson.

activities.title: Linked Reservoirs
activities.prompt: Why were most reservoirs at Dholavira joined by underground drains?
options: For water harvesting and sharing water
To carry water to brick wells
To make streets cleaner
To build new homes
activities.explanation: The underground drains helped with water harvesting and sharing water.

activities.title: Water from Brick Wells
activities.prompt: People in Mohenjo-daro took water from ______ of wells made of bricks.
activities.hint: The lesson says Mohenjo-daro had very many wells.
activities.explanation: Hundreds of brick wells gave people water in Mohenjo-daro.

activities.prompt: Homes had separate bathing areas. Their drains ran below streets and carried waste water away. Why did this help cleanliness?
options: It carried used water away from homes and streets.
It brought clean water into every nearby home.
It stored all used water inside each busy home.
It stopped people from washing inside their homes.

why.It brought clean water into every nearby: This mistakes drains for pipes carrying clean water.
why.It stored all used water inside each bus: This mistakes waste pipes for storage places.
why.It stopped people from washing inside th: This mistakes cleanliness for never washing at home.

activities.explanation: Removing waste water helped keep homes and streets clean.

activities.prompt: A map shows many wells in Mohenjo-daro. A source says these wells were made of bricks. What can we conclude?
options: Many brick wells gave people water in Mohenjo-daro.
All city water came from one shared underground reservoir.
Every house had its own private brick well.
Ponds, streams, and reservoirs covered the whole city.

why.All city water came from one shared unde: This adds a shared reservoir that the sources do not show.
why.Every house had its own private brick we: This assumes every house had a private well.
why.Ponds, streams, and reservoirs covered t: This confuses Mohenjo-daro with the other regions.

activities.explanation: The map and source support the many brick wells.

activities.prompt: Home bathing areas joined larger drains below the streets. These drains carried waste water away. If one drain became blocked, what might happen?
options: Waste water might stay near that part of the street.
The wells would immediately provide cleaner water.
The reservoirs would send water to every home.
All bathing areas would join into one network.

why.The wells would immediately provide clea: This wrongly links a blockage to the quality of well water.
why.The reservoirs would send water to every: This confuses drain blockage with reservoir distribution.
why.All bathing areas would join into one ne: This assumes blockage would connect every bathing area.

activities.explanation: A blocked drain could not carry waste water away as before.

lessons.title: Food, Farming and Trade

activities.prompt: Ready to discover how people grew food, made cloth, and traded together?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Food, Farming and Trade
activities.body:
Imagine you walk beside a river and see Harappan settlements nearby.
You see many settlements along both large and small rivers.
The rivers made the soil around them richer.
You see fields of barley, wheat, millets and sometimes rice.
Pulses and many kinds of vegetables also grow here.

You learn that Harappans were the first people in South Asia to grow cotton.
They wove this cotton into cloth and made farming tools, including the plough.
They domesticated animals for meat and caught fish in rivers and the sea.

You follow Harappan traders travelling by land, river and sea.
They exported ornaments, timber, daily-use objects, probably gold, cotton and perhaps foods.
Carnelian beads were among their most favoured ornaments.

You learn that Harappans mastered working copper and made bronze by adding tin.
At Lothal, a huge dockyard received and sent boats.
You now understand how Harappans grew food, made goods and traded.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: How Harappans Got Food and Trade
activities.body: Harappans lived beside rivers. River water made nearby soil richer. They grew cereals (grains like wheat), pulses (beans and lentils), vegetables and sometimes rice. They were the first cotton growers in South Asia. They made cloth from cotton. They kept animals for meat, and they fished. They made ploughs. They worked with copper and bronze. Traders travelled by land, river and sea. Lothal had a huge dockyard (a place for boats).
keyPoints: Rivers made the soil near them richer.
Harappans grew crops, kept animals and fished.
Traders used land, rivers and the sea.
activities.explanation: These facts show how rivers, farming and trade were linked.

activities.prompt: A family settles beside a small river. Why might this help farming?
steps: Harappans settled by small rivers, so this place fits farming life.
Rivers make nearby soil richer, which helps crops grow.
They can grow cereals, pulses and vegetables, with rice sometimes included.
So settling beside a small river could support a farming settlement.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Why Live Near Rivers?
activities.prompt: Why did many Harappan towns grow beside rivers?
options: Rivers made the soil poorer.
Rivers made nearby soil richer.
Rivers were used only for fishing.
Rivers were far from all the towns.
activities.explanation: River water made the soil around the towns richer. This was an important reason for farming.

activities.title: A Group of Crops
activities.prompt: Which group has barley, wheat, millets and rice?
options: Cereals
Farming tools
Ornaments
Trade routes
activities.explanation: Harappans grew cereals like barley, wheat and millets. They also sometimes grew rice.

activities.title: A Useful Farming Tool
activities.prompt: Harappans made farming tools, like the ______.
activities.hint: Use this tool while farming.
activities.explanation: The plough was one farming tool Harappans made.

activities.title: Grow, Make and Export
activities.prompt: Match each thing with its group, product, use or export.
activities.explanation: These matches show what Harappans grew, made and exported.

activities.title: Lothal's Busy Harbour
activities.prompt: What did Lothal have for boats to come in and go out?
options: A copper workshop
A cattle pen
A grain field
A big dockyard
activities.explanation: Lothal had a big dockyard. Boats came in and went out there. Harappan traders used rivers and the sea.

activities.title: Bronze-making Steps
activities.prompt: Put the steps to make bronze in order.
activities.explanation: Copper was worked first. Adding tin to copper made bronze.

activities.prompt: A family farms beside a small river. What change is most likely in the nearby soil?
options: The soil becomes richer.
The soil becomes useless.
The soil becomes harder.
The soil becomes salty.

This mistake thinks rivers make the soil useless.
This mistake thinks rivers make the soil harder.
This mistake thinks rivers make the soil salty.

activities.explanation: Rivers make the soil around them richer.

activities.prompt: A farm record lists barley, wheat, millets, pulses and many vegetables. What does this show?
options: These foods came from Harappan farming.
These objects came from Harappan metalwork.
These routes carried Harappan trade goods.
These objects were all Harappan ornaments.

why.These objects came from Harappan metalwo: This mistake treats food words as names of metal objects.
why.These routes carried Harappan trade good: This mistake treats crop names as routes for trade.
why.These objects were all Harappan ornament: This mistake treats food words as kinds of ornaments.

activities.explanation: Harappans grew these cereals, pulses and vegetables.

activities.prompt: A trader wants to export cotton cloth. Why can this item be made locally?
options: They grew cotton and wove it into cloth.
They added tin to copper and wove it.
They made a plough and wove it into cloth.
They exported soil and wove it into cloth.

This mistake mixes bronze-making with cotton weaving.
why.They made a plough and wove it into clot: This mistake mixes plough-making with cotton weaving.
why.They exported soil and wove it into clot: This mistake treats soil as the source of cloth.

activities.explanation: Harappans grew cotton and used it to weave cloth.

activities.prompt: A record shows a huge Lothal dockyard for boats. Maps show land and river routes. What do these sources show?
options: Harappan traders used land, rivers and the sea.
Harappan traders used land and rivers only.
Harappan traders used the sea and land only.
Harappan traders used boats but no other routes.

why.Harappan traders used land and rivers on: This mistake ignores the sea route and dockyard.
why.Harappan traders used the sea and land o: This mistake ignores the river route shown on the map.
why.Harappan traders used boats but no other: This mistake treats the dockyard as the only trade route.

activities.explanation: The dockyard supports boat trade, and routes included land, rivers and sea.

lessons.title: The Lives of the Ancients and the End of the Cities

activities.prompt: What happened when the Harappan cities began to grow quiet?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Harappan Journey
activities.body:
You begin among Harappan city ruins. Archaeologists have unearthed many objects made and used by the Harappans. Games and toys amused both adults and children. You imagine adults and children playing with their games and toys.

Then you ask why this civilisation began to fall apart despite its achievements. The cities were abandoned one by one. Many inhabitants adopted a rural lifestyle in the changed environment. Most Harappans scattered over hundreds or thousands of small rural settlements.

You find no trace of warfare or invasion. Harappans seem to have had no army or weapons of war. The available evidence suggests a relatively peaceful civilisation. It appears that the earlier government or administration no longer existed.

A climatic change caused reduced rainfall and a drier phase. Cities such as Kalibangan and Anauli were abandoned.

Yet much Harappan culture and technology survived. It passed on to the next phase of Indian civilisation. Your journey ends with the survival of Harappan culture and technology.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Life and Change
activities.body: Archaeologists have found many objects made by Harappans. They made games and toys for adults and children. Later, the Indus-Sarasvatī civilisation began to break down. It had many good things. But it still broke down. The climate changed. It had less rain and became drier. People left the cities one by one. Many people lived a rural life, in villages and the countryside. The evidence shows it was mostly peaceful.
keyPoints: Harappans made games and toys for adults and children.
Climate change brought less rain. Cities were left empty.
Many Harappans lived a peaceful, rural life.
activities.explanation: These facts help us picture Harappan life and how it changed.

activities.prompt: It rains less, and the Harappan environment becomes drier. What happens next?
steps: Less rain causes a drier phase, so the environment changes.
There is no trace of warfare, so invasion is not the clear explanation.
With the environment changed, many inhabitants adopt rural life.
Thus, cities are abandoned, but much Harappan culture survives onward.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Harappans made games and toys for adults and children.
activities.explanation: Games and toys were fun for both adults and children.

activities.title: Who Played Harappan Games?
activities.prompt: Harappans made games and toys for ______ and children.
activities.hint: Look for the people named next to children.
activities.explanation: Harappan games and toys were fun for both adults and children.

activities.title: Match Each Clue
activities.prompt: Match each question to its fact.
pairs: Who enjoyed Harappan games and toys?
What way of life did many people start?
It lived on and was passed on
activities.explanation: Each clue points to a fact about Harappan life or change.

activities.title: The End of the Cities
activities.prompt: Put these events in the right order.
items: The civilisation starts to break down
People leave the cities one by one
Many people start a rural lifestyle
Most Harappans spread out to villages
Culture and technology are passed on to later people
activities.explanation: The facts tell how the cities fell and what came next.

activities.prompt: Available evidence shows that Harappans had an army.
activities.explanation: There is no trace of warfare or invasion. Harappans seem to have had no army.

activities.prompt: Less rainfall made the phase drier. Why were the cities abandoned?
options: Many inhabitants adopted a rural lifestyle in the changed environment.
The earlier government kept the cities running through the dry phase.
Harappan games and toys made people abandon their cities.
The next civilisation forced everyone into small rural settlements.

why.The earlier government kept the cities r: This wrongly assumes that the earlier administration continued.
why.Harappan games and toys made people aban: This wrongly treats games and toys as causes of abandonment.
why.The next civilisation forced everyone in: This wrongly adds an invasion that the evidence does not show.

activities.explanation: This matches the rural change described after the climate changed.

activities.prompt: A source shows no trace of warfare. What careful conclusion is best?
options: The evidence supports a relatively peaceful civilisation.
The Harappans certainly owned a large army and many weapons.
Every Harappan lived peacefully throughout the entire civilisation.
Missing evidence proves that an invasion secretly caused the decline.

why.The Harappans certainly owned a large ar: This wrongly treats missing traces as proof of weapons.
why.Every Harappan lived peacefully througho: This wrongly turns general evidence into a claim about everyone.
why.Missing evidence proves that an invasion: This wrongly treats missing traces as proof of an invasion.

activities.explanation: This conclusion is careful because it follows the available evidence.

activities.prompt: The earlier administration no longer existed. Who would make city-wide rules?
options: No earlier government would make or enforce the city's rules.
The old government would secretly keep making all city rules.
Games and toys would become the city's new administration.
Armed groups would take over and rule the city.

why.The old government would secretly keep m: This wrongly assumes that the old government continued secretly.
why.Games and toys would become the city's n: This wrongly confuses games and toys with a government.
why.Armed groups would take over and rule th: This wrongly assumes that Harappans had an army.

activities.explanation: This follows the fact that the earlier administration no longer existed.

lessons.sceneCaption: A wheeled goat toy from Mohenjo-daro shows the Harappans’ playful side.

lessons.title: Test practice
lessons.sceneAlt: Excavated ruins of Mohenjo-daro show the Great Bath in the foreground and the granary mound in the background.
lessons.sceneCaption: Mohenjo-daro’s ruins show the Great Bath and granary, illustrating ancient urban planning and administration.

activities.context: A fast-growing city is building new homes and workshops. Its government and administration are managing public activities, while town planners are arranging water management and drainage. Craftspeople make goods from stone and metal. Traders exchange goods within the region and with distant places. The city also shows its culture through art, architecture, literature, oral traditions and social customs. Nearby productive agriculture provides enough food for the village and the growing city.
activities.prompt: If water collects around new homes, what should the town planners do next?
options: Improve the water system and drainage to support the growing city.
Build more homes without considering where the water will go.
Ask distant traders to solve the city's water problem.
Leave water management entirely to the craftspeople.

why.Build more homes without considering whe: More housing could increase the water problem.
why.Ask distant traders to solve the city's: Distant trade cannot manage the city's water.
why.Leave water management entirely to the c: Craftspeople are not responsible for town water systems.

activities.explanation: The planners should improve water management and drainage.

activities.context: A fast-growing city is building new homes and workshops. Its government and administration are managing public activities, while town planners are arranging water management and drainage. Craftspeople make goods from stone and metal. Traders exchange goods within the region and with distant places. The city also shows its culture through art, architecture, literature, oral traditions and social customs. Nearby productive agriculture provides enough food for the village and the growing city.
activities.prompt: As the city expands, what should the government and administration coordinate?
options: The city's many activities so that society remains organised.
Only the work of craftspeople making metal goods.
New housing while ignoring other community activities.
The end of all exchanges with distant regions.

why.Only the work of craftspeople making met: A civilisation has many crafts, so one craft is not enough.
why.New housing while ignoring other communi: Town growth must be managed along with other activities.
why.The end of all exchanges with distant re: Distant trade is part of the city's economic life.

activities.explanation: Government and administration manage society and its activities.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between local trade and distant trade.
activities.answer: Local trade involves exchanges within a city or region. Distant trade involves exchanges with other regions or parts of the world. Both are forms of trade, but distant trade connects the city with trading partners beyond its immediate area.
points: Local trade happens within a city or region.
Distant trade happens with other regions or parts of the world.
Both involve exchanging goods.
Distant trade extends beyond the local area.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: At a school exhibition, a student studies a river map showing the Indus with five main tributaries. Nearby, signs explain that important cities, including Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, grew along rivers. Other signs mark many sites beside the Sarasvatī River and state that this river is now called the Ghaggar in India and the Helmand in Afghanistan. The student also learns that Harappa in Sindh was the first city of the Harappan civilisation to be excavated.
activities.prompt: If a new account says that another city was excavated before Harappa, what should the student do with the display's excavation-order sentence?
options: Change the sentence to name the city described in the new account.
Keep Harappa in the sentence because it was an important city.
Keep Harappa in the sentence because it grew along a river.
Keep Harappa in the sentence because it was in Sindh.

why.Keep Harappa in the sentence because it: Being important does not determine excavation order.
Growing along a river does not determine excavation order.
Being in Sindh does not determine excavation order.

activities.explanation: The new account changes which city was excavated first.

activities.context: At a school exhibition, a student studies a river map showing the Indus with five main tributaries. Nearby, signs explain that important cities, including Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, grew along rivers. Other signs mark many sites beside the Sarasvatī River and state that this river is now called the Ghaggar in India and the Helmand in Afghanistan. The student also learns that Harappa in Sindh was the first city of the Harappan civilisation to be excavated.
activities.prompt: A display labels the inhabitants 'Indus people'. To use the specific name for these people, what should the student do?
options: Replace the label with the word Harappans.
Replace the label with Harappa because that is the people's name.
Replace the label with Mohenjo-daro because it was an important city.
Leave the label unchanged because Indus is also a name for the civilisation.

why.Replace the label with Harappa because t: Harappa was a city, not the name of the inhabitants.
why.Replace the label with Mohenjo-daro beca: Mohenjo-daro was an important city, not the inhabitants.
why.Leave the label unchanged because Indus: Indus names the civilisation, while Harappans names its inhabitants.

activities.explanation: The inhabitants of the Harappan civilisation were called Harappans.

activities.prompt: How does the lesson explain the location of important Harappan sites?
activities.answer: The lesson explains that important cities, including Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, grew along rivers. The Indus River had five main tributaries, and many other sites lay along the Sarasvatī River. These details connect the Harappan civilisation with river settlements and explain why the lesson links its sites to rivers.
points: Important cities grew along rivers.
The Indus River had five main tributaries.
Many sites were located along the Sarasvatī River.
The lesson links Harappan sites with river locations.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Imagine that a town-planning team is learning from Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, the first two Harappan cities to be discovered. Their planned layouts provide a model: streets towards the cardinal directions, fortification walls, and two distinct town areas. The upper town is intended for the local elite, while the lower town houses common people. The team also plans large buildings for collective purposes and chooses bricks as the usual material. The project follows precise planning methods used in large Harappan cities.
activities.prompt: If the town planner assigns common people to the upper town instead of the local elite, what would likely change?
options: The expected social arrangement of the two town parts would be reversed.
The two distinct town parts would merge into one.
The streets would no longer be placed towards the cardinal directions.
The large collective-purpose buildings would become separate houses.

why.The two distinct town parts would merge: Changing residents does not merge the two parts.
why.The streets would no longer be placed to: Changing housing does not change street directions.
why.The large collective-purpose buildings w: Changing residents does not change collective building purposes.

activities.explanation: This reverses the stated housing arrangement.

activities.context: Imagine that a town-planning team is learning from Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, the first two Harappan cities to be discovered. Their planned layouts provide a model: streets towards the cardinal directions, fortification walls, and two distinct town areas. The upper town is intended for the local elite, while the lower town houses common people. The team also plans large buildings for collective purposes and chooses bricks as the usual material. The project follows precise planning methods used in large Harappan cities.
activities.prompt: If the team wants its large collective-purpose buildings to follow the usual Harappan practice, what should it do?
options: Build most of those buildings with bricks.
Build all of those buildings with non-brick materials.
Use bricks for the walls but not for the collective buildings.
Leave the material undecided because the buildings serve collective purposes.

why.Build all of those buildings with non-br: This departs from the usual building practice.
why.Use bricks for the walls but not for the: The material choice concerns the buildings themselves.
why.Leave the material undecided because the: Collective use does not remove the usual material pattern.

activities.explanation: Most such buildings were generally made of bricks.

activities.prompt: Explain how the planned layout of large Harappan cities helped organise people and their surroundings.
activities.answer: Large Harappan cities were built according to precise plans. Many streets were placed towards the cardinal directions, and most cities had fortification walls and two distinct parts. The upper town probably housed the local elite, while common people lived in the lower town. Some large buildings served collective purposes.
points: Cities followed precise plans.
Many streets faced the cardinal directions.
Most cities had walls and two distinct parts.
The two parts housed different social groups.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student visits a home in Mohenjo-daro and notices a separate bathing area. The home's bathing area is connected to a larger network of drains below the streets, which carries waste water away. The student also learns that people drew water from hundreds of brick-built wells. At Dholavira, most large reservoirs are linked by underground drains for water harvesting and distribution.
activities.prompt: If a blockage stopped the larger drain from working, what would be the most likely result in the student's home?
options: Waste water could collect in the bathing area because it could not be carried away.
The home would receive more water from the surrounding wells.
The bathing area would become connected to a reservoir.
Waste water would be stored underground for later use.

why.The bathing area would become connected: The case mentions no reservoir connection.
why.Waste water would be stored underground: Nothing indicates that waste water was stored.

activities.explanation: This follows the drain's stated purpose.

activities.context: A student visits a home in Mohenjo-daro and notices a separate bathing area. The home's bathing area is connected to a larger network of drains below the streets, which carries waste water away. The student also learns that people drew water from hundreds of brick-built wells. At Dholavira, most large reservoirs are linked by underground drains for water harvesting and distribution.
activities.prompt: Suppose workers at Dholavira want to improve water harvesting and distribution between reservoirs. Which plan best matches the system described?
options: Connect most reservoirs with underground drains.
Give every reservoir a separate bathing area.
Connect each home to one reservoir but leave the reservoirs unlinked.
Replace the reservoir links with brick-built wells inside homes.

why.Connect each home to one reservoir but l: Home connections would not link reservoirs.
why.Replace the reservoir links with brick-b: Brick wells are associated with Mohenjo-daro.

activities.explanation: This matches the described reservoir network.

activities.prompt: Explain how Harappan bathing and drainage arrangements helped with water management and cleanliness.
activities.answer: Harappans gave great importance to water management and cleanliness. They often had separate bathing areas in their homes. These areas were connected to a larger network of drains below the streets. The drains carried waste water away, helping keep the home and its surroundings clean.
points: Harappans valued water management.
They valued cleanliness.
Homes had separate bathing areas.
Underground drains carried waste water away.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A family lives in a Harappan settlement beside a small river. The river enriches the soil around their fields, where they grow barley, pulses and vegetables. They also grow cotton and weave cloth from it, while making tools such as the plough for farming. At the busy dockyard nearby, traders receive and send boats carrying cotton, timber, ornaments and other goods. Some traders travel inland, while others use the river or the sea.
activities.prompt: Why is the family's choice to farm beside the river sensible?
options: The river can improve soil fertility and help crops grow well.
The river makes the soil poorer, so the family should move to another field.
The plough alone can enrich the soil even beside a river with poor soil.
The family can farm there because animals, rather than the river, improve the soil.

why.The river makes the soil poorer, so the: This reverses what rivers do to nearby soil.
why.The plough alone can enrich the soil eve: A plough is a farming tool, but it does not enrich soil by itself.
why.The family can farm there because animal: Domesticated animals provide meat; they do not improve the soil here.

activities.explanation: Richer soil gives crops better growing conditions.

activities.context: A family lives in a Harappan settlement beside a small river. The river enriches the soil around their fields, where they grow barley, pulses and vegetables. They also grow cotton and weave cloth from it, while making tools such as the plough for farming. At the busy dockyard nearby, traders receive and send boats carrying cotton, timber, ornaments and other goods. Some traders travel inland, while others use the river or the sea.
activities.prompt: If traders cannot use the river route, what should they consider doing with their goods?
options: Use land routes or the sea to carry the goods.
Keep all trade on the river because it is their only route.
Replace the boats with ploughs for moving the goods.
Stop trading at the dockyard and grow more food instead.

why.Keep all trade on the river because it i: Traders used several routes; the river was not the only one.
why.Replace the boats with ploughs for movin: Ploughs were farming tools, not means of transport.
why.Stop trading at the dockyard and grow mo: Growing more food would not transport goods to other settlements.

activities.explanation: Harappan traders used both land routes and the sea.

activities.prompt: Explain why Harappan settlements were often built along rivers and how farming benefited from this location.
activities.answer: Harappans settled along both large and small rivers. River water made the soil around them richer, helping crops such as barley, wheat, millets and sometimes rice grow. River locations also supported fishing and provided routes along which traders could move goods by boat.
points: Settlements were built along large and small rivers.
Rivers made the nearby soil richer.
The richer soil helped crops grow.
Rivers supported fishing and river transport.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a family discussion in Kalibangan, an adult points to the dry surroundings and explains that rainfall has reduced. The family remembers that the city’s earlier administration has disappeared. Archaeologists have found many objects made and used by Harappans, while the family also knows that Harappans designed games and toys for adults and children. As the community wonders what will happen next, they consider how people might move to the countryside and keep Harappan culture and technology alive.
activities.prompt: If reduced rainfall continues and the drier phase lasts, what is the most likely change in where the people of Kalibangan will live?
options: They will leave the city and settle in the surrounding countryside.
They will remain in the city and continue its old urban life.
They will settle in rural settlements but stop passing on their culture and technology.
They will remain in the city and build an army to guard it.

why.They will remain in the city and continu: Staying in the city ignores the pattern in which cities were abandoned one by one.
why.They will settle in rural settlements bu: Moving to rural settlements did not require people to lose their culture and technology.
why.They will remain in the city and build a: The evidence describes a relatively peaceful civilisation and gives no support for creating an army.

activities.explanation: Reduced rainfall and the drier phase make continued city life less likely, so moving to rural settlements fits the pattern.

activities.context: During a family discussion in Kalibangan, an adult points to the dry surroundings and explains that rainfall has reduced. The family remembers that the city’s earlier administration has disappeared. Archaeologists have found many objects made and used by Harappans, while the family also knows that Harappans designed games and toys for adults and children. As the community wonders what will happen next, they consider how people might move to the countryside and keep Harappan culture and technology alive.
activities.prompt: As people move from the city to rural settlements, what should they do with Harappan culture and technology?
options: Pass culture and technology to the next phase while living in rural settlements.
Stop passing on culture because the cities no longer exist.
Pass on only games and toys while leaving other achievements behind.
Wait for the earlier administration to return before sharing knowledge.

why.Stop passing on culture because the citi: The disappearance of cities did not mean that Harappan culture also disappeared.
why.Pass on only games and toys while leavin: Harappan culture and technology were broader than games and toys.
why.Wait for the earlier administration to r: The earlier administration no longer existed, so there is no evidence that it would return.

activities.explanation: This matches the evidence that Harappan culture and technology survived and passed on.

activities.prompt: Explain why the Harappan cities were abandoned despite the civilisation’s achievements.
activities.answer: The cities were abandoned as the civilisation fell apart during a climatic change that reduced rainfall and created a drier phase. There is no trace of warfare or invasion, so conquest does not explain the decline. Many inhabitants adopted rural lifestyles, and the earlier administration disappeared.
points: Reduced rainfall and a drier phase caused changes in the environment.
There is no evidence of warfare or invasion.
Cities were abandoned one by one.
Many inhabitants adopted rural lifestyles, and administration disappeared.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: The Beginnings of Indian Civilisation

activities.prompt: Civilisation means an advanced ______ of human society.
activities.hint: This word describes one part of society's journey.
activities.explanation: An advanced stage means a society with organised life and many activities.

activities.prompt: Match each Harappan place, material or bead to its fact.
activities.explanation: Each place or material was important. You matched them correctly!

activities.prompt: Put the steps for making bronze in order.
activities.explanation: Harappans learned to work copper well. Adding tin to copper made bronze.

activities.prompt: What did a climatic change cause in the Harappan civilisation?
options: Reduced rainfall and a drier phase
New trade routes across the sea
More cities in the Indus plains
A larger urban population

activities.explanation: The Indus River had five main tributaries. You remembered this well!

activities.explanation: Each part helps society work, grow or express itself. Nice matching!

units.title: Our Cultural Heritage and Knowledge Traditions

chapters.title: India's Cultural Roots
chapters.summary: In this chapter: india's cultural roots and the vedas; vedic society; upanishads, vedanta and yoga; buddhism and the buddha.

lessons.title: India's Cultural Roots and the Vedas

activities.prompt: What old stories shaped India's culture? What do the Vedas say?
activities.explanation: Read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of India’s Cultural Roots
activities.body:
Imagine standing along India’s cultural path, wondering where its earliest roots began. You find that Indian culture is thousands of years old.

Some roots lead to the Indus civilisation. You also meet schools of thought, which are groups of thinkers sharing similar ideas.

Now enter the world of the Vedas. The four are the Rig Veda, Yajur Veda, Sama Veda and Atharva Veda.

You listen as rishis and rishikas sing thousands of hymns, written as poems and songs. These hymns were composed in the Sapta Sindhava region.

You hear the hymns recited aloud, rather than written down. You see the texts memorised and passed on with very few changes. The hymns addressed deities such as Indra, Agni and Varuṇa. Finally, your tour reaches the last Rig Veda mantras, which call for unity among people.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Roots, Thinkers and Vedas
activities.body: Indian culture is thousands of years old. Some of its roots go back to the Indus civilisation. Schools of thought are groups of thinkers. They share similar ideas. The four Vedas are the Rig Veda, Yajur Veda, Sama Veda and Atharva Veda. They have thousands of hymns. Hymns are poems and songs. People said them out loud. People learned the texts by heart. They passed them on with very few changes.
keyPoints: Some cultural roots go back to the Indus civilisation.
Schools of thought share similar ideas.
The four Vedas contain thousands of hymns.
activities.explanation: These facts join India's long culture with its thinkers, Vedas and hymns.

activities.prompt: A child wonders how thousands of Vedic hymns survived when people did not write them down.
steps: The hymns were recited aloud, so people could pass them without writing.
The texts were memorised, so each singer could repeat them from memory.
The texts were passed on with very few changes, so the words stayed nearly the same.
Therefore, careful memory and oral sharing helped preserve thousands of hymns.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which words mean a group of thinkers who have similar ideas?
options: Schools of thought
Groups of pupils
Ancient trade routes
Types of Vedas
activities.explanation: A school of thought is a group of thinkers with similar ideas.

activities.prompt: Rishis and rishikas composed the hymns in an early form of ______.
activities.hint: Think of the language named in the lesson.
activities.explanation: Rishis and rishikas used an early form of Sanskrit.

activities.prompt: Match each fact to the idea it explains.
pairs: the language used by rishis and rishikas
gods that the hymns call to
a call for people to unite
activities.explanation: Great matching! Each pair links a place, language, group or message.

activities.prompt: Put the steps for passing on the hymns in order.
items: Rishis and rishikas made the hymns.
People said the hymns out loud.
People learned the texts by heart.
People passed the texts on with few changes.
activities.explanation: People made the hymns, said them out loud, learned them by heart, then passed them on.

activities.prompt: Why did the Vedic texts stay almost the same over time?
options: People wrote new versions every year.
People remembered them and passed them on.
People translated them into everyday language.
People sang only the last verse.
activities.explanation: People remembered the texts and passed them on with very few changes.

activities.prompt: A guide says the old Vedic texts stayed almost the same. Which fact explains why?
options: They were spoken to many gods.
They were poems and songs.
They were recited aloud, memorised and passed on.
They were made in the Sapta Sindhava region.
activities.explanation: Reciting aloud and memorising helped the texts stay almost the same.

activities.prompt: The hymns were recited aloud instead of being written down. People memorised and passed them on with very few changes. Why did this help preserve them?
options: Because each person repeated the words they had learned.
Because each person chose new words during every recital.
Because writing down the hymns was their main method.
Because people stopped passing the hymns to others.

why.Because each person chose new words duri: Choosing new words would change the hymns instead of preserving them.
why.Because writing down the hymns was their: The hymns were recited aloud, not written down.
why.Because people stopped passing the hymns: Passing hymns to others helps preserve them rather than stop them.

activities.explanation: Memorising and repeating the words kept the hymns nearly unchanged.

activities.prompt: One singer changes many words in every hymn. Another singer memorises and repeats the same words. Which singer passes the hymn on with fewer changes?
options: The second singer, because memorised words change less.
The first singer, because new words make the hymn richer.
The first singer, because changed words are easier to remember.
Neither singer, because every oral hymn must change greatly.

why.The first singer, because new words make: Changing words does not help keep the hymn nearly the same.
why.The first singer, because changed words: Changed words are not easier to remember than memorised words.
why.Neither singer, because every oral hymn: The facts show that oral hymns could pass on with very few changes.

activities.explanation: Memorised hymns were passed on with very few changes.

activities.prompt: The last Rig Veda mantras call for unity among people. Two classes want different games. What choice best follows this teaching?
options: They choose one game that both classes can play together.
They let one class choose while the other class waits.
They choose separate games so each class stays apart.
They pick a game that helps only one class win.

why.They let one class choose while the othe: Making one class wait does not show unity.
why.They choose separate games so each class: Keeping the classes apart does not follow the call for unity.
why.They pick a game that helps only one cla: Helping only one class win does not show unity among people.

activities.explanation: Unity means finding an activity that both classes can share.
