lessons.title: Vedic Society

activities.prompt: What would you discover on a journey into Vedic society?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Vedic Society
activities.body:
You begin your journey through Vedic society by meeting the janas, or clans. These groups formed early Vedic society. The Rig Veda lists more than 30 of them. You can imagine them spread across different regions.

As you travel, you hear about the Bharatas, Purus, Kurus and Yadus. Each clan was linked to a region in the northwest of the Subcontinent.

Now you arrive at a puzzling part of the tour. Here, you find that little is known about how the janas governed their society. The Vedas mention a king or ruler, using the word rājā. You also hear of the sabha and samiti, names for collective gatherings.

Next, you walk through a busy world of work. Vedic texts mention many different professions. Farmers, weavers, potters, builders and carpenters all appear. Here, you also find healers and priests.

As your tour ends, you see clans, regions, gatherings and workers. Every stop reminds you how varied Vedic society was. Some details remain hidden, especially about how clans governed themselves. The Vedas give you clues, but not a complete picture.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Clans, gatherings and work
activities.body: Early Vedic society had groups called janas. Janas were clans. The Rig Veda lists more than 30 janas. Bharatas, Purus, Kurus and Yadus are examples. Each clan was linked to an area. That area was in the northwest of the Subcontinent. The Vedas mention a king or ruler called rājā. Sabha and samiti were gatherings of people. Vedic society also had farmers, weavers, potters, builders, carpenters, healers and priests.
keyPoints: Janas were clans in early Vedic society.
The Vedas mention rulers, gatherings and many jobs.
Each clan was linked to an area in the northwest.
activities.explanation: These facts introduce clans, rulers, gatherings and work in Vedic society.

activities.prompt: A child wants to draw a picture of how people lived together in early Vedic society. How can the evidence guide the picture?
steps: Early Vedic society was organised into janas, so people belonged to clans.
Each clan had a link to a region, so the picture can show clans in different areas.
The Vedas mention collective gatherings, so the picture can show people meeting together.
We know little about how janas governed, so the picture cannot show every rule clearly.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which word names the clans in early Vedic society?
options: professions
janas
gatherings
regions
activities.explanation: Janas were the clans that organised early Vedic society.

activities.prompt: The Rig Veda names more than 30 janas.
activities.explanation: The Rig Veda names more than 30 janas.

activities.prompt: Early Vedic society was split into ______. These were clans.
activities.hint: The concept card explains this word.
activities.explanation: Janas were clans. They made up early Vedic society.

activities.prompt: Match each term with its description.
activities.explanation: The Vedas call a king or ruler rājā. Sabha and samiti are names for gatherings. Carpenters had a Vedic job.

activities.prompt: In the Vedas, what are Sabha and samiti?
options: farmers and priests
rājā and the Bharatas
meetings of many people
the Kurus and Yadus
activities.explanation: Sabha and samiti were names for meetings of many people.

activities.prompt: What can we say about how the janas ruled their society?
options: Their rule is fully described.
Every jana had the same ruler.
Only the Bharatas had rulers.
We know little about it.
activities.explanation: We know little about how the janas ruled their society.

activities.prompt: The Vedas clearly explain how each jana was ruled.
activities.explanation: We know little about how the janas ruled their society.

activities.prompt: Which statement about each jana's region is correct?
options: No jana was linked to a region.
Each was linked to a northwest region of the Subcontinent.
Each was linked to a southeast region.
Each was linked to a gathering.
activities.explanation: Each clan was linked to a region in the northwest of the Subcontinent.

activities.prompt: A clan has a shared problem and needs a group decision. What can we expect?
options: Members may meet in a collective gathering.
Members may gather alone and make no decision.
One member may speak for the whole clan.
Members may avoid speaking to anyone else.

why.Members may gather alone and make no dec: This wrongly assumes that groups could not make decisions.
This wrongly assumes one member always decided for everyone.
why.Members may avoid speaking to anyone els: This wrongly assumes clans did not use gatherings.

activities.explanation: Sabha and samiti were collective gatherings, so a group could meet.

activities.prompt: Two janas belong to regions in the northwest Subcontinent. What does this suggest?
options: Each clan had a connection to its own region.
Each clan moved constantly and had no region.
All janas shared exactly the same region.
Only one clan had any regional connection.

why.Each clan moved constantly and had no re: This wrongly treats regional links as if they did not exist.
why.All janas shared exactly the same region: This wrongly makes separate regions into one shared region.
why.Only one clan had any regional connectio: This wrongly thinks only one clan had a regional link.

activities.explanation: Each clan was linked to a region in the northwest.

lessons.title: Upanishads, Vedanta and Yoga

activities.prompt: How can old ideas help you understand yourself and the world?
activities.explanation: Read on to find out.

activities.title: Journey Through Upanishad Ideas
activities.body:
You begin with the Upanishads, which built on Vedic ideas and introduced new ideas. Imagine walking through a garden of questions about life, rebirth and what you truly are. Here, you learn about rebirth and the idea of karma.

Now you meet brahman, the divine essence. You also meet ātman, or the Self. The ātman is the divine essence present in every being.

As you wander further, you see that everything in the world is connected. One prayer wishes that all creatures may be happy. You imagine its wish reaching every creature.

Next, you enter the world of schools of thought. Several schools of thought grew from the Vedas. These schools became foundations of Hinduism as it is understood today.

Finally, you discover yoga. Yoga developed methods for realising brahman in your consciousness. Through these methods, you practise bringing your awareness within.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Ideas from the Upanishads
activities.body: The Upanishads built on Vedic ideas. They added new ideas. They taught about rebirth and karma. Rebirth means being born again after death. Brahman is the divine essence. Ātman means the Self. Ātman is in every living being. The Upanishads teach that everything is connected. One prayer asks for happiness for all creatures. Some schools grew from the Vedas. They became the base of Hinduism. Yoga developed ways to truly know brahman in the mind.
keyPoints: The Upanishads taught about rebirth and karma.
Brahman is the divine essence. Ātman is the Self.
Yoga developed ways to truly know brahman.
activities.explanation: These ideas show what the Upanishads thought about life and the Self.

activities.prompt: A child wonders why a school prayer wishes happiness for every creature.
steps: The prayer treats every creature as part of one connected world.
The Upanishads teach that everything in the world is connected.
This shared connection explains the prayer’s wish for all creatures.
Therefore, the prayer reflects Upanishad teaching about universal connection.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Ideas taught by the Upanishads
activities.prompt: Which idea comes from the Upanishads?
options: A belief in rebirth and karma
Life ends completely after death
A rule against any rebirth
Karma has no importance
activities.explanation: The Upanishads taught rebirth and karma.

activities.title: Everything is connected
activities.prompt: The Upanishads say everything in the world is connected.
activities.explanation: The Upanishads teach that everything in the world is connected.

activities.title: The meaning of ātman
activities.prompt: In the Upanishads, ātman means ______.
activities.hint: This is another name for the inner self.
activities.explanation: Ātman is another name for the Self.

activities.title: Ideas and their meanings

activities.explanation: Each pair matches an important idea with its correct word.

activities.title: Schools of thought
activities.prompt: Which sentence about schools of thought is true?
options: Several schools grew from the Vedas in the first millennium BCE.
Schools of thought grew only from later debates.
The Vedas stopped all schools from growing.
Only one school of thought grew from the Vedas.

activities.title: What Yoga is for
activities.prompt: Yoga was made to keep brahman apart from consciousness.
activities.explanation: Yoga made ways to realise brahman in one's consciousness.

activities.title: A wish for all creatures
activities.prompt: One prayer wants all creatures to be ______.
activities.hint: This word tells what the prayer wants for creatures.
activities.explanation: The prayer wants all creatures to be happy.

activities.title: Understanding our connections
activities.prompt: Which idea matches what the Upanishads teach about the world?
options: Everything in the world is connected.
Only people share the holy essence.
Each creature is totally separate.
All creatures are left out of the prayer.
activities.explanation: The Upanishads teach that everything in the world is connected.

activities.prompt: A child notices a prayer wishing every creature happiness. What idea about the world does this prayer show?
options: The child thinks every creature matters because all life is connected.
The child thinks happiness matters only for people in the school.
The child thinks creatures are connected only when they eat together.
The child thinks prayer works only when every person feels happy.

why.The child thinks happiness matters only: This mistake limits the prayer’s concern to people.
why.The child thinks creatures are connected: This mistake replaces a universal bond with one narrow action.
why.The child thinks prayer works only when: This mistake treats the prayer as a rule for people’s feelings.

activities.explanation: This is right because the Upanishads teach that everything is connected.

lessons.title: Buddhism and the Buddha

activities.prompt: How can we understand why people suffer?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Buddha’s Journey
activities.body:
You begin your journey in India. There, a school of thought does not accept Vedic authority. You meet Siddhārtha Gautama, born as a prince in Lumbini. Soon, you face questions about human suffering.

At twenty-nine, you see an old person, a sick person and a dead body. These sights make you leave palace life. You search for the cause of human suffering.

You follow his path beneath a pipal tree, where he attains enlightenment. He teaches that ignorance and attachment cause suffering. People need sincere inner discipline. He also teaches ahimsa, meaning non-hurting or non-injuring.

After enlightenment, you see him found the Sangha. This community includes monks and later nuns. Buddhism has enormous influence across India and Asia. You also learn about the Buddha’s former births through the Jataka tales.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Gautama's Search
activities.body: Buddhism is a school of thought. It is a set of shared ideas. It did not accept Vedic authority. Siddhārtha Gautama was born a prince in Lumbini. At 29, he saw an old person, a sick person and a dead body. He left the palace. He searched for the cause of human suffering. He sat under a pipal tree and meditated. He gained enlightenment. Enlightenment means deep understanding. He taught that ignorance and attachment cause suffering.
keyPoints: Gautama left the palace to search for the cause of suffering.
Ignorance and attachment cause suffering.
Ahimsa means not hurting or injuring.
activities.explanation: These ideas came from Gautama's search for the cause of suffering.

activities.prompt: A child sees old age, sickness, and death. The child asks why people suffer.
steps: Because he saw old age, sickness, and death, Gautama left palace life.
To find the cause of suffering, he meditated under a pipal tree.
After enlightenment, he taught that ignorance and attachment cause suffering.
Therefore, he taught ahimsa and asked for sincere inner discipline.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: A Prince in Lumbini
activities.prompt: What was Siddhārtha Gautama at birth?
options: A prince
A monk
A merchant
A farmer
activities.explanation: Gautama was born a prince in Lumbini.

activities.title: A Different Way of Thinking
activities.prompt: Buddhism did not accept ______ authority.
activities.hint: Pick the authority Buddhism said no to.
activities.explanation: Buddhism was a way of thinking that did not accept Vedic authority.

activities.title: Learning Buddhist Ideas
activities.prompt: Match each Buddhist idea or place with its meaning.
pairs: Group of monks and, later, nuns
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a meaning from this lesson.

activities.title: Gautama's Life
activities.prompt: Put these events from Gautama's life in order.
items: Gautama was born as a prince in Lumbini.
At 29, Gautama saw an old person, a sick person and a dead body.
Gautama left the palace and searched for the cause of human suffering.
After he meditated under a pipal tree, he reached enlightenment.
activities.explanation: Gautama searched for answers. He meditated, or sat quietly, under a pipal tree. He reached enlightenment.

activities.title: Stories from Earlier Lives
activities.prompt: What do the Jataka tales tell stories about?
options: The Sangha's daily work
Gautama's first day in the palace
The Buddha's earlier births
The pipal tree
activities.explanation: The Jataka tales tell stories about the Buddha's earlier births.

activities.prompt: At 29, Gautama saw old age, sickness, and death. Why did he leave palace life?
options: He wanted to find the cause of human suffering.
He disliked meeting older people near the palace.
He thought fighting illness would end human suffering.
He believed palace life was the best way to teach others.

why.He disliked meeting older people near th: This mistakes his search for understanding for dislike of older people.
why.He thought fighting illness would end hu: This mistakes his wish to understand suffering for a wish to fight it.
why.He believed palace life was the best way: This mistakes his search for the cause of suffering for confidence in palace teaching.

activities.explanation: This matches his search for the cause of human suffering.

activities.prompt: Two children argue, and one child wants to hit the other. Which response best follows ahimsa, meaning non-hurting?
options: Stop the hitting and speak without hurting anyone.
Hit back once so the fight feels fair for both.
Keep hitting until the other child finally apologises.
Promise revenge, even if you never hit anyone.

why.Hit back once so the fight feels fair fo: This mistakes fairness for permission to injure another person.
why.Keep hitting until the other child final: This treats an apology as a condition for stopping harm.
why.Promise revenge, even if you never hit a: This mistakes a threat of harm for non-hurting behaviour.

activities.explanation: Ahimsa means non-hurting, so stopping the hitting follows the teaching.

activities.prompt: A student follows every visible rule but hides careless choices inside. What does this show about inner discipline?
options: The student follows rules outside but lacks sincere inner discipline.
The student has sincere inner discipline because rules are followed.
The student shows that visible rules always change inner choices.
The student shows that inner discipline means hiding mistakes from others.

why.The student has sincere inner discipline: This assumes outward rule-following proves inner discipline is sincere.
why.The student shows that visible rules alw: This mistakes showing rules for changing inner choices.
why.The student shows that inner discipline: This mistakes hiding mistakes for practicing sincere inner discipline.

activities.explanation: Sincere inner discipline needs inner effort, not only outward rule-following.

activities.prompt: Buddhism did not accept Vedic authority. It had enormous influence across India and Asia. What does this show?
options: A school can gain wide influence without accepting Vedic authority.
Wide influence proves Buddhism later accepted Vedic authority.
Rejecting Vedic authority stops a school from gaining influence.
Only Vedic schools could influence places across Asia.

why.Wide influence proves Buddhism later acc: This assumes wide influence must mean accepting Vedic authority.
why.Rejecting Vedic authority stops a school: This treats rejection of Vedic authority as preventing influence.
why.Only Vedic schools could influence place: This wrongly limits wide influence to Vedic schools.

activities.explanation: The facts show that Buddhism gained wide influence while rejecting Vedic authority.

activities.prompt: A map marks Lumbini, Gautama's birthplace. It also marks Buddhist places across India and Asia. The Sangha had monks and later nuns. Which summary fits?
options: The Buddha, born in Lumbini, founded the Sangha in influential Buddhism.
A Buddhist community existed in every place marked on the map.
Gautama was born in Asia, while his Sangha stayed in Lumbini.
The map proves that only palace life influenced Buddhism across Asia.

why.A Buddhist community existed in every pl: This mistakes places marked Buddhist for places where the Sangha existed.
why.Gautama was born in Asia, while his Sang: This assumes a birthplace also fixed where the Sangha lived.
why.The map proves that only palace life inf: This wrongly credits palace life, which Gautama left.

activities.explanation: It connects the birthplace, Sangha, and Buddhism's enormous influence.

lessons.title: Jainism and Other Schools of Thought

activities.prompt: Ready to explore how different schools of thought see life?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Jainism and Other Schools
activities.body:
First, you hear that Jainism is said to have roots much older than Buddhism. Then you meet Prince Vardhamāna, born into a royal family. At thirty, he left home to seek spiritual knowledge. After twelve years, he achieved supreme wisdom. He became known as Mahāvīra, meaning “great hero”.

Your next stop reveals what “Jain” means. The word Jain comes from jina, meaning conqueror. This conquest means overcoming ignorance and attachments. You now follow his search for spiritual knowledge.

Back with Mahāvīra, you explore his teachings. They include ahimsa, anekāntavāda and aparigraha. Anekāntavāda teaches that truth has many aspects. Aparigraha means non-possession and limiting material belongings.

You then consider Jainism’s view of living things. It stresses the interconnectedness of all living creatures. In your mind, each living creature connects with others. You look beyond any one creature.

Finally, you visit the Chārvāka school. They believed that only the material world exists. You also learn that the Vedic, Buddhist and Jain schools shared important concepts.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Introducing Jainism
activities.body: Jainism is said to have roots much older than Buddhism. Prince Vardhamāna was born into a royal family. At 30, he left home to seek knowledge. After 12 years, he achieved supreme wisdom and became Mahāvīra, meaning great hero. Anekāntavāda teaches that truth has many aspects. Aparigraha means non-possession and limiting material belongings. Jainism stresses that all living creatures are interconnected. The Chārvāka school believed only the material world exists.
keyPoints: Jainism has roots much older than Buddhism.
Anekāntavāda teaches that truth has many aspects.
The Chārvāka school believed only the material world exists.
activities.explanation: These facts introduce Jainism, its teacher, and another school of thought.

activities.prompt: A child sees many things he does not need and feels pulled to buy them all. How should Jainism guide him?
steps: The child feels attached to many unnecessary things.
Jainism says real conquest means overcoming attachments.
So he should limit material belongings instead of collecting everything.
This follows aparigraha, which means non-possession.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What does jina mean?
options: A teacher
A conqueror
A king
A trader
activities.explanation: The word Jain comes from jina. Jina means conqueror.

activities.prompt: Aparigraha means ______.
activities.hint: This Jain teaching says to own few things.
activities.explanation: Aparigraha means non-possession. It means not keeping too many things.

activities.prompt: Match each word or phrase with its meaning.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a name or teaching and its meaning.

activities.prompt: What did Vardhamāna do at 30?
options: He was born into a royal family.
He became known as Mahāvīra.
He left home to look for spiritual knowledge.
He taught about things people own.
activities.explanation: At 30, Vardhamāna left home to look for spiritual knowledge.

activities.prompt: Put these events in the correct order.
items: A strong earthquake under the sea
The wave travels thousands of kilometres
Land near the coast is covered with water
activities.explanation: A strong earthquake can cause a tsunami. The wave travels far. It may cover land near the coast with water.

activities.prompt: Which statement about Jainism is true?
options: Jainism says all living creatures are connected.
Jainism teaches that truth has only one side.
Jainism teaches that only the material world exists.
Jainism teaches that people can own things with no limits.
activities.explanation: The lesson says Jainism stresses that living things are connected. The belief that only the material world exists belongs to the Chārvāka school.

activities.prompt: Prince Vardhamāna was born into a royal family. At thirty, he left home. What does this suggest?
options: He chose a spiritual path over royal life.
He chose royal life over a spiritual path.
He chose material wealth over royal duties.
He chose a palace over his family's advice.

why.He chose royal life over a spiritual pat: This wrongly says he chose royal life over spiritual knowledge.
why.He chose material wealth over royal duti: This wrongly turns his spiritual choice into a search for wealth.
why.He chose a palace over his family's advi: This wrongly guesses that he wanted a larger palace.

activities.explanation: He left home at thirty to seek spiritual knowledge.

activities.prompt: At a garden, a child pulls a living plant for fun. What does Jainism advise?
options: Leave the living plant completely unharmed.
Pull it because it is not a person.
Cut it to make himself a toy.
Save it only for his later use.

This wrongly thinks Jainism values only human life.
This focuses on using the plant instead of protecting it.
This delays harm instead of stopping it.

activities.explanation: Jainism stresses the interconnectedness of all living creatures.

activities.prompt: Two children see different sides of one disagreement. What does anekāntavāda advise?
options: Look for the many aspects of truth.
Trust one side without hearing the other.
Trust the other side without hearing one.
Call both children wrong without listening.

why.Trust one side without hearing the other: This chooses one side and ignores the other aspects.
why.Trust the other side without hearing one: This chooses the other side and ignores the first aspect.
why.Call both children wrong without listeni: This rejects both views instead of considering their aspects.

activities.explanation: Anekāntavāda teaches that truth has many aspects.

lessons.title: Folk and Tribal Roots

activities.prompt: How do communities pass traditions without using books?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Roots of Tradition
activities.body:
Imagine you walk through a community, following teachings passed by word of mouth. You hear teachings and practices shared without written texts. These form an oral tradition, where learning moves from person to person.

Next, you see how common people carry folk traditions. They pass these traditions on to one another. No written book is needed for this sharing.

Now you enter a tribal community. A tribe is a group of families or clans. They share a tradition of common descent. People often share culture and language and live close together. Some may live under a chief and hold no private property.

You look back at ancient India. There was no separate word for tribe there. Earlier biased judgements about tribal communities have mostly been abandoned. You also learn that, in 2011, India had 705 tribes with about 104 million people.

Finally, you notice threads joining folk, tribal and Hindu belief systems. Many concepts are similar across them. Deities, concepts, legends and rituals have moved between traditions. This long interaction has brought mutual enrichment. You leave remembering that mutual enrichment grows from long interaction.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: How Traditions Travel
activities.body: Oral traditions are teachings and practices passed on without written texts. Folk traditions pass through common people, while tribal traditions pass through tribes. A tribe includes families or clans with shared ancestry. These groups commonly share a culture and language and live close together. Some may have a chief and no private property. Folk, tribal and Hindu beliefs also share and exchange ideas.
keyPoints: Oral traditions need no written texts.
Folk traditions pass through common people.
Tribal traditions pass through tribes.
activities.explanation: Remember: these traditions are passed on through people and exchange.

activities.prompt: Children learn their village's customs from neighbours, not books. How can we understand this example?
steps: The people pass on teachings and practices by speaking and showing.
Because no written texts are used, this is an oral tradition.
Because common people pass them on, these customs are folk traditions.
Therefore, the village is preserving folk traditions through oral tradition.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which sentence describes oral traditions?
options: They are taught and passed on without writing.
They are taught only in written books.
Only one chief passes them on.
Only big cities use them.
activities.explanation: Oral traditions are passed on without writing.

activities.prompt: A ______ is a group of families or clans with shared ancestry.
activities.hint: This group has a shared tradition of common descent.
activities.explanation: A tribe can include families or clans with shared ancestry.

activities.prompt: Which sentence describes tribes?
options: They share a culture and language. They live close together.
They share a culture and language. They live far apart.
They live close together. They share no culture.
They own things alone. They live far apart.
activities.explanation: Tribes often share a culture and language. They live close together.

activities.prompt: Match each tradition with its description.
pairs: Teachings and practices passed on without written texts
Traditions passed on by common people
Folk, tribal and Hindu systems sharing similar concepts
activities.explanation: Each pair connects a tradition with the lesson's description.

activities.prompt: What happens when folk, tribal and Hindu beliefs share ideas?
options: They stay completely apart.
They help each other grow.
They all are written down.
They stop sharing ideas.
activities.explanation: Sharing between these beliefs has helped each one grow.

activities.prompt: In 2011, India had ______ tribes and about 104 million people.
activities.hint: This number counts India's tribes in 2011.
activities.explanation: The lesson says 705 tribes and about 104 million people.

activities.prompt: A teacher speaks and shows a craft. Learners follow without written lessons. What makes this an oral tradition?
options: Teaching and practice pass without written texts.
Only spoken words pass between learners.
Every learner must copy from a book.
The craft changes only after written notes.

This mistake treats oral tradition as spoken words only.
This mistake assumes written books are always needed.
why.The craft changes only after written not: This mistake assumes notes, not oral passing, cause the craft.

activities.explanation: This is correct because teachings and practices pass without written texts.

activities.prompt: Common people in a village share customs. Another group has families with shared descent. How does each group pass its traditions?
options: The first passes folk traditions; the second passes tribal traditions.
The first passes tribal traditions; the second passes folk traditions.
Both groups pass traditions only through written books.
Both groups pass traditions only to their leaders.

why.The first passes tribal traditions; the: This mistake swaps the two groups and confuses their identities.
why.Both groups pass traditions only through: This mistake assumes traditions need books instead of people passing them.
why.Both groups pass traditions only to thei: This mistake thinks only leaders can pass traditions.

activities.explanation: Common people pass folk traditions, while tribes pass tribal traditions.

activities.prompt: In 2011, India was counted as having 705 tribes. Ancient India had no separate word for tribe. What does this difference tell us?
options: The name and counting method differed between the times.
Ancient India had no communities sharing a descent.
Tribal communities began only after the year 2011.
Every ancient group was recorded as a separate tribe.

why.Ancient India had no communities sharing: This mistake confuses a missing name with missing communities.
why.Tribal communities began only after the: This mistake treats the 2011 record as the start of tribal communities.
why.Every ancient group was recorded as a se: This mistake assumes ancient groups were already counted as tribes.

activities.explanation: Ancient India lacked a separate name, while 2011 included a count.

activities.prompt: A community lives under a chief. It holds no private property. What can we say about its tribal life?
options: It matches two common features of tribal life.
It proves all tribes today have the same rules.
It means the community cannot share resources.
It shows private property is required for every chief.

why.It proves all tribes today have the same: This mistake turns a possibility into a rule for every tribe.
why.It means the community cannot share reso: This mistake assumes shared property prevents people from sharing resources.
why.It shows private property is required fo: This mistake assumes every chief must have private property.

activities.explanation: Chief leadership and no private property may occur in tribal life.

activities.prompt: Two traditions now share some deities, concepts, and legends. Rituals have also moved between them. Why can their beliefs and practices be similar?
options: Their long interaction has brought enrichment for both traditions.
One tradition completely destroyed all beliefs in the other.
Shared concepts prove that the two traditions are identical.
Similarities show that no exchange ever took place between them.

why.One tradition completely destroyed all b: This mistake imagines one tradition wiping out the other.
why.Shared concepts prove that the two tradi: This mistake thinks shared concepts make two traditions identical.
why.Similarities show that no exchange ever: This mistake says similarity proves no exchange took place.

activities.explanation: Long exchanges between traditions have brought mutual enrichment.

activities.context: A cultural club is preparing an oral presentation about India's ancient hymns. The club members have learned the verses by listening and repeating them, following the old practice of reciting the words aloud. Their teacher says the hymns were composed in the Sapta Sindhava region and preserved through memory with very few changes. They wonder whether writing every word on paper would change what the presentation represents.
activities.prompt: If the club replaces oral learning with copying every word onto paper, what would change?
options: The presentation would no longer follow the traditional way these hymns were preserved.
The club would preserve the words less carefully because writing them would remove the need to remember them.
The hymns would stop being songs because songs cannot be written as poems.
The Sapta Sindhava origin of the hymns would disappear because that origin was oral.

why.The club would preserve the words less c: Writing could assist memory, but it does not necessarily make people less careful.
why.The hymns would stop being songs because: The hymns were poems and songs even when they were recited aloud.
why.The Sapta Sindhava origin of the hymns w: A region's role in a hymn's origin does not depend on whether the hymn is written or spoken.

activities.explanation: The hymns were traditionally preserved through oral recitation, memorisation and passing them on.

activities.context: A cultural club is preparing an oral presentation about India's ancient hymns. The club members have learned the verses by listening and repeating them, following the old practice of reciting the words aloud. Their teacher says the hymns were composed in the Sapta Sindhava region and preserved through memory with very few changes. They wonder whether writing every word on paper would change what the presentation represents.
activities.prompt: The club wants its final statement to reflect the message of the last Rig Veda mantras. Which statement should it make?
options: People should work towards unity because the final Rig Veda mantras call for unity among people.
People should sing only to Agni because all the mantras address Agni.
People should keep the verses within the club because oral preservation works only when knowledge is hidden.
People should avoid discussing the deities because the final mantras reject all deity worship.

why.People should sing only to Agni because: The hymns address deities such as Agni, but not every hymn addresses Agni alone.
why.People should keep the verses within the: Oral preservation depended on memorisation and sharing, not on keeping verses hidden.
why.People should avoid discussing the deiti: The mantras call for unity and do not say that deity worship should be rejected.

activities.explanation: The last Rig Veda mantras specifically call for unity among people.

activities.prompt: How were the Vedas composed and passed on?
activities.answer: The Vedas contain thousands of hymns written as poems and songs. The Vedic hymns were recited aloud rather than being written down. Rishis and rishikas composed them in an early form of Sanskrit. The texts were memorised and passed on with very few changes.
points: The Vedas contain thousands of hymns.
The hymns are poems and songs.
They were recited aloud and composed in early Sanskrit.
They were memorised and passed on with very few changes.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Members of the Bharatas clan live in a region in the northwest of the Subcontinent. They need to discuss matters together, so they arrange a collective gathering. The Vedas use the word rājā for a king or ruler, although the clan’s own way of governing is not well known. When the gathering begins, the people also mention the many professions represented in their society, including farmers, weavers, potters, builders, carpenters, healers and priests.
activities.prompt: The Bharatas want to describe their gathering using a name found in the Vedic texts. What should they do?
options: Record the gathering as a sabha or samiti.
Record the gathering as a jana.
Record the gathering as a rājā.
Record the gathering as a profession.

A jana was a clan, not a meeting.
Rājā referred to a king or ruler.
Professions were kinds of work mentioned in Vedic society.

activities.explanation: Sabha and samiti were names for collective gatherings.

activities.context: Members of the Bharatas clan live in a region in the northwest of the Subcontinent. They need to discuss matters together, so they arrange a collective gathering. The Vedas use the word rājā for a king or ruler, although the clan’s own way of governing is not well known. When the gathering begins, the people also mention the many professions represented in their society, including farmers, weavers, potters, builders, carpenters, healers and priests.
activities.prompt: Why is it reasonable for farmers, weavers, potters, builders, carpenters, healers and priests to be connected with Vedic society?
options: The texts acknowledge many kinds of work and include every role in this group.
The texts acknowledge only one kind of work, so this group is too broad.
The texts use these job names for collective gatherings.
The texts list janas, so every occupation must be a clan.

why.The texts acknowledge only one kind of w: Farmers, weavers, potters, builders and carpenters were among them.
why.The texts use these job names for collec: Healers and priests were also mentioned.
why.The texts list janas, so every occupatio: These job names refer to work, not gatherings or clans.

activities.explanation: The Vedic texts mention many different professions.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between a jana and the terms sabha and samiti.
activities.answer: A jana was a clan, and the Rig Veda lists more than 30 janas. Bharatas, Purus, Kurus and Yadus were examples. Sabha and samiti were names for collective gatherings. Thus, jana refers to a social group, while sabha and samiti refer to meetings where people gathered together.
points: A jana was a clan.
The Rig Veda lists more than 30 janas.
Bharatas, Purus, Kurus and Yadus were examples.
Sabha and samiti were names for collective gatherings.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student was reading about the Upanishads and learned that they built on Vedic ideas while introducing new ideas about rebirth, karma, brahman and ātman. The student understood that ātman is the divine essence present in every being and that everything in the world is connected. On the way home, the student saw a small bird looking trapped near a bush. Remembering the prayer that all creatures may be happy, the student decided to free it carefully.
activities.prompt: Which response best shows how the student can apply the idea of connectedness to the bird?
options: Show care for the bird because ātman, the inner Self, is present in it too.
Leave the bird alone because only people possess ātman.
Help the bird only if it gives the student something in return.
Leave the bird alone because connectedness applies to ideas, not living beings.

why.Leave the bird alone because only people: Wrong: it wrongly limits ātman to people.
why.Help the bird only if it gives the stude: Wrong: it turns karma into a rule about rewards.
why.Leave the bird alone because connectedne: Wrong: it wrongly separates living beings from the idea of connectedness.

activities.explanation: Correct: every being, including the bird, has ātman.

activities.context: A student was reading about the Upanishads and learned that they built on Vedic ideas while introducing new ideas about rebirth, karma, brahman and ātman. The student understood that ātman is the divine essence present in every being and that everything in the world is connected. On the way home, the student saw a small bird looking trapped near a bush. Remembering the prayer that all creatures may be happy, the student decided to free it carefully.
activities.prompt: What should the student do if the bird cannot be freed safely alone?
options: Pull harder, because wanting happiness justifies any method.
Wait, because the bird's ātman means it needs no help.
Move away, because connectedness does not require action.
Ask another person for help so the bird can be released safely.

why.Pull harder, because wanting happiness j: Wrong: a wish for happiness does not justify harmful action.
why.Wait, because the bird's ātman means it: Wrong: having ātman does not remove the need for practical help.
why.Move away, because connectedness does no: Wrong: connectedness supports care rather than passivity.

activities.explanation: Correct: seeking help can allow the bird to be freed carefully.

activities.prompt: Explain how the ideas of brahman, ātman and Yoga are related.
activities.answer: Brahman is the divine essence, and ātman is that same essence as it is present in every being. Yoga developed methods for realizing brahman in one's own consciousness. Therefore, a person can use Yoga to become aware of the brahman within, which is also described through the idea of ātman.
points: Brahman is described as the divine essence.
Ātan is the divine essence present in every being.
Yoga developed methods for realizing brahman in consciousness.
Realizing brahman connects the ideas of Yoga and ātman.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: While preparing a school play about the Buddha, one student suggested hurting another actor during a disagreement to prove the meaning of ahimsa. Another said that the actors should first understand the teaching and discipline themselves. The play also shows Siddhārtha Gautama leaving palace life after seeing an old person, a sick person and a dead body, and later attaining enlightenment under a pipal tree.
activities.prompt: How should the students settle their disagreement while following the teaching of ahimsa?
options: Choose actions and words that do not injure anyone.
Make the threatened actor experience pain so everyone understands the lesson.
Ask the audience to decide whether the threat is acceptable.
Ignore the disagreement because only the final performance matters.

why.Ask the audience to decide whether the t: The students should make the decision themselves rather than pass it to the audience.
why.Ignore the disagreement because only the: Avoiding the disagreement would not put ahimsa into practice.

activities.explanation: This follows the teaching that ahimsa means non-hurting or non-injuring.

activities.context: While preparing a school play about the Buddha, one student suggested hurting another actor during a disagreement to prove the meaning of ahimsa. Another said that the actors should first understand the teaching and discipline themselves. The play also shows Siddhārtha Gautama leaving palace life after seeing an old person, a sick person and a dead body, and later attaining enlightenment under a pipal tree.
activities.prompt: If the actors memorize their lines but do not practise sincere inner discipline, what may happen according to the Buddha's teaching?
options: They may remain unaware of their attachments, so suffering can continue.
They will fully understand the teaching simply because they remember the words.
Their performance will prove that attachment is the only cause of every problem.
They will lose the need for discipline once the play ends.

why.They will fully understand the teaching: Memorizing words alone does not provide inner discipline.
why.Their performance will prove that attach: The teaching does not claim that attachment causes every problem.
why.They will lose the need for discipline o: The need for discipline does not disappear after a performance.

activities.explanation: Ignorance and attachment are taught to be causes of suffering.

activities.context: Prince Vardhamāna was born into a royal family. At 30, he left home to seek spiritual knowledge, and after 12 years he achieved supreme wisdom. People began calling him Mahāvīra, the “great hero,” while his followers took the name Jains from jina, “conqueror.” His teaching called for nonviolence, accepting many aspects of truth, limiting possessions, and respecting the connection among all living creatures. For them, conquest meant being free from ignorance and not clinging to things.
activities.prompt: A follower of Mahāvīra owns many material belongings and wants to follow his teaching more closely. What should the follower do?
options: Keep acquiring possessions without considering their effects on others.
Limit how many material belongings he keeps.
Use every possession only to gain a higher social position.
Keep all possessions because material objects are the only reality.

why.Keep acquiring possessions without consi: Aparigraha teaches limiting possessions, not endless acquisition.
why.Use every possession only to gain a high: Jain teaching does not make social position or greater possession the aim.
why.Keep all possessions because material ob: That reasoning follows the Chārvāka belief, not the Jain teaching on possessions.

activities.explanation: This directly follows the teaching about non-possession and material belongings.

activities.context: Prince Vardhamāna was born into a royal family. At 30, he left home to seek spiritual knowledge, and after 12 years he achieved supreme wisdom. People began calling him Mahāvīra, the “great hero,” while his followers took the name Jains from jina, “conqueror.” His teaching called for nonviolence, accepting many aspects of truth, limiting possessions, and respecting the connection among all living creatures. For them, conquest meant being free from ignorance and not clinging to things.
activities.prompt: A follower is about to harm a small living creature to take something. What should the follower do?
options: Leave the creature unharmed and respect its life.
Harm it when obtaining possessions seems more important.
Harm it because the material world is all that exists.
Set it aside while claiming that living beings have no connection.

why.Harm it when obtaining possessions seems: Jain conquest means overcoming attachments rather than placing possessions above life.
why.Harm it because the material world is al: The Chārvāka belief is different from the Jain teaching on life.
why.Set it aside while claiming that living: Jainism stresses that all living creatures are interconnected.

activities.explanation: Ahimsa supports avoiding harm, and Jainism stresses the connection among living creatures.

activities.context: Prince Vardhamāna was born into a royal family. At 30, he left home to seek spiritual knowledge, and after 12 years he achieved supreme wisdom. People began calling him Mahāvīra, the “great hero,” while his followers took the name Jains from jina, “conqueror.” His teaching called for nonviolence, accepting many aspects of truth, limiting possessions, and respecting the connection among all living creatures. For them, conquest meant being free from ignorance and not clinging to things.
activities.prompt: After Vardhamāna achieved supreme wisdom, why was the name Jain suitable for his followers?
options: Their victory was over ignorance and emotional clinging.
It showed that their leader had gained supreme wisdom.
It showed that their aim was to collect material belongings.
It showed that their leader accepted only the material world.

why.It showed that their leader had gained s: Supreme wisdom explains the title Mahāvīra, but not the meaning of Jains.
why.It showed that their aim was to collect: Conquest is not the collecting of belongings, which Jainism teaches followers to limit.
why.It showed that their leader accepted onl: Only the material world is the Chārvāka view, not the meaning of Jainism.

activities.explanation: Jina means conqueror, and conquest means overcoming ignorance and attachments.

activities.prompt: Explain how Vardhamāna’s life and the name “Jain” are connected.
activities.answer: Vardhamāna’s life shows a search for spiritual knowledge rather than royal life. He left home at 30 and, after 12 years, achieved supreme wisdom. He became Mahāvīra, meaning “great hero.” The name Jains came from jina, “conqueror,” describing conquest of ignorance and attachments.
points: Vardhamāna was born into a royal family.
He left home at 30 to seek spiritual knowledge.
After 12 years, he achieved supreme wisdom.
Jains comes from jina, meaning conqueror.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A group of families living close together shares a common descent, culture and language. Elders pass beliefs, legends and rituals to children through spoken teaching and community practices. People from nearby villages tell folk stories, and some families also follow Hindu beliefs. Children compare the stories, learn rituals from both sides, and combine ideas. As a result, the communities begin exchanging customs more often and learning from one another.
activities.prompt: What is likely to happen as the communities continue sharing customs and ideas?
options: The traditions may become mutually richer through continued interaction.
The traditions will remain completely separate because they began differently.
Only the tribal tradition will survive because it is shared by a tribe.
The folk tradition will disappear because its stories are not written down.

why.The traditions will remain completely se: The case already shows that different traditions can interact.
why.Only the tribal tradition will survive b: Folk traditions are also passed on, so they need not disappear.
why.The folk tradition will disappear becaus: A lack of written texts does not prevent traditions from being shared.

activities.explanation: Continued exchange allows each tradition to gain from the other.

activities.context: A group of families living close together shares a common descent, culture and language. Elders pass beliefs, legends and rituals to children through spoken teaching and community practices. People from nearby villages tell folk stories, and some families also follow Hindu beliefs. Children compare the stories, learn rituals from both sides, and combine ideas. As a result, the communities begin exchanging customs more often and learning from one another.
activities.prompt: If the communities exchange concepts, legends and rituals in both directions, what would be a reasonable result?
options: Each tradition could gain from the other.
Only the tradition that existed first would gain.
The traditions would gain nothing because they are different.
One tradition would have to disappear for both to continue.

why.Only the tradition that existed first wo: The given facts do not suggest that only one tradition benefits.
why.The traditions would gain nothing becaus: The case shows different traditions learning from one another.
why.One tradition would have to disappear fo: Mutual enrichment does not require a tradition to disappear.

activities.explanation: Exchange between traditions has brought mutual enrichment.

activities.prompt: How can oral tradition spread beliefs, legends and rituals among different communities?
activities.answer: Beliefs, legends and rituals can be transmitted through oral tradition, which does not require written texts. When folk, tribal and Hindu traditions exchange their ideas and practices, each can gain from the other. This long interaction has brought mutual enrichment while allowing different traditions to continue.
points: Oral tradition passes on teachings and practices without written texts.
Beliefs, legends and rituals can move between communities.
Exchange between traditions brings mutual enrichment.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

chapters.title: Unity in Diversity, or 'Many in the One'
chapters.summary: In this chapter: india’s rich diversity; food for all; textiles and clothing; festivals galore.

lessons.title: India’s Rich Diversity

activities.prompt: What will you discover on a journey across India?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: India’s Rich Diversity
activities.body:
Imagine boarding a train for a journey across India. You watch the land change. You see many kinds of dress and food. You hear languages that may sound familiar or unfamiliar. You also spot different scripts as your journey continues.

You may even meet people from other parts within your own region. People from different places may have different customs and traditions. You may notice their clothing, food and languages during your travels.

This variety of landscapes, cultures and ways of life is called India’s rich diversity. India has over 1.4 billion people, making such diversity unsurprising.

Have you heard of the Anthropological Survey of India? It is a national organisation. The survey covered 4,635 communities across all States of the country. It counted 325 languages written using 25 scripts.

Here, a migrant is someone living away from their birthplace or original community. India is presented as an example of unity in diversity.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: India’s Many Differences
activities.body: India’s rich diversity means its many landscapes, cultures and ways of life. A train journey shows changing landscapes, different dress and varied food. Languages you know or do not know may be heard. Scripts are different ways of writing languages. Customs and traditions are ways people live. People from other regions may live near you. India is an example of unity in diversity.
keyPoints: Train journeys show changing landscapes, dress and food.
Travellers may hear different languages and see different scripts.
People from other regions may share your region.
India’s variety is called its rich diversity.
activities.explanation: These facts show why India’s many differences can exist together.

activities.prompt: Why can people meet different cultures even in their own region?
steps: Other regions' people may live nearby, so diversity appears close to home.
Different places have different languages, scripts, customs and traditions.
India has over 1.4 billion people, so such differences are unsurprising.
These differences make India an example of unity in diversity.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Studying India's Communities
activities.body: The Anthropological Survey of India is a national group. It studied 4,635 communities in all States. It counted 325 languages. They are written in 25 scripts. India has over 1.4 billion people. This chapter says a migrant does not live near their birthplace or first community.
keyPoints: The survey studied communities in all States.
It counted languages and their scripts.
A migrant does not live near their birthplace or first community.
activities.explanation: The survey counted India's languages. This chapter also explains the word 'migrant'.

activities.prompt: Which example shows India’s rich diversity?
options: Seeing the same landscape, clothes and food everywhere
Seeing different landscapes, clothes and food
Finding that everyone has the same customs
Hearing only one language
activities.explanation: A trip across India shows many differences in scenery, clothes and food.

activities.prompt: Travellers hear only languages they know.
activities.explanation: Travellers may hear languages they know or do not know.

activities.prompt: Which person is a “migrant”?
options: Someone who lives near their birthplace and original community
Someone who lives beside their birthplace and original community
Someone who does not live near their birthplace or original community
Someone who stays near their birthplace and original community
activities.explanation: A migrant does not live near their birthplace or original community.

activities.prompt: Match each term with its meaning.
pairs: Someone who does not live near their birthplace or original community
Many different lands, cultures and ways of life
activities.explanation: Each pair matches a key term with its meaning in the lesson.

activities.prompt: The Anthropological Survey of India covered ______ communities in every State.
activities.hint: The survey reached communities in every State.
activities.explanation: The survey covered 4,635 communities in every State in the country.

activities.prompt: Put these ideas in order, from journey observations to India’s big idea.
activities.explanation: The journey shows India’s variety before the chapter names its central idea.

activities.prompt: One train crosses several regions. A traveller sees new foods, dress, languages and scripts. What does this journey show?
options: India has many kinds of people, places, languages and customs.
Every place in India has the same food, dress and language.
Only faraway places in India show signs of diversity.
Train journeys hide the differences between Indian regions.

why.Every place in India has the same food,: This mistake believes all Indian places are identical.
why.Only faraway places in India show signs: This mistake thinks diversity exists only far from home.
why.Train journeys hide the differences betw: This mistake believes train travel makes regional differences disappear.

activities.explanation: This is right because one journey reveals many differences across India.

activities.prompt: Within one region, a child meets people from another part of India. What does this show?
options: Every person in one region comes from the same place.
People from different parts can live close to home.
People from other parts never live near their birthplace.
Diversity appears only when someone crosses India's borders.

why.Every person in one region comes from th: This mistake thinks everyone in one region has one birthplace.
why.People from other parts never live near: This mistake thinks people never live near their birthplace.
why.Diversity appears only when someone cros: This mistake believes diversity appears only outside the country.

activities.explanation: This is right because people from other parts may live nearby.

activities.prompt: Different languages, customs and landscapes exist together in India. Why is 'unity in diversity' a fitting description?
options: India is diverse only when people stop sharing one country.
Different ways of life can exist within one shared country.
India shows diversity because all its people live alike.
Unity in diversity means every region has identical traditions.

why.India is diverse only when people stop s: This mistake thinks diversity and sharing a country cannot coexist.
why.India shows diversity because all its pe: This mistake thinks diversity means everyone lives in the same way.
why.Unity in diversity means every region ha: This mistake thinks unity requires identical traditions in every region.

activities.explanation: This is right because many differences can exist within one country.

lessons.title: Food for All

activities.prompt: How can shared ingredients create so many different dishes?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Indian Food
activities.body:
Imagine you begin a food tour across India. You will taste foods from different regions. Your journey starts with grains, the basic food for most Indians. You are ready to learn.

You explore a shared food landscape. You will find thousands, or even lakhs, of dishes and preparations. Some food grains are common throughout almost the whole country. Rice, barley and wheat are among the common cereals.

You also find pearl millet, sorghum and finger millet among the millets. Dals are among the pulses eaten in India.

Next, you meet familiar spices on your journey. Turmeric, cumin, cardamom and ginger are common spices used across India.

Here is the special secret of Indian food. Different combinations of shared ingredients create an endless variety of dishes. You return home with a new wonder. You now know how shared ingredients create endless variety. Your curiosity has led you to a delicious discovery.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.prompt: Two Indian families use many shared ingredients. Why can their meals still be very different?
steps: People eat foods from different regions, so their dishes may differ.
Shared grains and spices give cooks similar starting ingredients.
Different combinations of those ingredients create endless variety.
Thus, common ingredients and regional choices together explain India's many dishes.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which group has only common cereals?
options: Rice, barley and wheat
Pearl millet, sorghum and ginger
Turmeric, cumin and cardamom
Dals, barley and turmeric
activities.explanation: Rice, barley and wheat are common cereals.

activities.prompt: Staple grains are the basic food for most ______.
activities.hint: This word names the people who live in India.
activities.explanation: Staple grains provide the basic food for most Indians.

activities.prompt: What makes so many kinds of dishes possible?
options: Different mixes of shared ingredients
One shared recipe for every region
Only whole grains in every dish
Only one spice in every dish
activities.explanation: Shared ingredients can be mixed in different ways. This makes many kinds of dishes.

activities.prompt: Match each food description with its example.
activities.explanation: Staple grains, cereals, millets and pulses are grouped as shown.

activities.prompt: Put these foods in this order: cereal, pulse, spice.
activities.explanation: Wheat is a cereal. Dals are pulses. Turmeric is a spice.

activities.prompt: A cook mixes the same foods in different ways. What can the cook make?
options: Endless kinds of dishes
The same dish in every place
A dish with no shared foods
Only basic grains with no spices
activities.explanation: Different mixes of the same foods make endless kinds of dishes.

activities.prompt: A cook mixes dal, rice, and shared spices. What can the cook make?
options: Many dishes with different combinations.
Only one dish from these ingredients.
Only dishes found in one region.
No dish without a new ingredient.

This mistake thinks shared ingredients have only one possible combination.
This mistake thinks shared ingredients cannot differ across regions.
This mistake thinks every dish needs an ingredient from outside the shared list.

activities.explanation: Different combinations of shared ingredients create endless variety.

activities.prompt: A food map shows rice in one area and millets in another. What does the map show?
options: People's foods can differ across India's regions.
All regions eat exactly the same dishes.
Only millets are eaten across India.
Food choices never change between regions.

This mistake ignores the regional differences shown on the map.
This mistake treats one grain as the only food across India.
why.Food choices never change between region: This mistake thinks regional food choices never change.

activities.explanation: People eat foods from different regions, so their foods can differ.

activities.prompt: A family menu lists dal, rice, and wheat. What can we learn from the menu?
options: It includes a pulse and common cereals.
It includes spices and a common cereal.
It includes millets and a common spice.
It includes pulses and regional dishes.

This mistake treats dal as a spice and rice as something else.
This mistake treats the foods as millets and spices.
This mistake treats rice and wheat as regional dishes.

activities.explanation: Dal is a pulse, while rice and wheat are common cereals.

activities.prompt: Place A lists rice as basic food. Place B lists wheat. What can we say about both?
options: They are common cereals in India.
They are common spices in India.
They are examples of millets.
They are dals among pulses.

This mistake mixes up cereals with spices.
This mistake mistakes common cereals for examples of millets.
This mistake mixes up cereals with pulses.

activities.explanation: Rice and wheat are both among the common cereals.

lessons.title: Textiles and Clothing

activities.prompt: What can a length of cloth tell us about a place?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Indian Textiles
activities.body:
You begin your journey among Indian clothing. You see styles from many regions and communities. Each has developed its own style.

Traditional clothes differ in material, yet they share some features. A sari is a plain, unstitched length of cloth worn as clothing.

Saris may be made from cotton, silk or synthetic fabrics. Famous silk types include Banarasi, Kanjivaram, Paithani, Patan Patola, Muga and Mysore. You find hundreds of varieties, each with its own colours. Some designs are woven into the cloth, while others are printed afterwards.

Now, travel back to when Indian textiles were exported as far away as Europe. Chintz, a type of printed cotton, became very popular there.

England and France later banned imports of Indian chintz. They wanted to protect their own products. Your tour ends beside these traditions, each distinct, yet sharing some features.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Clothes Around India
activities.body: Every Indian region and community has developed its own clothing styles. Traditional Indian clothes share some features, even when their materials differ. A sari is a plain, unstitched length of cloth. Saris may use cotton, silk or synthetic fabrics. Their designs may be woven in or printed later. Indian textiles were once exported to Europe. Chintz became popular there. England and France later banned Indian chintz imports.
keyPoints: Indian regions and communities have developed their own clothing styles.
Traditional Indian clothes share some features.
A sari is a plain, unstitched length of cloth.
activities.explanation: Indian clothing styles vary, while traditional clothes still share some features.

activities.prompt: A child visits a cloth shop and sees saris made from cotton, silk and synthetic fabrics. They wonder why the saris can look very different.
steps: Saris can use cotton, silk or synthetic fabrics, because these are common sari materials.
They can still share some features, because traditional Indian clothes share features even when materials differ.
Their patterns can be woven in or printed later, because sari designs can be made in different ways.
Their colours can also vary greatly, so saris come in many varieties.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What Is a Sari?
activities.prompt: Which description matches a sari?
options: A plain, unstitched length of cloth
A type of printed cotton
A famous silk sari type
A design woven into cloth
activities.explanation: A sari is a plain, unstitched length of cloth worn as clothing.

activities.title: Common Sari Materials
activities.prompt: Saris are often made from cotton, silk or ______ cloth.
activities.hint: This is another common material for saris.
activities.explanation: Cotton, silk and synthetic cloth are all common sari materials.

activities.title: Famous Silk Saris
activities.prompt: Which one is a famous kind of silk sari?
options: Banarasi
Chintz
Cotton fabric
Plain length of cloth
activities.explanation: Banarasi is one of the famous silk saris.

activities.title: Clue Pairs
activities.prompt: Match each clue to the right answer.
pairs: A plain piece of cloth with no stitches
One way to make some sari designs
A reason to ban Indian chintz imports
activities.explanation: Each clue matches one fact about saris, chintz or cloth trade.

activities.title: Cloth Trade Events
activities.prompt: Put these events in the order they happened.
items: Chintz became very popular in Europe
England and France banned Indian chintz imports
activities.explanation: Cloth was sent to Europe first. Chintz became popular before the ban.

activities.title: Why Was Chintz Banned?
activities.prompt: Why did England and France ban imports of Indian chintz?
options: To protect their own products
To change chintz into a sari
To make every sari with no stitches
To stop weaving designs into cloth
activities.explanation: The ban was made to protect things made in England and France.

activities.prompt: Saris from two Indian regions use cotton and silk. What can we conclude?
options: Some traditional clothes can share features despite different materials.
Every sari must have exactly the same colours.
All Indian regions must wear one identical style.
Saris cannot be made from synthetic fabrics.

why.Every sari must have exactly the same co: This confuses shared features with identical colours.
why.All Indian regions must wear one identic: This confuses different regional styles with one identical style.
why.Saris cannot be made from synthetic fabr: This ignores that saris can also use synthetic fabrics.

activities.explanation: Traditional Indian clothes can share features even when their materials differ.

activities.prompt: A government wants to protect local cloth makers. What rule fits?
options: Ban imports of Indian chintz cloth.
Give free silk to every family.
Stop people from buying all cloth.
Make every sari exactly the same.

This gives material instead of following the import ban.
This stops too much buying instead of protecting one product.
This changes sari designs instead of controlling imports.

activities.explanation: England and France banned Indian chintz imports to protect their own products.

activities.prompt: England and France ban Indian chintz imports. What is likely next?
options: Imports of Indian chintz would likely fall.
Imports of Indian chintz would likely rise.
Every European shop would keep selling chintz.
Chintz would become only an Indian style.

why.Imports of Indian chintz would likely ri: This predicts the opposite effect of an import ban.
why.Every European shop would keep selling c: This ignores that banned chintz cannot enter freely.
why.Chintz would become only an Indian style: This changes the place of chintz instead of following its import ban.

activities.explanation: A ban on imports would reduce the amount of Indian chintz entering those countries.

lessons.title: Festivals Galore

activities.prompt: Ready to discover what India's festival map can show you?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Festival Tour of India
activities.body:
Imagine a festival tour of India. You will find an immense variety of festivals. You follow a map and imagine visiting celebrations across the country.

First, you visit places where a few festivals are celebrated across India. These common festivals are often celebrated at about the same time.

Your guide shows you a map. It displays similar festivals with different names across India around the same date. You begin to see the pattern.

During your journey, you learn about Makara Sankrānti. This festival marks the beginning of the harvest season in many parts of India. It is celebrated in many parts of India on or around January 14.

You continue exploring and see that many major festivals take place during October and November. The map helps you spot similar celebrations around the same date. You discover that similar festivals can have different names in different regions.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Festivals Across India
activities.body: India has many kinds of festivals. Some festivals are celebrated all over India. Common festivals often happen at about the same time. Similar festivals can have different names in different places. Makara Sankrānti starts the harvest season (the time when crops are cut) in many parts of India. It is celebrated on or around January 14. Many big festivals happen in October and November.
keyPoints: India has many different festivals.
Some festivals are celebrated all over India.
Similar festivals can have different names.
Makara Sankrānti starts the harvest season in many parts.
activities.explanation: Festivals bring different places together. This is true even if names or dates are different.

activities.prompt: Different festival names appear near January 14. Why might they be linked?
steps: The map shows similar festivals around one date, so names may differ.
Makara Sankrānti is one example of this pattern.
It is celebrated in many parts around January 14, showing the pattern.
Different names therefore do not always mean unrelated festivals.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What does the lesson say about festivals in India?
options: India has many kinds of festivals.
India has only one festival.
India has no festivals.
India celebrates festivals only in October.
activities.explanation: India has many kinds of festivals. So there are many celebrations to enjoy.

activities.prompt: Some festivals are celebrated across India.
activities.explanation: Yes, some festivals are celebrated across India.

activities.prompt: Makara Sankrānti marks the start of the ______ season in many parts of India.
activities.hint: Think about when farmers pick their crops.
activities.explanation: Makara Sankrānti marks the start of the harvest season in many parts of India.

activities.prompt: Match each place or time with its fact.
pairs: Similar festivals can have different names here.
This festival starts the harvest season in many parts.
activities.explanation: Each pair joins a place or time with a festival fact.

activities.prompt: Why can festivals in different places seem connected?
options: They may be celebrated at about the same time.
They must have exactly the same name.
They happen in the same month every year.
They are all harvest festivals.
activities.explanation: Common festivals are often celebrated at about the same time across India.

activities.prompt: What does the map show about festivals across India?
options: Similar festivals can have different names about the same date.
Every festival has one name everywhere.
Festivals only happen in one place.
All festivals mark the start of the harvest season.
activities.explanation: The map shows similar festivals with different names across India at about the same date.

activities.prompt: A map places festivals near one date. What might their names show?
options: The festivals may be similar but have different regional names.
The festivals must belong to completely different traditions.
One festival may be much older than the other.
The map proves both festivals happen in every region.

why.The festivals must belong to completely: This mistake treats different names as proof of different festivals.
why.One festival may be much older than the: This mistake gives the map meanings that it does not show.
why.The map proves both festivals happen in: This mistake assumes the map proves festivals happen everywhere.

activities.explanation: This is right because similar festivals can have different regional names.

activities.prompt: Makara Sankrānti begins the harvest season in many parts. Why celebrate it?
options: It marks the start of a new harvest season.
It marks the end of every festival in India.
It shows that harvest seasons never change.
It proves that all regions use one festival name.

why.It marks the end of every festival in In: This mistake assumes it ends all festivals in India.
why.It shows that harvest seasons never chan: This mistake assumes the harvest season never changes.
why.It proves that all regions use one festi: This mistake assumes every region must use one name.

activities.explanation: This is right because it marks the harvest season's beginning.

activities.prompt: Two common festivals happen together. What might a family need to do?
options: Choose between them, because their times may overlap.
Join both, because common festivals never happen together.
Join neither, because overlapping festivals cannot be similar.
Wait until January, because common festivals end early.

why.Join both, because common festivals neve: This mistake assumes common festivals never share a time.
why.Join neither, because overlapping festiv: This mistake assumes overlapping festivals must be unrelated.
why.Wait until January, because common festi: This mistake assumes all common festivals end before January.

activities.explanation: This is right because common festivals are often celebrated together.
