lessons.title: An Epic Spread

activities.prompt: How can stories spread so widely and still feel close to home?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Stories That Spread
activities.body:
Imagine opening two enormous storybooks. The Rāmāyaṇa and Mahābhārata might fill about 7,000 pages together.

In one, the Pāṇḍavas fight their cousins, the Kauravas, with Kṛiṣhṇa’s help. In the other, Rāma receives help from his brother Lakṣhmaṇa and from Hanuman.

Within these epics, shorter stories focus on values. They often ask what is right and what is wrong. These questions invite you to think about right and wrong.

Now visit the Pañchatantra, a collection of stories with animals as the main characters. These stories have been adapted into almost every Indian language. About 200 adaptations exist in more than 50 languages.

Next, listen to folk versions of the two great epics. Many communities have their own versions of the Rāmāyaṇa and the Mahābhārata. This variety shows how Indian culture values diversity while keeping sight of the unity that supports it.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Stories Across India
activities.body: The Rāmāyaṇa and Mahābhārata are two Sanskrit epics. Together, they might fill about 7,000 pages. They contain shorter stories about values, right and wrong, and people helping one another. The Pañchatantra uses animals as main characters. Its stories have many adaptations. Folk versions show that Indian culture values diversity and unity.
keyPoints: The two Sanskrit epics might fill about 7,000 pages together.
Shorter stories ask what is right and wrong.
Indian culture values diversity and unity.
activities.explanation: Great stories spread through many versions, languages and communities.

activities.prompt: Two children read an animal story. They read it in different Indian languages. Why is this possible?
steps: Different versions exist because Pañchatantra is adapted in almost every Indian language.
This reach happens because about 200 versions exist in over 50 languages.
These many forms show diversity, while Indian culture keeps sight of unity.
So children can share animal stories even when their language versions differ.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Two Great Epics
activities.prompt: Two epics together might fill about 7,000 pages. Which two epics are they?
options: The Rāmāyaṇa and Mahābhārata
The Pañchatantra and Rāmāyaṇa
The Rāmāyaṇa and Panchatantra
The Mahābhārata and Panchatantra
activities.explanation: The Rāmāyaṇa and Mahābhārata might fill about 7,000 pages together.

activities.title: Main Characters
activities.prompt: The Pañchatantra is a book of stories. Its main characters are ______.
activities.hint: Think of the main characters in a jungle story.
activities.explanation: Animals are the main characters in Pañchatantra stories.

activities.title: Match the Epic Facts
activities.prompt: Match each story with its fact.
pairs: Rāma gets help from Lakṣhmaṇa and Hanuman
The Pāṇḍavas fight their cousins, the Kauravas
Many groups have their own versions
activities.explanation: Each pair matches a story with a fact about it.

activities.title: Stories Across Languages
activities.prompt: Into which languages have Pañchatantra stories been adapted (retold)?
options: Only Sanskrit
Almost every Indian language
Only foreign languages
No Indian languages
activities.explanation: Pañchatantra stories have been retold in almost every Indian language.

activities.title: Build the Epic Fact
activities.prompt: Put the pieces in order to make a sentence about the Mahābhārata.
activities.explanation: The Pāṇḍavas fight their cousins, the Kauravas, with Kṛiṣhṇa’s help.

activities.prompt: Compare animal stories with Sanskrit epics. What is the main difference?
options: Animal stories use animals as their main characters.
Sanskrit epics use animals as their main characters.
Animal stories are about 7,000 pages together.
Sanskrit epics are collections of animal stories.

why.Sanskrit epics use animals as their main: This wrongly gives the Pañchatantra’s animal characters to the Sanskrit epics.
why.Animal stories are about 7,000 pages tog: This wrongly gives the epics’ possible length to the animal-story collection.
why.Sanskrit epics are collections of animal: This wrongly makes the epics a collection of animal stories.

activities.explanation: This is right because the Pañchatantra has animals as its main characters.

activities.prompt: A story asks what is right and wrong. What does this show?
options: The story is focused on values.
The story is focused on animal characters.
The story is focused on many language versions.
The story is focused on helping cousins fight.

why.The story is focused on animal character: This confuses values with the Pañchatantra’s animal characters.
why.The story is focused on many language ve: This confuses values with the stories’ many language adaptations.
why.The story is focused on helping cousins: This confuses values with the fight between the cousin groups.

activities.explanation: This is right because stories asking right and wrong focus on values.

activities.prompt: Children read folk epics and Pañchatantra versions. Many Indian languages are used. What big idea fits?
options: Indian culture values diversity while keeping sight of unity.
Indian culture values only one fixed story version.
Indian culture lets communities lose their shared unity.
Indian culture keeps every story in one language.

why.Indian culture values only one fixed sto: This wrongly assumes that diversity leaves only one fixed version.
why.Indian culture lets communities lose the: This wrongly assumes that different versions must remove unity.
why.Indian culture keeps every story in one: This wrongly assumes that different language versions do not belong together.

activities.explanation: This is right because many versions exist within a culture that values unity.

activities.context: During a train journey across India, a student sees changing landscapes, different kinds of dress and food, and people using different languages and scripts. In one region, the student meets people from other parts of the country and notices different customs and traditions. The Anthropological Survey of India studied 4,635 communities across all States and counted 325 languages written using 25 scripts, showing the country’s rich diversity.
activities.prompt: Why does the student notice unfamiliar languages, different scripts, and varied customs during the journey?
options: These differences are signs of India’s cultural variety.
All communities must follow exactly the same customs and traditions.
Only the landscapes change, while the communities remain culturally the same.
The journey must have crossed separate countries rather than one country.

why.All communities must follow exactly the: Incorrect: The journey shows customs that differ from place to place.
why.Only the landscapes change, while the co: Incorrect: Languages, scripts, dress, food, and customs also reveal differences.
why.The journey must have crossed separate c: Incorrect: The journey is across India and illustrates variety within one country.

activities.explanation: Correct: It connects several cultural differences with India’s diversity.

activities.context: During a train journey across India, a student sees changing landscapes, different kinds of dress and food, and people using different languages and scripts. In one region, the student meets people from other parts of the country and notices different customs and traditions. The Anthropological Survey of India studied 4,635 communities across all States and counted 325 languages written using 25 scripts, showing the country’s rich diversity.
activities.prompt: What does the survey’s finding of 325 languages written using 25 scripts suggest about India’s communities?
options: Many communities use languages and scripts that differ from one another.
All communities use one language and one script, so there is no variety.
Most communities speak without using any script at all.
The findings show only changing landscapes, not linguistic or cultural variety.

why.All communities use one language and one: Incorrect: One language and script would contradict the survey’s findings.
why.Most communities speak without using any: Incorrect: The finding specifically includes languages written using scripts.
why.The findings show only changing landscap: Incorrect: The survey results provide evidence of language and script diversity.

activities.explanation: Correct: The large number of languages and scripts indicates cultural variety.

activities.prompt: What does the term ‘migrant’ mean in this chapter, and how can a person fit this description?
activities.answer: In this chapter, a migrant is a person who does not live near their birthplace or original community. A person fits this description when they live away from the place where they were born or from the community to which they originally belonged.
points: Defines where a migrant lives.
Uses ‘birthplace’ correctly.
Uses ‘original community’ correctly.
Explains how the description applies to a person.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: At a family meal in India, a student sees rice and wheat served beside dals, pearl millet, and dishes seasoned with turmeric, cumin, cardamom, and ginger. The cook explains that staple grains are the basic food for most Indians, while shared ingredients are being combined in different ways. The student wonders why one meal can include so many different dishes and preparations.
activities.prompt: Why can one meal include many different dishes even when several ingredients are shared?
options: Changing the combinations of shared ingredients can produce many different preparations.
Shared ingredients always lead to one fixed dish across India.
The number of dishes depends only on how many spices are present.
Different dishes arise only when no ingredients are shared.

why.Shared ingredients always lead to one fi: It wrongly assumes shared ingredients always give one result.
why.The number of dishes depends only on how: It ignores combinations involving ingredients other than spices.
why.Different dishes arise only when no ingr: It wrongly says that different dishes require no shared ingredients.

activities.explanation: This applies the idea that changing combinations creates variety.

activities.context: At a family meal in India, a student sees rice and wheat served beside dals, pearl millet, and dishes seasoned with turmeric, cumin, cardamom, and ginger. The cook explains that staple grains are the basic food for most Indians, while shared ingredients are being combined in different ways. The student wonders why one meal can include so many different dishes and preparations.
activities.prompt: If the cook removes the dals but keeps the cereals and spices, what would happen at the meal?
options: A pulse-based dish would be missing, while cereal and spice dishes could remain.
Every grain-based dish would disappear because dals are the only grains.
The meal would stay unchanged because dals and cereals are the same food group.
Only the spice dishes would remain because spices can replace dals.

why.Every grain-based dish would disappear b: This wrongly treats dals as the only grains.
why.The meal would stay unchanged because da: This wrongly places dals and cereals in the same food group.
why.Only the spice dishes would remain becau: This wrongly suggests that spices can take the place of pulses.

activities.explanation: Dals are pulses, so removing them removes that kind of food from the meal.

activities.context: At a family meal in India, a student sees rice and wheat served beside dals, pearl millet, and dishes seasoned with turmeric, cumin, cardamom, and ginger. The cook explains that staple grains are the basic food for most Indians, while shared ingredients are being combined in different ways. The student wonders why one meal can include so many different dishes and preparations.
activities.prompt: What should the student conclude about Indian food after noticing both regional foods and shared ingredients?
options: Indian food can vary by region while still relying on ingredients shared across the country.
Indian food cannot vary because the same ingredients are used everywhere.
Indian food varies only because each region refuses to share ingredients.
Shared ingredients prevent regional foods from developing different dishes.

why.Indian food cannot vary because the same: This wrongly assumes common ingredients make all foods identical.
why.Indian food varies only because each reg: This wrongly says regional food variety results from refusing to share.
why.Shared ingredients prevent regional food: This wrongly claims that shared ingredients stop different dishes from developing.

activities.explanation: People eat foods from different regions, but some ingredients are shared widely.

activities.prompt: How are millets different from pulses such as dals?
activities.answer: The lesson places pearl millet, sorghum, and finger millet among millets, which are food grains. Dals, by contrast, are among the pulses eaten in India. Thus, both are eaten in India, but the lesson identifies them as different kinds of foods.
points: Pearl millet, sorghum, and finger millet are millets.
Millets are food grains.
Dals are among the pulses eaten in India.
Millets and dals are identified as different kinds of foods.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: How are woven and printed sari designs different?
activities.answer: A woven design is formed as part of the cloth during its making. A printed design is added to the cloth afterwards. Therefore, the timing and method of adding the design are different, even though both can be sari designs.
points: A woven design is formed into the cloth.
A printed design is added afterwards.
Both methods can be used for sari designs.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student is preparing a display about India's festivals. Family members from different regions use different names for similar festivals, so the student checks the chapter's map. It shows these festivals around the same date. The student also sees that Makara Sankrānti is celebrated in many parts on or around January 14. They wonder whether every region uses the same festival name and plan to mention that many major festivals occur during October and November.
activities.prompt: The student must show that similar festivals in different regions can have different names. What is the best way to complete the chart?
options: Use one name for every region and leave out the map.
Include only the festivals from October and November.
Label each regional name and show the nearby festival date.
Replace all the regional names with Makara Sankrānti.

why.Use one name for every region and leave: This removes the regional differences that the chart should show.
why.Include only the festivals from October: It leaves out an important part of India's festival calendar.
why.Replace all the regional names with Maka: This erases the different names shown on the map.

activities.explanation: This presents both the names and the timing clearly.

activities.context: A student is preparing a display about India's festivals. Family members from different regions use different names for similar festivals, so the student checks the chapter's map. It shows these festivals around the same date. The student also sees that Makara Sankrānti is celebrated in many parts on or around January 14. They wonder whether every region uses the same festival name and plan to mention that many major festivals occur during October and November.
activities.prompt: Suppose the display mentions only the major festivals from October and November. What should the student do to avoid leaving out Makara Sankrānti?
options: Include a map entry showing Makara Sankrānti around January 14.
Delete the October and November entries because the display should show one month.
Change Makara Sankrānti to an October festival without checking the map.
Leave it out because festivals in January are not common in India.

why.Delete the October and November entries: It removes useful information that the student planned to include.
why.Change Makara Sankrānti to an October fe: It gives the festival a date that is not supported by the chapter.
why.Leave it out because festivals in Januar: It confuses a well-celebrated festival with one that is uncommon.

activities.explanation: This places the festival correctly using the date given in the chapter.

activities.context: During a school reading week, Meera chooses a story about Rāma, who gets help from Lakṣhmaṇa and Hanuman. Her friend Arjun chooses an animal story from the Pañchatantra and learns that it has been adapted into many Indian languages. The class also compares folk versions of the Rāmāyaṇa and Mahābhārata. A student wonders whether these very different stories show that Indian culture ignores unity.
activities.prompt: What should the student conclude after comparing the different stories and folk versions?
options: Different communities can keep their own epic versions while sharing a sense of cultural unity.
Only one community's version can be treated as the correct version of an epic.
Different versions show that Indian culture values separation rather than unity.
Animal stories and epic stories belong to separate cultures and cannot be compared.

why.Only one community's version can be trea: The facts do not say that only one version is correct.
why.Different versions show that Indian cult: Different versions do not mean that culture values separation.
why.Animal stories and epic stories belong t: Both animal stories and epic stories are part of Indian culture.

activities.explanation: This recognizes diversity while keeping unity in view.

activities.context: During a school reading week, Meera chooses a story about Rāma, who gets help from Lakṣhmaṇa and Hanuman. Her friend Arjun chooses an animal story from the Pañchatantra and learns that it has been adapted into many Indian languages. The class also compares folk versions of the Rāmāyaṇa and Mahābhārata. A student wonders whether these very different stories show that Indian culture ignores unity.
activities.prompt: Meera wants to find a shorter part of the two epics that helps her class think about values. What should she look for?
options: A shorter story that asks what is right and what is wrong.
A passage listing how many pages the two epics might fill.
A passage about the Pāṇḍavas fighting the Kauravas.
A passage about the number of Pañchatantra adaptations in different languages.

why.A passage listing how many pages the two: The page count does not directly help the class think about values.
why.A passage about the Pāṇḍavas fighting th: The conflict is part of the epic but does not directly answer the question asked.
why.A passage about the number of Pañchatant: The number of adaptations does not directly address values or right and wrong.

activities.explanation: The shorter stories in the epics focus on values and ask what is right and wrong.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between folk versions of the two great epics and adaptations of the Pañchatantra?
activities.answer: Folk versions are countless versions of the Rāmāyaṇa and Mahābhārata, and many communities have their own versions. Pañchatantra versions are adapted animal stories; about 200 adaptations exist in more than 50 languages. The key difference is the source stories and the kind of versions.
points: Folk versions belong to the two great epics.
Many communities have their own epic versions.
Pañchatantra stories use animals as main characters.
About 200 adaptations exist in more than 50 languages.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

chapters.title: Family and Community
chapters.summary: In this chapter: family types and relationships; family roles, duties and support; tenzing’s family and shared responsibilities; what is a community?.

lessons.title: Family Types and Relationships

activities.prompt: What makes each family different, yet connected?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Family Life
activities.body:
Imagine beginning a tour of the many homes where people live. Almost everyone lives in a family, so family shapes surround you each day. The family is the oldest and most basic unit of society. As you explore, you will meet different family types.

First, stop at a joint family home. Several generations live together, and you see them moving through the same home.

Next, visit a nuclear family. It mainly includes a couple and their children. Sometimes, it includes one parent and children instead. These arrangements show you that family life can take different shapes.

Now, listen closely to family words in Indian languages. They often include more words for relationships than English. Curiously, most have no special word for cousin. Cousins are treated as brothers and sisters because all the children are closely connected.

As your tour ends, look at the children around you. Family ties create deep bonds among them. You now see different family types and relationships. You can recognise these bonds wherever you meet them.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Different Family Types
activities.body: Families are the oldest and most basic group in society. Almost everyone lives in a family. A joint family has several generations living together. Generations means grandparents, parents and children. A nuclear family is mostly two parents and their children. Sometimes, a nuclear family has one parent and children. Family ties create strong bonds between all the children.
keyPoints: A joint family has several generations living together.
A nuclear family is mostly two parents and their children.
Family ties create strong bonds between all the children.
activities.explanation: This card shows family types and how family members are connected.

activities.prompt: A child asks, “I have one parent. Am I still in a family?”
steps: The child lives with one parent, so this home fits a nuclear family.
This is possible because a nuclear family can have one parent and children.
It fits society because the family is its oldest, most basic unit.
Therefore, the child is still in a family.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which group is a joint family?
options: A couple and their children
Many generations living together
One parent and children
A group of friends
activities.explanation: A joint family has many generations living together.

activities.prompt: A nuclear family mainly includes a couple and their children.
activities.explanation: This is the main description of a nuclear family.

activities.prompt: In most Indian languages, there is no special word for ______.
activities.hint: Think about children whose parents are brothers or sisters.
activities.explanation: Most Indian languages have no special word for cousin.

activities.prompt: Why are cousins treated as brothers and sisters?
options: Because they live in different cities
Because all the children are closely connected
Because they have the same surname
Because they go to different schools
activities.explanation: Cousins are treated as brothers and sisters because all the children are closely connected.

activities.prompt: What is true about Indian languages and family members?
options: They often have more words for family members than English
They have fewer words for family members than English
They have no words for family members
They use the same word for every family member
activities.explanation: Indian languages often have more words for family members than English.

activities.prompt: In most Indian languages, cousins have a special word.
activities.explanation: False. In most Indian languages, there is no special word for cousin.

activities.prompt: A home has a couple, children, and grandparents. Another has one parent and children. How do the homes differ?
options: The first is a joint family; the second is a nuclear family.
The first is a nuclear family; the second is a joint family.
Both are joint families because children live in each home.
Both are nuclear families because each home has children.

why.The first is a nuclear family; the secon: The first has several generations, but the second has one parent and children.
why.Both are joint families because children: Having children does not make every home a joint family.
why.Both are nuclear families because each h: This wrongly treats any home with children as nuclear.

activities.explanation: Several generations mean joint; one parent with children can be nuclear.

activities.prompt: Indian languages have more family words than English. Most have no special word for cousin. How can both facts fit?
options: Many family words can exist while cousins are still treated like siblings.
More family words mean cousins are treated like strangers.
No cousin word means cousins have no close family bond.
Many family words mean only cousins receive special names.

why.More family words mean cousins are treat: This wrongly links more words with distance between cousins.
why.No cousin word means cousins have no clo: This wrongly thinks the missing word removes their close bond.
why.Many family words mean only cousins rece: This wrongly assumes that only cousins have family names.

activities.explanation: The children are closely connected, so cousins can act like siblings.

activities.prompt: A source says most Indian languages lack a special cousin word. What family practice does this suggest?
options: Cousins are treated like brothers and sisters.
Cousins are treated like neighbours.
Cousins are treated like grandparents.
Cousins are treated like strangers.

The source points to siblings, not neighbours.
The source points to siblings, not grandparents.
The source points to closeness, not distance between family members.

activities.explanation: Without a separate word, cousins can be treated as brothers and sisters.

activities.prompt: One parent and children live together. The child asks, “Is our home still a family?” What is the best answer?
options: Yes, because one parent and children can form a nuclear family.
No, because every family must have a couple.
No, because every family must have several generations.
Yes, because every family includes one parent and children.

why.No, because every family must have a cou: This wrongly assumes every family needs a couple.
why.No, because every family must have sever: This wrongly treats the joint-family rule as a rule for all.
why.Yes, because every family includes one p: This wrongly treats one family arrangement as the rule for all.

activities.explanation: One parent and children can form a nuclear family.

lessons.title: Family Roles, Duties and Support

activities.prompt: How does a family help each other grow?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Family Life Tour
activities.body:
Imagine you are visiting a family and watching its everyday life. Family relationships rest on love, care, cooperation and interdependence. Cooperation means working together. You see family members caring for one another.

You see parents raising children to become happy and responsible members of society. Children take on more responsibilities in the home as they grow up. Daily practice helps them take part in household life.

You watch children learn traditions and practices that their families follow. Doing one's duty is an important principle of Indian culture. The family teaches values such as ahimsa, dāna, sevā and tyāga.

Family members often give up their own needs to care for the family. Now you meet Shalini, whose family showed support by sharing what they had. Shalini was happy when everyone could get new clothes.

Before you leave, you remember that duties connect family life. You see cooperation, responsibility and support shaping family life. Families depend on love, care, cooperation and interdependence.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: How Families Help Each Other
activities.body: Families grow close through love, care, cooperation and interdependence. Cooperation means working together. Interdependence means depending on each other. Parents must raise happy, responsible children. As children grow, they do more work at home. They learn by doing it every day. Families also pass on traditions and values. Doing your duty is important in Indian culture. Family members may give up things they need. Shalini's family shared what they had.
keyPoints: Love, care, cooperation and interdependence help families grow close.
Children learn duties and traditions by doing them every day.
Family members help each other by sharing and caring.
activities.explanation: Every family member helps the family be happy and responsible.

activities.prompt: A family shares what it has so everyone can eat. What does this reveal about family life?
steps: The family shares what it has, so each member's need matters to everyone.
This is cooperation because the members are working together.
Their care shows interdependence because each member depends on the others.
Therefore, sharing what they have is a way of showing family support.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Working Together
activities.prompt: Which action shows cooperation at home?
options: Keeping all the work to yourself
Sharing work with your family
Not wanting to work with others
Caring only for your own needs
activities.explanation: Cooperation means working together.

activities.title: Meaning of Cooperation
activities.prompt: Cooperation means working ______.
activities.hint: Think about what people do when they cooperate.
activities.explanation: The lesson says cooperation means working together.

activities.title: Parents’ Duty
activities.prompt: What is the duty of parents?
options: Keeping children away from household life
Stopping children from learning family traditions
Raising children to become happy and responsible members of society
Giving children fewer duties as they grow up
activities.explanation: Parents must raise children who are happy and responsible members of society.

activities.title: Family Roles
activities.prompt: Match each family role with its part.
activities.explanation: Each family member has duties that support the whole family.

activities.title: Showing Family Support
activities.prompt: How did Shalini’s family show support?
options: They shared what they had.
They kept all the clothes for one person.
They stopped caring for one another.
They refused to share anything.
activities.explanation: Shalini’s family showed support by sharing what they had.

activities.title: A Moment of Family Support
activities.prompt: Put Shalini’s family moment in order.
items: The family shares what they had.
activities.explanation: Sharing helped everyone get new clothes, and Shalini felt happy.

activities.prompt: A child is growing older. What change should happen in the child's role at home?
options: The child should take on more home responsibilities.
The child should stop learning how the home works.
The child should care only about personal needs.
The child should leave all household work to others.

why.The child should stop learning how the h: This wrongly suggests that children stop learning household life.
why.The child should care only about persona: It ignores that children learn by taking part in home life.
why.The child should leave all household wor: It misses the family's shared responsibilities and cooperation.

activities.explanation: Growing older brings more responsibilities in the home.

activities.prompt: Two children live in the same home. The older child helps more. Why is this likely?
options: The older child has learned to take part in household life.
The older child has learned to avoid all family duties.
The younger child has no chance to learn at home.
Household practice matters less as children grow up.

why.The older child has learned to avoid all: This mistake says practice makes children less involved.
why.The younger child has no chance to learn: This wrongly treats younger children as unable to learn.
why.Household practice matters less as child: This reverses the effect of growing up on responsibilities.

activities.explanation: Daily practice helps children learn household life.

activities.prompt: A family plans the work together and completes it side by side. What does this show?
options: The family is cooperating by working together.
The family is avoiding shared household responsibilities.
Each family member is working completely alone.
The family is teaching children to ignore cooperation.

why.The family is avoiding shared household: This wrongly says working together avoids responsibilities.
why.Each family member is working completely: This mistakes separate work for cooperation.
why.The family is teaching children to ignor: This ignores what cooperation means in family life.

activities.explanation: Cooperation means working together, and this family is doing that.

activities.prompt: A child completes a duty even when it takes effort. What principle does this action show?
options: Doing one's duty is important in Indian culture.
Family duties matter less when they are difficult.
Children should only work when others watch.
Doing a duty means giving up family love.

why.Family duties matter less when they are: This wrongly says effort makes a duty unimportant.
why.Children should only work when others wa: This thinks a duty matters only when others notice it.
why.Doing a duty means giving up family love: This confuses doing a duty with rejecting family care.

activities.explanation: Doing one's duty is an important principle of Indian culture.

activities.prompt: A family teaches children ahimsa, dāna, sevā and tyāga. What should children understand?
options: These family values guide how they live with others.
These values matter only outside the family.
These values mean children should avoid helping others.
These values replace all learning about family traditions.

why.These values matter only outside the fam: This wrongly limits family values to life outside the home.
why.These values mean children should avoid: This misunderstands values that guide caring for others.
why.These values replace all learning about: This wrongly says family values remove other family learning.

activities.explanation: The family teaches these values to guide life within the family.

activities.prompt: Shalini's family shared what they had. Everyone could get new clothes. Why was Shalini happy?
options: Everyone received clothes, so the family's support reached her.
She wanted the family to keep everything for itself.
She was unhappy that family members shared.
She liked hearing that clothes were not shared.

why.She wanted the family to keep everything: This mistake shows she valued keeping needs for herself.
why.She was unhappy that family members shar: This directly opposes her happiness when everyone received clothes.
why.She liked hearing that clothes were not: This wrongly suggests that sharing caused her unhappiness.

activities.explanation: Shalini was happy because everyone could get new clothes.

lessons.title: Tenzing’s Family and Shared Responsibilities

activities.prompt: How do Tenzing’s family members share responsibilities?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Sharing at Home and Beyond
activities.body:
You meet Tenzing’s father, who runs a small grocery store. You also see him helping with household chores. His mother became busy working in a local handicraft cooperative. When she did, Tenzing’s father joined in cleaning the house. You watch responsibilities being shared.

His parents discuss special expenses together. You hear how they try to save money for unexpected needs.

Next, you meet his grandmother, an interesting storyteller. Her stories contain humour and wisdom. You listen carefully and enjoy her stories.

You then meet his grandfather, who helps Tenzing with his homework. He is active in social work in the colony. During a power failure, he registers a complaint at the nearby office. You see him helping the community beyond his home.

After a storm damaged a neighbour’s house, you see his grandfather collect money for repairs. His care reaches neighbours as well as his relatives. You finish your visit noticing how each family member shares different responsibilities. Some help at home, while others support the wider community.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: A Family That Helps Together
activities.body: Tenzing’s family shares many jobs. His father runs a small grocery shop. He also helps with housework. His mother works at a local handicraft cooperative (a group that makes crafts). Now she is often busy. When she is busy, his father helps clean the house. His grandmother tells fun stories. They are funny and wise. His grandfather helps with homework. He also does social work (helps people) in the colony. The family talks about big costs. They save money for surprise needs.
keyPoints: Family members share work at home and in the colony.
Grandparents help with homework, stories and social work.
The family plans costs and saves for surprise needs.
activities.explanation: Tenzing’s family shows that everyone can share jobs.

activities.prompt: Tenzing’s mother becomes busy at the cooperative. How should the family share housework?
steps: Mother’s busy cooperative work leaves the family less time for housework.
Father joins cleaning because the house still needs care.
Father already helps with chores, so cleaning fits his shared duty.
The family shows that responsibilities are shared when someone becomes busy.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Family Shop
activities.prompt: What does Tenzing’s father run?
options: A small grocery store
A handicraft cooperative
A nearby complaint office
A colony social club
activities.explanation: Tenzing’s father runs a small grocery store.

activities.title: Fill the Shop Word
activities.prompt: Tenzing’s father runs a small ______ store.
activities.hint: The blank describes the kind of shop he runs.
activities.explanation: the lesson says that his father runs a small grocery store.

activities.title: Helping at Home
activities.prompt: Tenzing’s father joined in cleaning the house when his mother became busy.
activities.explanation: Yes. He joined in cleaning when his mother became busy with her work.

activities.title: Why Did Father Help?
activities.prompt: Why did Tenzing’s father help to clean the house?
options: Because his grandmother started work at the cooperative.
Because his grandfather made a complaint.
Because his mother became busy with work at the cooperative.
Because a storm damaged the house.
activities.explanation: His mother became busy with work at the cooperative. So his father helped to clean the house.

activities.title: Family Roles
activities.prompt: Match each family member with the fact about their work.
pairs: Works in a local handicraft cooperative
Is active in social work in the colony
activities.explanation: Each family member contributes through work, stories or community service.

activities.title: After the Storm
activities.prompt: A storm damaged a neighbour’s house. What did Tenzing’s grandfather do?
options: He collected money for repairs.
He made a complaint about a power failure.
He joined the local handicraft cooperative.
He cleaned his small grocery store.
activities.explanation: He collected money for repairs. This helped the neighbour after the storm.

activities.prompt: Tenzing’s mother becomes busy at the local handicraft cooperative. What is most likely to happen at home?
options: Tenzing’s father joins in cleaning the house.
Tenzing’s father stops helping with household chores at home.
Tenzing’s grandmother stops telling interesting stories to everyone.
Tenzing’s grandfather stops helping Tenzing with his homework.

why.Tenzing’s father stops helping with hous: This wrongly thinks extra work makes father stop his chores.
why.Tenzing’s grandmother stops telling inte: This wrongly links mother’s work to stopping grandmother’s stories.
why.Tenzing’s grandfather stops helping Tenz: This wrongly links mother’s work to stopping grandfather’s help.

activities.explanation: Mother’s busier work time led father to join the cleaning.

activities.prompt: A family-life map shows each family member’s daily work. It includes store work, housework, homework help, and social work. What shared idea do these entries support?
options: Family members take different responsibilities for home and colony.
Only parents are responsible for home and colony.
Family members work only for themselves and their jobs.
Grandparents have no responsibility toward Tenzing or others.

why.Only parents are responsible for home an: This wrongly leaves children and grandparents out of family duties.
why.Family members work only for themselves: This wrongly treats every responsibility as separate and self-focused.
why.Grandparents have no responsibility towa: This wrongly treats grandparents as people without family duties.

activities.explanation: Different family members contribute to home and colony life.

activities.prompt: Tenzing’s parents discuss special expenses together. The family also saves money for unexpected needs. What does this show about their shared responsibility?
options: The family shares responsibility for future money needs.
The family makes each special money choice separately.
The family plans only for expenses they already know.
The family avoids discussing special expenses with each other.

why.The family makes each special money choi: This wrongly treats shared planning as separate decision-making.
why.The family plans only for expenses they: This wrongly says saving ignores possible future needs.
why.The family avoids discussing special exp: This wrongly denies the family’s shared expense discussions.

activities.explanation: Discussing expenses and saving together share money responsibility.

lessons.title: What Is a Community?

activities.prompt: What helps people live and work together in a community?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Community Life
activities.body:
Imagine walking through a village with your family. You meet other families and people nearby, all connected in different ways. Your family is connected with other families and the people around you. Such a group of connected people may be called a community.

You come together for different reasons. Some village people work together to support one another. You may also work together on land preparation, sowing and harvesting.

Your village community may share natural resources. These can include water, grazing lands and forest produce. Many community practices were rarely written down, but they are called rules. These rules give communities secure access to resources.

You see how communities organise festivals, feasts, weddings and other events. You also see members coming together for different reasons.

For smooth working, each member must perform their duties. Without this, a community cannot function smoothly. You can see people connect, organise events, share resources and follow rules. This is how a community works together.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Understanding a community
activities.body: Families are connected with other families and the people around them. A group of connected people may be called a community. Community members come together for different reasons. They organise festivals, feasts, weddings and other events. Members also perform duties, so their community can function smoothly.
keyPoints: Families are connected with other families.
Connected people may form a community.
Members come together and perform duties.
activities.explanation: Communities work better when members share tasks and perform their duties.

activities.prompt: How can shared land, rules, and work make a community?
steps: Several families use shared grazing land.
They are connected because they share resources.
They follow rules because these give secure access.
They work together, so they may be called a community.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What may a group of connected people be called?
options: A family
A community
One person
A building
activities.explanation: A group of connected people may be called a community. Families are connected with people around them.

activities.prompt: Shared natural resources can include water, grazing lands and forest ______.
activities.hint: Think of what comes from a forest.
activities.explanation: Forest produce is one of the shared natural resources listed.

activities.prompt: Match each example with its group.
activities.explanation: Festivals are community events. Water is shared. Rules are community practices.

activities.prompt: Put these village tasks in the correct order.
activities.explanation: Village communities can work together through land preparation, sowing and harvesting.

activities.prompt: A member skips their duty. What may happen?
options: The community may work better.
Members need fewer things.
The community cannot work well.
Rules are not needed.
activities.explanation: Members must do their duties to work well. Skipping a duty may stop this.

activities.prompt: Shared grazing land is used by many families. How do community rules help?
options: Give all members secure access to resources.
Make every family prepare and harvest fields.
Stop village members from sharing land.
Choose the village's festival and feast.

why.Make every family prepare and harvest fi: This confuses rules for resources with duties for work.
This wrongly treats rules as a way to remove access.
This mistakes community rules for plans for celebrations.

activities.explanation: This is what the rules do: give secure access to resources.

activities.prompt: One village works together to sow. Another works together to harvest. Why might they do this?
options: Their shared work can help them support one another.
To keep most families away from farm work.
Because every village has identical daily duties.
Because village work must happen without help.

why.To keep most families away from farm wor: This wrongly assumes families should stay away from shared work.
why.Because every village has identical dail: This confuses sharing a task with having identical duties.
why.Because village work must happen without: This wrongly treats shared work as something to avoid.

activities.explanation: Shared work can help village people support one another.

activities.prompt: A written list gives each village member a duty. What can we learn from it?
options: Members have duties that help the community function.
The community has no shared work to organise.
Every member has the same kind of job.
Written rules are more important than community events.

why.The community has no shared work to orga: This wrongly assumes the community has no shared work.
This confuses having duties with having identical duties.
why.Written rules are more important than co: This wrongly makes written rules more important than community events.

activities.explanation: The list shows duties, and members must perform them to function smoothly.

activities.prompt: A rule guides families' use of shared water. How does this rule help?
options: Give members secure access to shared water.
Make every family prepare and harvest fields.
Turn shared water into a village festival.
Stop families from using the water together.

why.Make every family prepare and harvest fi: This confuses access rules with duties for farm work.
why.Turn shared water into a village festiva: This wrongly treats a resource rule as an event plan.
why.Stop families from using the water toget: This wrongly says rules prevent shared use.

activities.explanation: Rules give communities secure access to shared resources.

activities.prompt: Families and neighbours share food at a village feast. Why can this be called a community?
options: Connected people are sharing an event together.
Only families, not neighbours, share the feast.
The feast must become a written rule.
Each neighbour has the same daily duties.

why.Only families, not neighbours, share the: This wrongly treats a community as involving only families.
This confuses a feast with a rule that guides behaviour.
why.Each neighbour has the same daily duties: This mistakes taking part together for having identical duties.

activities.explanation: Connected families and neighbours are taking part in a shared event.

activities.prompt: If members stop doing their duties, what is likely to happen?
options: The community cannot function smoothly.
All members will perform more duties.
The village will organise another feast.
Shared resources will disappear.

This wrongly links stopping duties with taking more duties.
This assumes failure will lead to another feast.
This wrongly treats stopped duties as the loss of resources.

activities.explanation: Communities need members to perform their duties to function smoothly.

lessons.title: Communities Acting for Others

activities.prompt: How can communities help people and nature?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Communities Acting for Others
activities.body:
You begin by visiting a halma gathering. Here, people come together to support one another. Anyone facing a crisis receives this support. The tradition’s main aim is to serve Mother Earth.

Now, you meet the Bhils who worked together. You watch them dig trenches to conserve rainwater. They did this work without payment. It was their duty to their community and the environment.

Next, you visit private, spiritual and religious groups. You see them cooking large quantities of food. The groups distributed this food to people who needed it.

Later, you meet Kamal Parmar after his work. He began teaching children every evening. He also gave the children a free dinner. Soon, 150 children regularly attended his classes.

Finally, you notice older pupils joining the classes. Some joined as volunteers to teach in the classes.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Helping the Community
activities.body: Halma is a tradition. It brings people together. Its main aim is to serve Mother Earth. The Bhils dug trenches to save rainwater. They did this work without pay. It was their duty to help the community and the environment. Other groups cooked food. They gave the food to people in need. Kamal Parmar taught children every evening. Kamal Parmar gave them dinner. Later, older students helped as volunteers.
keyPoints: Halma brings people together to help anyone in trouble.
The Bhils saved rainwater through community service.
Kamal Parmar helped children by teaching them and giving free meals.
activities.explanation: These actions show people helping communities, the environment and children.

activities.prompt: People cook meals, dig water trenches, and teach children. Why might they all be helping?
steps: In a crisis, halma brings people together so they can support others.
Its main aim is to serve Mother Earth, so saving rainwater fits it.
The Bhils worked unpaid because it was their duty.
Cooking food, sharing meals, and teaching children show service in daily life.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Digging Trenches
activities.prompt: Who dug trenches to conserve rainwater?
options: The Bhils
Private, spiritual and religious groups
Older pupils
Kamal’s children
activities.explanation: The Bhils dug the trenches as unpaid community service.

activities.title: Saving Rainwater
activities.prompt: The Bhils dug trenches to conserve ______.
activities.hint: This is water saved for later use.
activities.explanation: Their trenches helped conserve rainwater.

activities.title: Why Work Without Pay?
activities.prompt: Why did the Bhils work without pay?
options: Their duty to the community and environment
To get money from the government
To sell rainwater in the market
To become leaders who get paid
activities.explanation: They saw the work as their duty to the community and environment.

activities.title: Community Actions
activities.prompt: Match each action with the person or group who did it.
activities.explanation: Each pair matches an action with the right group or person.

activities.title: Sharing Food
activities.prompt: What did the groups do with a lot of food?
options: They gave it to people who needed it
They kept it for themselves
They sold it in the market
They used it only for the cooks
activities.explanation: The groups shared their food with people who needed it.

activities.title: Supporting Kamal’s Classes
activities.prompt: Which detail shows older pupils supporting Kamal’s work?
options: They joined as volunteers to teach in the classes
They paid Kamal for every evening class
They stopped attending after receiving dinner
They cooked food only for themselves
activities.explanation: Some older pupils became volunteer teachers in Kamal’s classes.

activities.prompt: Suppose a crisis affects a community. The halma tradition brings people together. What will they most likely do?
options: Support people who face the crisis.
Keep all help inside one household.
Stop helping when payment ends.
Ask every person to work alone.

This mistake keeps community support inside one household.
This mistake assumes help depends on getting payment.
This mistake turns a shared tradition into separate work.

activities.explanation: This is right because halma brings people together to support anyone facing a crisis.

activities.prompt: The Bhils dug trenches as a duty to their community and environment. Kamal taught children and gave them dinner. What do both examples show?
options: Treat helping as a shared community duty.
Help only after receiving some payment.
Act mainly to protect their own money.
Keep their useful work away from others.

This mistake thinks community duty appears only when people are paid.
This mistake wrongly treats helping as a way to gain money.
This mistake assumes service is kept away from the community.

activities.explanation: Both examples show service to other people in different ways.

activities.prompt: Private, spiritual and religious groups cooked large amounts of food. Suppose many people need meals. Where should this food go?
options: Go to people in the community who need meals.
Stay with the groups that cooked the food.
Wait until the cooking groups need food.
Go to one family, even if others need meals.

why.Stay with the groups that cooked the foo: This mistake keeps the food from reaching people in need.
This mistake ignores the needs of hungry people.
why.Go to one family, even if others need me: This mistake helps one family while ignoring other people.

activities.explanation: The food was meant for people who needed it.

activities.prompt: Soon, 150 children regularly attended Kamal’s classes. Later, older pupils joined as volunteers. What could this change?
options: Share the teaching work with more people.
Make every child pay to attend class.
End the free dinner when volunteers came.
Leave all teaching to one older pupil.

This mistake wrongly assumes volunteering requires every child to pay.
why.End the free dinner when volunteers came: This mistake connects volunteers with ending a helpful meal.
This mistake ignores the help that volunteers could give Kamal.

activities.explanation: Older pupil volunteers could share Kamal’s teaching work.

lessons.title: Different Communities and Interdependence

activities.prompt: How do people in your area depend on each other?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Communities
activities.body:
You begin in an urban neighbourhood, where you may see a Residents’ Welfare Association. New types of communities have appeared in recent decades.

In this community, you find rules for everyday life. The rules may cover waste, common-area cleanliness and pet care. People help make these rules together.

Now you visit a trading community. Residents’ Welfare Associations depend on the trading community for supplies. You also see municipal workers who handle waste. These visits show how communities depend on one another.

Next, you learn that a community can change with the situation. You may hear the word jāti, which is also often called a community. People sharing a religion, region, work or interest may form one. At school, you may belong to a class community and a sports community. In complex societies, everyone depends on other people and communities.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Communities Help One Another
activities.body: A community is people who share religion, region, work or interest. New types of communities have appeared in recent decades. A Residents’ Welfare Association is an urban community. Its members help make rules about waste, cleanliness and pet care. Such communities need a trading community for supplies and municipal workers for waste. In complex societies, everyone depends on other people and communities.
keyPoints: Residents’ Welfare Associations are urban communities.
Members help make rules about waste, cleanliness and pet care.
Communities depend on a trading community, municipal workers and one another.
activities.explanation: Different communities have different roles, but they need one another.

activities.prompt: Why does a Residents’ Welfare Association need outside help?
steps: Residents help make its rules, so members share responsibility for the association.
These rules matter because they cover waste, cleanliness and pet care.
It needs the trading community for supplies and municipal workers for waste.
This dependence shows that communities ultimately depend on one another.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: An Urban Community
activities.prompt: Which one is an example of an urban community?
options: Residents’ Welfare Association
Municipal workers
Common-area cleanliness
Waste collection
activities.explanation: Residents’ Welfare Associations are examples of urban communities.

activities.title: Supplies for the Community
activities.prompt: Residents’ Welfare Associations depend on the trading community for supplies.
activities.explanation: The trading community provides supplies that Residents’ Welfare Associations need.

activities.title: Complete the Dependency
activities.prompt: They depend on the ______ community for supplies.
activities.hint: Think of the community that provides supplies.
activities.explanation: Residents’ Welfare Associations depend on the trading community for supplies.

activities.title: Why Trading Communities Matter
activities.prompt: Why do Residents’ Welfare Associations depend on the trading community?
options: They need common-area cleanliness.
They need pet-care rules.
They need supplies.
They need municipal workers.
activities.explanation: The trading community provides supplies that Residents’ Welfare Associations depend on.

activities.title: More Than One Community
activities.prompt: A child is in a class community and a sports community. What does this show?
options: Communities must stay apart.
Only work communities exist in schools.
The child can belong to more than one community.
A community never changes when the situation changes.
activities.explanation: A child can be in both a class community and a sports community at school.

activities.title: School Communities
activities.prompt: A child at school can be in a sports community. The child cannot be in a class community.
activities.explanation: A child can be in both a class community and a sports community at school.

activities.prompt: A Residents’ Welfare Association wants clean common areas. What should residents do?
options: Follow the cleanliness rule they helped make.
Leave all waste for municipal workers alone.
Ask the trading community to make every rule.
Choose pet-care rules instead of cleanliness rules.

why.Leave all waste for municipal workers al: Residents share responsibility for common-area cleanliness.
why.Ask the trading community to make every: The trading community supplies the association but does not make its rules.
why.Choose pet-care rules instead of cleanli: Cleanliness and pet care are separate rules, so one cannot replace the other.

activities.explanation: Residents help make association rules, including cleanliness rules.

activities.prompt: If trading supplies do not come, what may happen to an association?
options: It may have difficulty getting needed supplies.
It may lose the power to make its rules.
It may need fewer municipal workers.
It may stop needing other communities altogether.

A supply problem does not change who helps make its rules.
A supply problem does not show that fewer waste workers are needed.
why.It may stop needing other communities al: The association still depends on other communities for supplies and waste help.

activities.explanation: The association depends on the trading community for supplies.

activities.prompt: A map shows an association needing help. What does this show?
options: The association depends on other communities.
The association controls other communities' rules.
Other communities depend only on the association.
The association has no common-area duties.

why.The association controls other communiti: Needing help does not mean controlling other communities.
why.Other communities depend only on the ass: The association itself depends on the trading community and municipal workers.
why.The association has no common-area dutie: Association rules can cover common-area cleanliness.

activities.explanation: The association depends on the trading community and municipal workers.

activities.prompt: Residents made a pet-care rule. A resident ignores it. What shows respect?
options: Follow it because residents helped make it.
Leave it because trading supplies matter more.
Ask municipal workers to enforce every pet rule.
Replace it with a rule about waste.

why.Leave it because trading supplies matter: Trading supplies do not make local rules less important.
why.Ask municipal workers to enforce every p: Municipal workers handle waste, not every pet-care rule.
Waste and pet care are separate parts of the association's rules.

activities.explanation: People in the association help make the rules, so they should follow them.

activities.prompt: A jāti and a class group are both communities. What does this show?
options: The word community can include different kinds of groups.
Only one kind of group should be called a community.
A jāti and class group must serve the same purpose.
The word community must always mean one fixed group.

why.Only one kind of group should be called: The facts show that many kinds of groups can be communities.
why.A jāti and class group must serve the sa: A jāti and a class community can be different community kinds.
why.The word community must always mean one: The idea of a community can change according to the situation.

activities.explanation: A jāti is called a community, and class and sports groups are communities too.
