lessons.sceneAlt: A harmonious Indian joint family shares love and memories, with every member contributing to the strength of the whole across generations.
lessons.sceneCaption: Members of an Indian joint family share love, memories, and togetherness across generations.

sceneCredit.text: Unity in Tradition The Joint Indian Family by Jaydevm, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
sceneCredit.creator: Jaydevm

activities.context: A boy lives with his parents, sister, grandparents, and aunt in the same home. His cousin visits, and the children call one another brothers and sisters because they are closely connected. The family speaks an Indian language that has more relationship words than English but no separate word for cousin. They wonder how clearer labels might affect the bonds among the children.
activities.prompt: Why does the boy’s home fit the idea of a joint family?
options: Several generations live under the same roof.
It includes one couple and their children only.
The cousin has a separate relationship word in the language.
It contains one parent and the children.

why.It includes one couple and their childre: This describes a nuclear family, but more than one generation lives there.
why.The cousin has a separate relationship w: The case says the language has no separate word for cousin.
Both parents are present, so this does not describe the home.

activities.explanation: This directly matches the defining feature of a joint family.

activities.context: A boy lives with his parents, sister, grandparents, and aunt in the same home. His cousin visits, and the children call one another brothers and sisters because they are closely connected. The family speaks an Indian language that has more relationship words than English but no separate word for cousin. They wonder how clearer labels might affect the bonds among the children.
activities.prompt: Why are the boy and his cousin treated like brothers and sisters?
options: There is no separate cousin word in the language, and the children’s close connection makes cousins seem like siblings.
Living together in a joint family automatically makes every child a sibling.
The language has fewer relationship words than English, so cousins need one general word.
Cousins count as siblings only when they belong to a nuclear family.

why.Living together in a joint family automa: The shared home explains who lives together, not why visiting cousins are treated alike.
why.The language has fewer relationship word: This reverses the fact that Indian languages often have more such words than English.
why.Cousins count as siblings only when they: The reason is closeness and language, not the family’s type.

activities.explanation: This connects both the language and the close bonds among the children.

activities.context: A boy lives with his parents, sister, grandparents, and aunt in the same home. His cousin visits, and the children call one another brothers and sisters because they are closely connected. The family speaks an Indian language that has more relationship words than English but no separate word for cousin. They wonder how clearer labels might affect the bonds among the children.
activities.prompt: If the grandparents and aunt moved out while the parents and children stayed, what would the home mainly be?
options: A nuclear family, mainly made up of the parents and their children.
A joint family, because the parents and children are different generations.
A one-parent family, because only one adult would remain.
A joint family, because the cousin still belongs to the family.

why.A joint family, because the parents and: Two generations do not make the several generations required for a joint family.
why.A one-parent family, because only one ad: Both parents would remain, so it would not be a one-parent family.
why.A joint family, because the cousin still: A cousin who visits does not make several generations live together.

activities.explanation: The parents and their children mainly form a nuclear family.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between a joint family and a nuclear family.
activities.answer: A joint family has several generations living together. A nuclear family mainly includes a couple and their children. Sometimes a nuclear family has one parent and children. The main difference is that a joint family includes several generations, while a nuclear family mainly stays within parents and children.
points: A joint family includes several generations.
A nuclear family mainly includes a couple and their children.
A nuclear family may sometimes have one parent and children.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Shalini’s family showed support by sharing what they had. Family members gave up some of their own needs to care for one another, and everyone worked together. Shalini was happy when everyone could get new clothes. The children took part in household life through daily practice and learned the traditions their family followed. As they grew older, they took on more responsibilities at home.
activities.prompt: If Shalini’s family stopped working together and each member focused only on personal needs, what would most likely change?
options: Mutual care within the family would become less likely.
Children would learn cooperation more quickly and take on more duties.
Parents would have less duty to raise happy and responsible children.
Family traditions and practices would become clearer to every child.

why.Children would learn cooperation more qu: Without cooperation, children would not learn cooperation more quickly.
why.Parents would have less duty to raise ha: Parents’ duty to raise responsible children would remain important.
why.Family traditions and practices would be: Ignoring family needs would not make traditions clearer.

activities.explanation: Working together and caring for one another strengthen family support.

activities.context: Shalini’s family showed support by sharing what they had. Family members gave up some of their own needs to care for one another, and everyone worked together. Shalini was happy when everyone could get new clothes. The children took part in household life through daily practice and learned the traditions their family followed. As they grew older, they took on more responsibilities at home.
activities.prompt: If the children stopped joining daily household life, what would most likely happen?
options: They would have fewer chances to learn responsibilities.
They would learn their duties sooner because they had more free time.
Family traditions would be learned more quickly without them.
They would become more cooperative without taking part.

why.They would learn their duties sooner bec: More free time would not itself provide practice in taking responsibility.
why.Family traditions would be learned more: Family practices are learned through participation, so exclusion would not speed learning.
why.They would become more cooperative witho: A lack of participation would weaken, not strengthen, cooperation.

activities.explanation: Children learn household duties through daily practice; avoiding it removes that learning.

activities.prompt: Explain how family life helps children learn duties and responsibilities.
activities.answer: Children learn responsibilities by taking part in household life every day. As they grow older, they take on more duties and practise cooperation with family members. They also learn the traditions and practices followed by their family, so daily participation helps them become responsible members of society.
points: Children take part in household life.
Daily practice develops responsibility.
Children learn family traditions and practices.
Responsibility grows with age.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Tenzing’s mother became busy working in a local handicraft cooperative, so his father joined in cleaning the house and helps with household chores. His grandmother tells stories containing humour and wisdom. Tenzing’s grandfather helps with his homework and is active in social work in the colony. He registers a complaint at the nearby office during a power failure and collects money after a storm damages a neighbour’s house. Tenzing’s parents discuss special expenses together and save money for unexpected needs.
activities.prompt: If Tenzing’s mother becomes busy at the cooperative again, what should his father do?
options: Continue helping with cleaning and other household tasks
Leave every household task to Tenzing’s mother
Do only the cleaning and refuse other chores
Wait until Tenzing’s mother returns before helping

why.Leave every household task to Tenzing’s: This wrongly leaves all housework to one person.
why.Do only the cleaning and refuse other ch: This ignores the other chores his father helps with.
why.Wait until Tenzing’s mother returns befo: This unnecessarily delays the sharing of housework.

activities.explanation: This reflects the support his father already gives.

activities.context: Tenzing’s mother became busy working in a local handicraft cooperative, so his father joined in cleaning the house and helps with household chores. His grandmother tells stories containing humour and wisdom. Tenzing’s grandfather helps with his homework and is active in social work in the colony. He registers a complaint at the nearby office during a power failure and collects money after a storm damages a neighbour’s house. Tenzing’s parents discuss special expenses together and save money for unexpected needs.
activities.prompt: If a power failure occurs while Tenzing’s grandfather is doing social work in the colony, what should he do?
options: Make a formal complaint about the power supply at the nearby office
Try to repair the colony’s electrical wiring himself
Wait for a storm before reporting the problem
Ask each neighbour to complain separately

why.Try to repair the colony’s electrical wi: This is not his responsibility and may be unsafe.
why.Wait for a storm before reporting the pr: A storm is not needed before reporting a power failure.
why.Ask each neighbour to complain separatel: Sharing complaints does not replace making one himself.

activities.explanation: This matches the action he takes during power failures.

activities.prompt: How do Tenzing’s parents share responsibility for money?
activities.answer: Tenzing’s parents discuss special expenses together, so decisions about family costs are shared rather than made by one person alone. They also try to save money for unexpected needs, helping the family prepare for surprises.
points: Special expenses are discussed together.
Both parents take part in financial decisions.
The family saves money for unexpected needs.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: In a village, families are connected with one another and with the people around them. Some residents join together because they need help with farming. They prepare land, sow seeds, and harvest crops. The village also shares water, grazing lands, and forest produce. When people organize a feast or wedding, they follow shared practices. These practices were rarely written down, but they guide members' duties and help the village work smoothly.
activities.prompt: If one member regularly avoids a duty, what is the most likely result for the community?
options: Shared tasks may be completed less effectively.
The village will no longer need any shared practices.
Members will have more secure access to shared resources.
Every member will be free from all responsibilities.

why.The village will no longer need any shar: Avoiding duties does not remove the need for shared practices.
why.Members will have more secure access to: Reduced participation does not automatically increase secure access to resources.
why.Every member will be free from all respo: Avoiding one duty does not remove every member's responsibilities.

activities.explanation: A community cannot function smoothly unless its members perform their duties.

activities.context: In a village, families are connected with one another and with the people around them. Some residents join together because they need help with farming. They prepare land, sow seeds, and harvest crops. The village also shares water, grazing lands, and forest produce. When people organize a feast or wedding, they follow shared practices. These practices were rarely written down, but they guide members' duties and help the village work smoothly.
activities.prompt: Before a feast, some members are unsure what they should do. What should they do next?
options: They should follow the community's shared practices and carry out their duties.
They should wait for every practice to be written down before acting.
They should leave the feast to the members who arrived first.
They should ignore their responsibilities because the practices are unwritten.

why.They should wait for every practice to b: Many community practices were rarely written down but are still called rules.
why.They should leave the feast to the membe: Shared practices guide members' responsibilities during community events.
why.They should ignore their responsibilitie: Unwritten practices still guide what community members should do.

activities.explanation: Community members must perform their duties so the community can function smoothly.

activities.prompt: Explain how community rules and members' duties help a community function.
activities.answer: Community rules can give members secure access to shared resources. Duties tell members what they are expected to do. When members perform those duties, the community can organise events, work together on farming, and function more smoothly. This is why cooperation and responsibility are important.
points: Rules give secure access to shared resources.
Members are expected to perform their duties.
Community events and farming work need cooperation.
Performing duties helps the community function smoothly.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: In a crisis, the halma tradition brought people together to support anyone facing it. Private, spiritual and religious groups cooked large quantities of food and distributed it to people who needed it. The Bhils dug trenches to conserve rainwater, doing the work without payment as their duty to the community and environment. Kamal Parmar began teaching children every evening after his work and gave them free dinner. Soon, 150 children attended regularly, and some older pupils became volunteers.
activities.prompt: What is most likely to happen in Kamal’s classes after older pupils become volunteers?
options: More children can receive support as the older pupils share what they have learned.
Kamal may give less attention to the classes because the volunteers take over.
The free dinner may end because the older pupils now share the teaching work.
Regular attendance may fall because the children no longer need evening classes.

why.Kamal may give less attention to the cla: Their help can strengthen support for the children.
why.The free dinner may end because the olde: Nothing says that they replace Kamal.
why.Regular attendance may fall because the: The classes grew as more children attended.

activities.explanation: The older pupils joined specifically to teach.

activities.context: In a crisis, the halma tradition brought people together to support anyone facing it. Private, spiritual and religious groups cooked large quantities of food and distributed it to people who needed it. The Bhils dug trenches to conserve rainwater, doing the work without payment as their duty to the community and environment. Kamal Parmar began teaching children every evening after his work and gave them free dinner. Soon, 150 children attended regularly, and some older pupils became volunteers.
activities.prompt: If more people needed food during the crisis, what should the groups do next?
options: Prepare enough extra meals and share them with everyone in need.
Keep the original amount and choose only some people to receive it.
Give the extra meals first to the older pupil volunteers.
Keep preparing food, but delay sharing it until the crisis is over.

why.Keep the original amount and choose only: The purpose is to help anyone facing the crisis.
why.Give the extra meals first to the older: Selecting only some people would leave others without needed support.
why.Keep preparing food, but delay sharing i: The older pupils volunteered to teach, not because they needed meals more.

activities.explanation: More people in need require more food.

activities.context: Residents in an urban neighbourhood formed a Residents’ Welfare Association and made rules about waste, common-area cleanliness and pet care. The association relied on the trading community for supplies and on municipal workers to handle waste. At school, a child belonged to both a class community and a sports community. The residents saw that their community depended on other people and communities, and that the idea of community could change with the situation.
activities.prompt: If the trading community stopped providing supplies, what would be the likely result?
options: The association would have difficulty obtaining the supplies it needs.
Municipal workers would take over supplying the association.
The association’s waste-handling work would immediately stop.
The pet-care rule would become its only responsibility.

why.Municipal workers would take over supply: This wrongly makes municipal workers the source of supplies.
why.The association’s waste-handling work wo: This confuses the supply dependency with the waste-handling dependency.
why.The pet-care rule would become its only: It wrongly treats one rule as the association’s only responsibility.

activities.explanation: The association relies on the trading community for supplies.

activities.context: Residents in an urban neighbourhood formed a Residents’ Welfare Association and made rules about waste, common-area cleanliness and pet care. The association relied on the trading community for supplies and on municipal workers to handle waste. At school, a child belonged to both a class community and a sports community. The residents saw that their community depended on other people and communities, and that the idea of community could change with the situation.
activities.prompt: If the child could no longer take part in the sports community, which conclusion would be best?
options: The child would still belong to the class community but would not be active in the sports community.
The child would lose membership in every school community.
The child would automatically become part of the Residents’ Welfare Association.
The Residents’ Welfare Association would replace both school groups.

why.The child would lose membership in every: This wrongly removes membership of all communities when one group is lost.
why.The child would automatically become par: This wrongly treats an urban association as a school community.
why.The Residents’ Welfare Association would: This wrongly assumes that one community can simply replace another.

activities.explanation: A child may belong to separate class and sports communities.

activities.prompt: Explain how the Residents’ Welfare Association shows interdependence.
activities.answer: The RWA shows interdependence because residents make rules about waste, common-area cleanliness and pet care, yet the association still needs help from outside groups. The trading community provides supplies, while municipal workers handle waste. If either group stopped helping, the association would face difficulty in obtaining supplies or managing waste.
points: Residents help make the association’s rules.
The trading community supplies the association.
Municipal workers handle the association’s waste.
Communities ultimately depend on one another.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

chapters.title: Grassroots Democracy - Part 1: Governance
chapters.summary: In this chapter: rules, governance and government; the three organs of government; separation of powers and three tiers; government at local, state and national levels.

lessons.title: Rules, Governance and Government

activities.prompt: How can a community work well when people disagree?
activities.explanation: Read on to find out.

activities.title: Keeping Communities Together
activities.body:
You arrive in a community where people have lived together for a very long time. Daily life brings questions about how everyone should act. Sometimes people disagree, and disorder can begin. Without shared rules, society could not function.

You first notice family life. Families usually expect children to follow simple rules at home. At school, rules apply to both students and teachers. During examinations, students must follow certain rules too.

You then step outside and join other road users. Road users must obey traffic rules. Some rules are especially important and are called laws. A government makes rules and makes sure they are followed. Governance means making decisions, organising society and ensuring rules are followed.

You may wonder whether these rules stay unchanged forever. They do not, because rules and laws can be changed. Citizens can also have a say about laws and rules governing society. By understanding rules, governance and government, you can see how communities work together.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: How rules help us live together
activities.body: People have lived in communities for a very long time. Living together can cause arguments and disorder. Society could not work if nobody followed rules. Families, schools, exams and roads all have rules. Governance means making decisions and organising society. It also makes sure rules are followed. A government makes rules. It makes sure people follow them. Laws are very important rules. Rules and laws can change. Citizens, the people of a country, can have a say about them.
keyPoints: Communities need rules to work.
Governance organises society. It makes sure rules are followed.
Citizens can have a say about laws and rules.
activities.explanation: Rules help people live together. Governance helps rules work.

activities.prompt: A child asks: Why do families, schools, and roads all need rules?
steps: Human beings have lived in communities for a very long time.
Living together can cause disagreements and disorder.
Communities therefore need rules to reduce disorder.
Governance therefore makes decisions and makes sure rules are followed.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What do families usually expect children to do?
options: Follow simple rules at home
Make decisions for the whole country
Avoid all rules
Change traffic rules
activities.explanation: Families usually expect children to follow simple rules at home. These rules help people live together.

activities.prompt: Governance makes decisions, organises society and makes sure ______ are followed.
activities.hint: Think about what governance helps people follow.
activities.explanation: Governance is the process of making sure rules are followed.

activities.prompt: Schools have rules for students and teachers.
activities.explanation: Yes. Schools have rules for both students and teachers.

activities.prompt: Match each group with the rules it follows.
activities.explanation: Each place or activity has its own rules. These include home, school, examination and traffic rules.

activities.prompt: What can people do about the rules in their country?
options: They can give their opinion about them
They must never think about them
They can remove all rules
They cannot change them
activities.explanation: People can give their opinion about the laws and rules.

activities.prompt: Families expect children to follow simple rules. Why do families expect this?
options: So children can become rulers at home.
So the family no longer needs rules.
So disagreements and disorder can be reduced.
So schools can ignore their examination rules.

This wrongly thinks children gain power by following rules.
This mistakes following rules for having no need for rules.
why.So schools can ignore their examination: This wrongly connects family rules with school examination rules.

activities.explanation: This fits because living together can cause disagreements and disorder.

activities.prompt: Families use simple rules at home. Schools have rules for students and teachers. What do both places show?
options: Only children need to follow simple rules.
People need rules in many different communities.
Schools and families use exactly the same rules.
Rules matter only within school buildings.

why.Only children need to follow simple rule: This wrongly thinks only children need rules.
why.Schools and families use exactly the sam: This assumes both places use exactly the same rules.
why.Rules matter only within school building: This wrongly limits rules to school buildings.

activities.explanation: This fits because society needs people to follow rules.

activities.prompt: A school notice lists separate rules for pupils and teachers. Why does it include both groups?
options: So only pupils know how the school works.
So teachers do not need any school rules.
So each group can ignore the other's rules.
So both groups can follow clear rules together.

why.So only pupils know how the school works: This wrongly leaves teachers outside the school rules.
why.So teachers do not need any school rules: This treats teachers as exempt from school rules.
why.So each group can ignore the other's rul: This thinks separate rules allow one group to ignore the other.

activities.explanation: This fits because the source lists rules for both groups.

activities.prompt: People want a traffic rule changed. They believe citizens should have a say. What should they do?
options: Keep the traffic rule fixed for ever.
Follow the traffic rule only when convenient.
Ask the government to change the rule.
Say that citizens cannot ask for changes.

This assumes rules must stay fixed for ever.
why.Follow the traffic rule only when conven: This confuses having a say with choosing when to obey.
why.Say that citizens cannot ask for changes: This wrongly denies that citizens can have a say.

activities.explanation: This fits because citizens can ask the government for a change.

activities.prompt: An old community rule no longer suits the people. What can happen next?
options: The rule must be hidden from all people.
The rule must stay fixed for ever.
The rule can change without any decision.
Citizens can ask for the rule to change.

This mistakes changing a rule for hiding it.
This assumes rules can never change.
why.The rule can change without any decision: This wrongly thinks rules can change without decisions.

activities.explanation: This fits because rules can change and citizens can have a say.

lessons.title: The Three Organs of Government

activities.prompt: How can government help stop digital crime?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Tour of Three Branches
activities.body:
Imagine you are visiting a classroom about digital crime. You hear that criminals can now steal money through digital methods. Digital technology has opened new ways for criminals to steal money. Learning about this case will show you how all three branches of government work together.

You first enter the legislature. An assembly of representatives of the people makes and updates laws. Lawmakers make new laws to fight cybercrime. They can also update or remove existing laws.

Next, you visit the executive. It implements or executes laws. This branch puts the new laws into action, helping the country fight digital crime.

Then, you arrive at the judiciary. Courts decide whether someone has broken the law. They can decide what action a person should face for breaking the law. Cybercriminals can be fined and sent to jail.

Before the tour ends, the courts check their work. They check whether a law is fair. They also check whether an executive decision is right. You now see how the three branches work together.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: How the Three Branches Work Together
activities.body: Digital tools give criminals new ways to steal money. Cybercrime means crime done with digital tools. Governments have made new laws to fight cybercrime. The legislature is a group of representatives (people who speak for others). It makes and updates laws. The executive puts these laws into action. The judiciary uses courts to decide if someone broke a law. These three branches of government work together.
keyPoints: Crime done with digital tools is cybercrime.
New laws can fight cybercrime.
Each branch has a different job.
Three branches work together.
activities.explanation: Different jobs help the government handle cybercrime.

activities.prompt: A thief steals money using a digital method. How can the three branches of government stop this crime?
steps: This is cybercrime because the crime uses digital methods.
The legislature can make new laws, because digital theft needs a legal response.
The executive can implement laws, because passing a law is not enough.
Courts decide guilt and action, so all three branches work together against cybercrime.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Law-Making Branch
activities.prompt: Which branch makes new laws?
options: The executive
The legislature
The judiciary
Cybercriminals
activities.explanation: The legislature makes new laws. It can also update or remove existing laws.

activities.title: Match the Jobs
activities.prompt: Match each job with the part of government that does it.
pairs: Decide if someone broke a law
Check if a law is fair
activities.explanation: Each part of government has a different job. Together, they help solve problems about law.

activities.title: The Law Action Branch
activities.prompt: The ______ implements or executes laws.
activities.hint: This branch puts laws into action.
activities.explanation: The executive carries out laws. The legislature makes them first.

activities.title: A Court's Job
activities.prompt: Which action belongs to the courts?
options: Make new laws against online crime
Decide what happens to a person who breaks a law
Find new ways to steal money
Carry out laws against online crime
activities.explanation: Courts decide what should happen after someone breaks the law. Other parts make or carry out laws.

activities.title: Branches Working Together
activities.prompt: Put these steps in order. They show how the three branches work together against cybercrime.
items: New digital technology gives criminals new ways to steal money.
The legislature makes new laws to fight cybercrime.
The executive carries out the new laws.
The judiciary decides if someone broke the law.
Courts decide what should happen to a person who broke the law.
activities.explanation: The legislature makes the law. The executive puts it into action. The judiciary then decides if the law was broken.

activities.title: After a Law Is Broken
activities.prompt: A cybercrime law is in place. A person breaks it. What can the courts do?
options: Make a new law without the legislature
Carry out the law instead of the executive
Decide if the person broke the law, and what comes next
Make new digital ways to steal money
activities.explanation: Courts decide if the person broke the law. They also decide what should happen next. The other branches do other work.

activities.prompt: Digital methods let criminals steal money. How should governments respond?
options: The legislature should make laws against cybercrime.
The executive should make laws against cybercrime.
The judiciary should make laws against cybercrime.
No branch should make laws against cybercrime.

why.The executive should make laws against c: This mistakes the executive for the law-making branch.
why.The judiciary should make laws against c: This mistakes the judiciary for the law-making branch.
why.No branch should make laws against cyber: This wrongly thinks the branches cannot fight cybercrime.

activities.explanation: The legislature makes laws, and new laws can fight cybercrime.

activities.prompt: A new cybercrime problem needs a new law. Which branch should act?
options: The legislature should make the new law.
The executive should make the new law.
The judiciary should make the new law.
No branch should make a new law.

This mistakes the executive for the law-making branch.
This mistakes the judiciary for the law-making branch.
This wrongly thinks no branch can make a needed law.

activities.explanation: The legislature makes new laws when new problems need rules.

activities.prompt: A cybercrime law is now in force. Which branch should carry it out?
options: The executive should implement the cybercrime law.
The legislature should implement the cybercrime law.
The judiciary should implement the cybercrime law.
No branch should implement the cybercrime law.

why.The legislature should implement the cyb: This mistakes the legislature for the branch that carries out laws.
why.The judiciary should implement the cyber: This mistakes the judiciary for the branch that carries out laws.
why.No branch should implement the cybercrim: This wrongly thinks a law does not need to be carried out.

activities.explanation: The executive implements or executes laws, including cybercrime laws.

activities.prompt: A person committed cybercrime. What can a court do next?
options: Fine the person or send the person to jail.
Allow the person to choose any punishment.
Make new laws against all digital methods.
Check only whether the executive decision is right.

why.Allow the person to choose any punishmen: This wrongly lets criminals choose their own punishment.
why.Make new laws against all digital method: This gives the law-making job to the court instead of the legislature.
why.Check only whether the executive decisio: This misses the court’s power to check whether a law is fair.

activities.explanation: Courts can decide what action a cybercrime offender should face.

lessons.title: Separation of Powers and Three Tiers

activities.prompt: How can three government parts stay separate and still cooperate?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Government
activities.body:
Imagine you visit a government building and meet three separate organs. Good governance begins when they remain separate. Each organ has an expected role, and none should act beyond it. You watch each one stay within its role.

Yet the organs still interact and work together. Each organ can check what another organ is doing. You see them act like careful teammates, without taking one another's roles.

You notice how checking helps create balance. When the organs are not working together properly, they can restore balance. Working together and checking one another helps them do this.

Now you travel across India's levels of democratic government. A democratic government works at several levels. In India, it functions at three levels. You see local, state or regional, and national tiers.

Each level deals with different matters. A problem at home is usually checked at home before going to higher authorities. You now see why good governance needs separation, cooperation, and careful checks.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Working Together, Staying Separate
activities.body: Good government needs the three organs of government to stay separate. The organs are the three main parts of government. Each organ should do its own job. But the organs also work together. They check each other. They can bring back balance when things go wrong. India's government works at three levels: local, state or regional, and national. Each level handles different things.
keyPoints: Each organ should do its own job.
The organs work together and check each other.
India has three levels: local, state or regional, and national.
activities.explanation: Staying separate and working together both help good government.

activities.prompt: One government organ starts doing another organ's work. How should the organs respond?
steps: Each organ should stay in its expected role because no organ should act beyond it.
The organs should still work together because separate organs must also interact.
Each organ can check another organ's work because checks help correct imbalance.
They can restore balance together, so separation and teamwork can both exist.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Separate Government Organs
activities.prompt: How should the three organs of government act in good governance?
options: They should stay separate.
They should make all decisions together.
They should ignore each other.
They should act outside their jobs.
activities.explanation: Good governance needs the three organs to stay separate.

activities.title: Government Levels
activities.prompt: India’s democratic government functions at ______ levels.
activities.hint: Think of local, state or regional, and national.
activities.explanation: India’s democratic government functions at three levels.

activities.title: Government Connections
activities.prompt: Match each idea to its correct partner.
activities.explanation: Separation, checking, and different matters all support good governance.

activities.title: Order the Government Tiers
activities.prompt: Put India's government tiers in order from local to national.
activities.explanation: The three tiers are local, state or regional, and national.

activities.title: An Organ Does Another Job
activities.prompt: One organ does work that is not its job. What should it do?
options: Do the job of every other organ.
Stop all contact between the organs.
Stop and do only its own job.
Take away another organ's checking power.
activities.explanation: An organ should not do work that is not its job.

activities.title: Restore Balance
activities.prompt: The organs are not working together properly. What can they do?
options: Stop checking one another.
Give up all separate roles.
Ignore the problem completely.
Restore balance.
activities.explanation: The organs can restore balance when they are not working together properly.

activities.prompt: A colony reports a problem to local officials first. Why might this be the right step?
options: Local problems are usually checked at home before higher authorities.
Higher authorities always know local problems better than local offices.
Every problem belongs only to the highest level of government.
Going higher first prevents local offices from doing their work.

why.Higher authorities always know local pro: This mistake thinks higher authorities know local problems better.
why.Every problem belongs only to the highes: This mistake thinks each level does not have different matters.
why.Going higher first prevents local office: This mistake thinks local offices should not check home problems.

activities.explanation: This is right because home problems are usually checked at home first.

activities.prompt: One government organ takes over another organ's task. What should it do?
options: Stop and return to its expected role.
Keep taking every task that it can find.
Ask the other organ to stop working too.
Wait for higher authorities to make all choices.

This mistake thinks one organ may take over every role.
This mistake thinks separation means all organs should stop working.
why.Wait for higher authorities to make all: This mistake thinks cooperation means higher authorities control everything.

activities.explanation: This is right because an organ should not act beyond its expected role.

activities.prompt: A person carries a home problem straight to higher authorities. Why is this usually unwise?
options: A home problem should usually be checked at home first.
Higher authorities have no power over any problems.
Local offices check problems but never help solve them.
Home problems must always be sent to every level.

why.Higher authorities have no power over an: This mistake wrongly says higher authorities cannot handle problems.
why.Local offices check problems but never h: This mistake says local offices check problems without helping.
why.Home problems must always be sent to eve: This mistake thinks every level must always receive every problem.

activities.explanation: This is right because home problems are usually checked at home first.

activities.prompt: Two areas send different matters to different government levels. Why can this happen?
options: Each level of government deals with different matters.
Different levels must always handle identical matters.
One level has no matters while another has many.
Only the local level has powers over government matters.

why.Different levels must always handle iden: This mistake assumes every level handles the same work.
why.One level has no matters while another h: This mistake wrongly gives all matters to only some levels.
why.Only the local level has powers over gov: This mistake wrongly removes powers from higher levels.

activities.explanation: This is right because each level deals with different matters.

activities.prompt: Three organs work together, and each checks the others. Why is this good governance?
options: They stay separate, cooperate, and check one another.
They stay separate, so they should never cooperate.
They cooperate, so they no longer need checks.
They check each other, so roles no longer matter.

why.They stay separate, so they should never: This mistake wrongly treats separation as complete separation from teamwork.
why.They cooperate, so they no longer need c: This mistake thinks working together removes the need for checks.
why.They check each other, so roles no longe: This mistake thinks checking makes expected roles unimportant.

activities.explanation: This is right because good governance needs separation, cooperation, and checks.

lessons.title: Government at Local, State and National Levels

activities.prompt: Who helps people, and how are governments organised?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of India’s Governments
activities.body:
Imagine you are touring India and learning about its governments. You see local, State and Central levels. Each level has a different role during a flood, and you can follow their help.

You first visit a local government, which exists in India. Local authorities may deal with a small flood. When a flood affects several towns and villages, you look to the State Government. It can send rescue teams to help.

For a massive flood affecting vast areas, you look to Central Government help. This help can include relief supplies and the army.

Now you meet the Central Government. The President of India is the nominal head of the Central executive. The Prime Minister is the executive head of the Central Government. You also see the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha working together. They formulate national laws.

Next, you visit a State Government. Its assembly is called the Vidhan Sabha. The Governor is the nominal head of the State Government. The Chief Minister is its executive head. You finish your tour knowing that different levels can help during floods.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Three Levels of Government
activities.body: India has local, State, and Central governments. Local authorities can deal with small floods. The State Government can send rescue teams. The Central Government can help with huge floods. Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha make national laws. The President is the nominal head of the Central executive. Nominal means head in name only. The Prime Minister is the executive head of the Central Government. The Governor is the nominal head of a State Government. The Chief Minister is the executive head of a State Government.
keyPoints: Local authorities can deal with a small flood.
The State Government can send rescue teams.
The Central Government can help in a huge flood.
activities.explanation: Each level of government has its own duties for floods and leadership.

activities.prompt: A flood grows bigger. Which government should help at each stage?
steps: Local authorities may handle a small flood because the problem is small.
State rescue teams help when several towns and villages are affected.
The Central Government can help when a massive flood affects vast areas.
Therefore, wider floods need help from higher levels of government.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which level of government can deal with a small flood?
options: Local authorities
State Government
Central Government
President of India
activities.explanation: Local authorities may be able to deal with a small flood.

activities.prompt: The Prime Minister is the executive head of the ______ Government.
activities.hint: This level is also called the Union Government.
activities.explanation: The Prime Minister is the executive head of the Central Government.

activities.prompt: Who is the nominal head (head in name only) of the Central executive?
options: The Prime Minister
The Governor
The President of India
The Chief Minister
activities.explanation: The President is the nominal head of the Central executive.

activities.prompt: Match each group or leader to its work or role.
activities.explanation: Each pair matches the given assembly or leader with its stated role.

activities.prompt: Put these flood responses in order, from a small flood to a vast flood.
items: Local authorities deal with a small flood
State Government sends rescue teams when several towns and villages are affected
Central Government helps when a massive flood affects vast areas
activities.explanation: The responses grow from a small flood to a flood affecting vast areas.

activities.prompt: Which leader and role are correctly matched?
options: The President of India — executive head of the Central Government
The Prime Minister — nominal head of the Central executive
The Governor — nominal head of a State Government
The Chief Minister — nominal head of a State Government
activities.explanation: The Governor is the nominal head of a State Government. The Chief Minister is the executive head.

activities.prompt: A flood affects a small area in one town, and local authorities may act. Why is this suitable?
options: The problem is local, and local authorities may handle a small flood.
The problem is local, but the State Government always sends rescue teams.
The problem is local, but the Central Government must bring the army.
The problem is local, but the Governor must lead the rescue work.

why.The problem is local, but the State Gove: This mistake thinks every flood needs State rescue teams.
why.The problem is local, but the Central Go: This mistake thinks even one small flood needs the army.
why.The problem is local, but the Governor m: This mistake thinks a nominal head leads everyday rescue work.

activities.explanation: Local authorities may handle a small flood in their own area.

activities.prompt: A flood affects several towns and villages, so the State Government can send rescue teams. Why?
options: Several towns and villages need help beyond one small flood.
One town is flooded, so local authorities should do all the work.
Vast areas are affected, so the Central Government should send the army.
The Governor is nominal, so the Governor must send the teams.

why.One town is flooded, so local authoritie: This mistake ignores that the flood affects several towns and villages.
why.Vast areas are affected, so the Central: This mistake treats several towns like vast areas needing Central help.
why.The Governor is nominal, so the Governor: This mistake thinks a nominal head must do the rescue work.

activities.explanation: Several towns and villages make the flood wider than one small flood.

activities.prompt: A source places relief supplies and the army under Central help during a vast flood. What can we infer?
options: Central help can support a massive flood affecting vast areas.
Only a one-town flood needs Central help.
State law-making must include relief supplies and the army.
A nominal State head must organise all flood relief.

why.Only a one-town flood needs Central help: This mistake confuses one town with vast areas.
why.State law-making must include relief sup: This mistake mixes law-making with Central flood help.
why.A nominal State head must organise all f: This mistake thinks nominal heads lead all relief work.

activities.explanation: The source connects Central help with a vast flood and wide support.

activities.prompt: A group wants to make a law for the whole country. Which path can make it?
options: Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha can work together to formulate the law.
Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha should each make separate national laws.
The Vidhan Sabha should make this law for the whole country.
The Governor and Chief Minister should make the national law together.

why.Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha should each ma: This mistake thinks Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha should work separately.
why.The Vidhan Sabha should make this law fo: This mistake treats a State assembly as a national law-maker.
why.The Governor and Chief Minister should m: This mistake gives State leaders the work of making national laws.

activities.explanation: Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha work together to formulate national laws.

activities.prompt: A report calls the President the nominal head of Central executive. Who should lead Central Government work?
options: The Prime Minister, because the Prime Minister is the executive head.
The President, because the President leads daily Central Government work.
The Governor, because the Governor runs the Central Government.
The Chief Minister, because the Chief Minister runs the Central Government.

why.The President, because the President lea: This mistake thinks a nominal head leads daily Central work.
why.The Governor, because the Governor runs: This mistake mixes the State Governor with the Central Government.
why.The Chief Minister, because the Chief Mi: This mistake mixes the State Chief Minister with the Central Government.

activities.explanation: The Prime Minister is the executive head of the Central Government.

activities.prompt: A report calls the Governor the nominal head of a State Government. Who should lead State Government work?
options: The Chief Minister, because the Chief Minister is the executive head.
The Governor, because the Governor leads daily State Government work.
The Prime Minister, because the Prime Minister runs every State Government.
The President, because the President is the nominal head of every State.

why.The Governor, because the Governor leads: This mistake thinks a nominal head leads daily State work.
why.The Prime Minister, because the Prime Mi: This mistake gives the Prime Minister power over each State Government.
why.The President, because the President is: This mistake gives the President power over each State Government.

activities.explanation: The Chief Minister is the executive head of a State Government.

lessons.title: Leadership and Service to the People

activities.prompt: How can someone use knowledge and humility to serve a whole nation?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Leader for the People
activities.body:
You begin in Rameswaram, Tamil Nadu, where Dr A.P.J. Abdul Kalam was born in 1931. You learn that his family was humble. The story introduces you to a scientist who later served the people.

He became a renowned scientist. You soon understand why he was called the Missile Man of India. You explore his important role in India's space and missile programmes.

Next, you see him serve as India's 11th President from 2002 to 2007. Even as President, he remained connected to the people. You recognise that national leadership did not separate him from those he served.

Your tour also shows why he cared about good education and innovation. Although his presidential position was nominal, he could make a positive difference. His example demonstrates the impact a leader can have.

His humility and dedication inspired many people. He encouraged young Indians to dream big and work hard. You finish by recognising his power to impact countless lives.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: A Leader Who Served People
activities.body: Dr Abdul Kalam came from a humble family in Rameswaram, Tamil Nadu. He was a renowned scientist called the Missile Man of India. He played an important role in India’s space and missile programmes. As the 11th President, he remained connected to the people. He cared about good education and innovation. Innovation means new ideas. He encouraged young Indians to dream big and work hard.
keyPoints: He was a renowned scientist and the Missile Man of India.
He remained connected to people as President.
He encouraged education, new ideas, and hard work.
activities.explanation: Dr Abdul Kalam showed leadership by serving people and inspiring others.

activities.prompt: A student becomes class leader and wants to serve classmates. How should the student lead?
steps: Dr Kalam stayed connected to people, even as President, so a leader should listen.
He cared about education and innovation, so the student should support learning and new ideas.
His humility and dedication inspired others, so the student should work hard and encourage others.
This is leadership and service: the student helps people while staying humble.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Making a Positive Difference
activities.body: He was the President. He stayed close to the people. He cared about good education and innovation. Innovation means new ideas. He told young Indians to have big dreams and work hard. His humility (not thinking he was better than others) and hard work inspired many people. His position was nominal (it had little real power). Yet he made a positive difference.
keyPoints: He stayed close to the people.
He told young Indians to dream big and work hard.
He made a positive difference, even though his position was nominal.
activities.explanation: A good leader can inspire people and make a positive difference.

activities.prompt: What was Dr Abdul Kalam called?
options: The Father of Indian Space
The Missile Man of India
The Young People's Teacher
The Rameswaram Leader
activities.explanation: Yes! He was called the Missile Man of India.

activities.prompt: Dr Abdul Kalam was the ______ President of India. He served from 2002 to 2007.
activities.hint: Think about where he is in the list of Presidents.
activities.explanation: Well done! Dr Abdul Kalam was the 11th President of India.

activities.prompt: Dr Abdul Kalam was born in a humble family.
activities.explanation: Yes! He was born in a humble family in Rameswaram, Tamil Nadu.

activities.prompt: Match each part of his life with its description.
activities.explanation: You matched his early life, public work, and leadership qualities.

activities.prompt: Put these moments in time order.
items: His presidential term continued through 2002 to 2007
activities.explanation: The dates help you place his presidential term in the correct order.

activities.prompt: Which one best shows how Dr Abdul Kalam helped the people?
options: By caring about learning and new ideas
By avoiding people while in office
By telling young people not to dream
By caring only about his title as president
activities.explanation: Correct! He cared about learning, new ideas, and what people needed.

activities.prompt: Dr Kalam listened to people even while serving as President. What was the likely result?
options: People felt heard and supported by their President.
People felt ignored and distant from their President.
People gained less help from their President.
People stopped believing education and innovation mattered.

why.People felt ignored and distant from the: This reverses the effect of listening and caring for people.
why.People gained less help from their Presi: Listening gives the President more understanding, not less help.
why.People stopped believing education and i: Staying connected supports education and innovation instead of stopping care.

activities.explanation: Staying connected helps people feel heard and supported, which is right.

activities.prompt: Dr Kalam led science work and later served as President. Which quality helped in both?
options: Humility and dedication inspired people in every role.
Formal office gave him more power in every role.
Missile work made him care less about people.
Being President made him stop learning about science.

why.Formal office gave him more power in eve: Formal office was not what made his lasting personal impact.
why.Missile work made him care less about pe: His dedication to people continued alongside his missile work.
why.Being President made him stop learning a: This wrongly treats his two roles as opposing each other.

activities.explanation: Humility and dedication inspired people across his different roles.

activities.prompt: A museum panel shows his humble childhood and later national service. What does this source show?
options: He moved from a humble beginning to important national service.
His childhood mattered more than all his later service.
His later service began before his humble childhood began.
His early family life had no connection to his later service.

why.His childhood mattered more than all his: The source shows his later service, not that childhood mattered more.
why.His later service began before his humbl: His later work came after the humble childhood shown by the source.
why.His early family life had no connection: The source brings both parts together, so denying connection misunderstands it.

activities.explanation: The source places his humble family life before his major service.

activities.prompt: If the President has only a nominal position, what can Dr Kalam still do?
options: Use the office to encourage education, innovation, and public service.
Use the office to order every citizen to change jobs.
Do nothing, because a nominal position has no influence.
Stop listening, because formal power belongs only to the office.

why.Use the office to order every citizen to: This mistakes leadership for unlimited control over citizens.
why.Do nothing, because a nominal position h: This assumes a nominal position cannot make any positive difference.
why.Stop listening, because formal power bel: This wrongly says listening and public service need formal power.

activities.explanation: Even a nominal position can positively encourage education and service.

activities.prompt: Why did Dr Kalam keep meeting and listening to people as President?
options: He understood that real leadership begins with staying connected to people.
He believed that ordinary people should not influence national decisions.
He wanted people to forget their needs while government work continued.
He thought listening to people would remove his knowledge and experience.

why.He believed that ordinary people should: This mistakes staying connected for shutting people out.
why.He wanted people to forget their needs w: This reverses his care; he listened rather than ignored needs.
why.He thought listening to people would rem: This wrongly assumes listening removes knowledge and experience.

activities.explanation: He remained connected to people because that supported his leadership.

activities.prompt: A student wants to follow Dr Kalam's example and serve others. What should the student do?
options: Listen to others, work hard, and encourage big dreams.
Wait for a formal office before helping anyone.
Focus only on personal fame and avoid working with others.
Ask everyone to stop dreaming and leave difficult work undone.

why.Wait for a formal office before helping: This wrongly thinks service must wait for formal power.
why.Focus only on personal fame and avoid wo: This mistakes fame for the humble service he demonstrated.
why.Ask everyone to stop dreaming and leave: This reverses his message to dream big and work hard.

activities.explanation: He listened, worked hard, and encouraged others to dream big.

lessons.title: Democracy and Grassroots Democracy

activities.prompt: How can ordinary people influence decisions about the country they live in?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Your Journey Through Democracy
activities.body:
Imagine your journey beginning with the word democracy. It comes from two Greek words. The word kratos means rule or power. Together, they mean the rule of the people. Democracy is a foundation stone of governance in most countries.

At State and national levels, you vote for elected representatives. MLAs represent people at State level, while MPs represent them nationally. These elected members discuss laws, problems and solutions in assemblies. India is a representative democracy.

Imagine yourself visiting an assembly. Elected members discuss laws and consider problems. They also search for solutions. In direct democracy, every participant's opinion is taken into account when a decision is made.

During elections in 2024, India had about 970 million voters. If you are an Indian citizen above 18, you can participate in elections. Your vote helps choose MLAs at State level and MPs nationally.

Now compare representative and direct democracy. In representative democracy, you elect members to represent you. In direct democracy, every participant's opinion is taken into account. Which route seems closer to democracy's literal meaning, rule by the people?
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: What is democracy?
activities.body: Democracy is the base of how most countries are governed. The word democracy comes from two Greek words. Kratos means rule or power. Democracy means rule of the people. India is a representative democracy. At state level and national level, people vote for representatives. MLAs represent people at state level. MPs represent people at national level.
keyPoints: Democracy means rule of the people.
India is a representative democracy.
MLAs and MPs represent people at different levels.
activities.explanation: Democracy lets people choose representatives by voting.

activities.prompt: People at state level want a new law. Should they decide everything themselves or vote for representatives?
steps: At state level, people vote for elected representatives because the people need representation.
MLAs represent people at state level because they are elected members.
MLAs discuss laws, problems and solutions in assemblies because that is their work.
Therefore, people vote for MLAs, and the MLAs discuss the new law in an assembly.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What does democracy literally mean?
options: The rule of the people
The power of one leader
The rule of a small group
The work of elected representatives
activities.explanation: The word democracy literally means the rule of the people.

activities.prompt: The Greek word kratos means rule or power.
activities.explanation: Kratos is one of the Greek words used to form democracy.

activities.prompt: Democracy literally means the rule of the ______.
activities.hint: Think about who holds the power.
activities.explanation: Democracy means the rule of the people.

activities.prompt: Match each idea with its matching fact.
activities.explanation: MLAs work at State level, while MPs work at national level.

activities.prompt: Put these ideas in order from word roots to voting.
items: Democracy comes from two Greek words
Democracy means the rule of the people
activities.explanation: The word's meaning leads to the idea of people choosing representatives.

activities.prompt: Which elected member represents people at State level?
options: An MLA
An MP
Both an MLA and an MP
Neither an MLA nor an MP
activities.explanation: MLAs represent people at State level, and MPs represent people nationally.

activities.prompt: Indian citizens older than 18 can take part in elections.
activities.explanation: The lesson says citizens older than 18 can take part in elections.

activities.prompt: What happens in a direct democracy when people make a decision?
options: Every person's opinion is counted
Only one person's opinion is counted
Only elected leaders decide
No person's opinion is counted
activities.explanation: In a direct democracy, every person's opinion is counted.

activities.prompt: India had about 970 million voters in 2024. Why does this not show direct democracy?
options: Because people vote for elected representatives at state and national levels.
Because only elected representatives vote in elections.
Because direct democracy uses only elected representatives.
Because all voters discuss laws in assemblies.

why.Because only elected representatives vot: This wrongly says only elected representatives can vote.
why.Because direct democracy uses only elect: This wrongly makes representatives part of direct democracy.
why.Because all voters discuss laws in assem: This wrongly treats every voter as an assembly member.

activities.explanation: India is representative democracy, so voters choose representatives rather than decide directly.

activities.prompt: Many people vote at state and national levels. Why do they choose representatives instead of making every decision alone?
options: Because representatives discuss laws, problems and solutions in assemblies.
Because direct democracy also uses elected representatives.
Because voting for representatives means voting on every law.
Because all voters meet to discuss laws in assemblies.

why.Because direct democracy also uses elect: This wrongly treats elected representatives as part of direct democracy.
why.Because voting for representatives means: This confuses choosing representatives with deciding on every law.
why.Because all voters meet to discuss laws: This wrongly assumes that every voter joins an assembly.

activities.explanation: Representatives discuss laws, problems and solutions in assemblies after people vote for them.

activities.context: During a school examination, a student notices that rules apply to both students and teachers. Before leaving home, the student followed the simple rules expected by the family. On the way to school, road users obeyed traffic rules. The student wonders how society is governed, whether its rules can change, and whether citizens can have a say.
activities.prompt: What should the student do when a school rule is different from a rule expected at home?
options: Follow the rules that apply in each place.
Follow only the home rules because families make them.
Ignore school rules whenever they differ from home rules.
Treat traffic rules as optional on the way to school.

why.Follow only the home rules because famil: Home rules do not replace the rules that apply at school.
why.Ignore school rules whenever they differ: Students must follow school rules as well as family rules.
why.Treat traffic rules as optional on the w: Road users must obey traffic rules.

activities.explanation: Different rules apply in different places, such as homes and schools.

activities.context: During a school examination, a student notices that rules apply to both students and teachers. Before leaving home, the student followed the simple rules expected by the family. On the way to school, road users obeyed traffic rules. The student wonders how society is governed, whether its rules can change, and whether citizens can have a say.
activities.prompt: A group of citizens wants a change to a law. What can they do?
options: They can express their views about changing it.
They must keep silent because citizens cannot have a say.
They can make any law change they want immediately.
They must accept that laws must always remain fixed forever.

why.They must keep silent because citizens c: Citizens do have a say, even though government makes the rules.
why.They can make any law change they want i: Citizens can raise their views but do not make any change immediately.
why.They must accept that laws must always r: Laws and rules can be changed instead of remaining fixed forever.

activities.explanation: Citizens can have a say about the laws and rules governing society.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between rules and laws, and say whether they can change.
activities.answer: Rules guide how people behave in places such as homes, schools, examinations and roads. Laws are especially important rules. Both rules and laws can be changed when people decide they should be changed. Governance organises society and helps make sure that rules are followed.
points: Rules apply in homes, schools, examinations and on roads.
Laws are especially important rules.
Rules and laws can be changed.
Governance helps ensure that rules are followed.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A criminal used digital technology to steal money, so the activity became cybercrime. The legislature, made up of an assembly of representatives of the people, passed a new law against cybercrime and can update or remove it. The executive put the law into action. When the case reaches court, the judiciary decides whether the criminal broke the law and what action should be taken. Cybercriminals can be fined and sent to jail.
activities.prompt: What should happen when the cybercrime case reaches the courts?
options: The court determines whether the digital theft broke the law and chooses the consequence.
The legislature hears the case and decides the sentence.
The executive investigates the case and decides whether jail is needed.
The representatives of the people update the law before deciding the case.

why.The legislature hears the case and decid: Making and updating laws is the legislature’s work.
why.The executive investigates the case and: The executive implements laws rather than deciding cases.
why.The representatives of the people update: The legislature makes laws rather than judging individual cases.

activities.explanation: The judiciary decides whether someone broke the law and what action they should face.

activities.context: A criminal used digital technology to steal money, so the activity became cybercrime. The legislature, made up of an assembly of representatives of the people, passed a new law against cybercrime and can update or remove it. The executive put the law into action. When the case reaches court, the judiciary decides whether the criminal broke the law and what action should be taken. Cybercriminals can be fined and sent to jail.
activities.prompt: Which power can the courts exercise while dealing with the cybercrime law?
options: They can check whether the law is fair and whether an executive decision was right.
They can remove the cybercrime law from the records.
They can write a replacement law for the legislature.
They can carry out the law by arranging the punishment.

why.They can remove the cybercrime law from: The legislature can sometimes update or remove existing laws.
why.They can write a replacement law for the: The legislature makes and updates laws.
why.They can carry out the law by arranging: The executive implements or executes laws.

activities.explanation: Courts can check the fairness of laws and the correctness of executive decisions.

activities.prompt: Explain how the cybercrime example shows the three branches of government working together.
activities.answer: The legislature makes new laws and can update or remove existing laws. The executive implements or executes those laws. The judiciary decides whether someone has broken a law and what action the person should face. Cybercrime shows all three branches working together to deal with a new criminal problem.
points: The legislature makes and can update or remove laws.
The executive implements or executes laws.
The judiciary decides whether a law was broken and what action should follow.
The example shows all three branches working together.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A resident takes a problem at home to the local level of government. The local organ deals with the matter, while the state or regional and national organs handle their own different responsibilities. Later, one organ tries to act beyond its expected role. Another organ examines what it has done, and the organs work together again so that government remains balanced.
activities.prompt: Where should the resident's home problem usually be dealt with first?
options: The tier closest to the person's home
The state or regional tier
The national tier
All three tiers at the same time

why.The state or regional tier: Wrong: The state or regional tier is a higher level.
why.The national tier: Wrong: The national tier is also a higher level.
why.All three tiers at the same time: Wrong: A home problem is not normally sent everywhere at once.

activities.explanation: Correct: A problem at home is usually checked at home first.

activities.context: A resident takes a problem at home to the local level of government. The local organ deals with the matter, while the state or regional and national organs handle their own different responsibilities. Later, one organ tries to act beyond its expected role. Another organ examines what it has done, and the organs work together again so that government remains balanced.
activities.prompt: If the three organs stop working together properly, what should they do?
options: Each organ should check the others and help bring the system back into balance
One organ should handle every organ's responsibilities
Every problem should be sent to the national level without any checking
Each organ should work alone without interacting with the others

why.One organ should handle every organ's re: Wrong: Giving one organ every duty would remove separation.
why.Every problem should be sent to the nati: Wrong: This ignores the usual home-first approach.
why.Each organ should work alone without int: Wrong: Working alone removes interaction and checking.

activities.explanation: Correct: The organs can check one another and restore balance.

activities.prompt: Explain why the organs of government should remain separate but still work together.
activities.answer: Separation keeps each organ within its expected role. Cooperation allows the organs to work together even though they remain separate. By checking what the others are doing, each organ can help restore balance when things go wrong. This supports democratic government at local, state or regional, and national levels.
points: Each organ stays within its expected role.
The organs interact and cooperate.
Each organ can check the work of the others.
They can restore balance when cooperation weakens.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: Explain how the local, State and Central governments can help during different scales of flooding.
activities.answer: At the local level, authorities can deal with a small flood. When several towns and villages are affected, the State Government can send rescue teams. If a massive flood affects vast areas, the Central Government can help, including by providing relief supplies and the army.
points: Local authorities can deal with a small flood.
The State Government can send rescue teams to several affected towns and villages.
The Central Government can help when a massive flood affects vast areas.
Central help can include relief supplies and the army.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: When Dr Abdul Kalam became President, he could have used his authority to distance himself. His concern for education and innovation would become weaker.

why.His connection with people would become: He could remain connected to people through other forms of service.
why.His service would matter less than his p: His service already mattered more to him than the formal title.

activities.context: When Dr Abdul Kalam became President, he could have used his authority to distance himself. Instead, he remained connected to the people and cared about good education and innovation. Talking with young Indians, he encouraged them to dream big and work hard. The limited power of his office gave him complete freedom to act.

why.The limited power of his office gave him: A nominal position did not provide unlimited control or authority.
why.His scientific fame automatically made e: Scientific renown alone could not guarantee effective leadership.
why.His formal title mattered more than his: His influence came from personal service rather than the title alone.

activities.prompt: How did Kalam's humility and dedication help him serve and influence people?

His dedication expressed itself through his concern for good education and innovation and through encouraging young Indians to dream big and work hard. These qualities inspired many people, helping him make a positive difference in countless lives.
points: He remained connected despite his presidential position.
He cared about good education and innovation.
He encouraged young Indians to dream big and work hard.

activities.context: A neighbourhood group in India wants to discuss a local problem. why.A representative process, because the gr: Election of one person is a feature of representative democracy.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between representative democracy and direct democracy.
activities.answer: In representative democracy, people vote for representatives. These members represent people at State or national level and discuss laws, problems and solutions in assemblies.
