lessons.title: Citizen Voice and Shared Responsibility

activities.prompt: What can your voice change about the place where you live?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Your Voice, Your Community
activities.body:
Imagine you are walking through a busy city. Tall buildings rise around you, and crowds fill the streets. Many people rush past you, and the noise can feel louder than village life.

City residents may live independently and might not know their neighbours well. Yet you can still show community spirit when someone needs help. After heavy rains, a house collapsed. Dozens of people gathered to clear the rubble and check that nobody was trapped. Their community spirit shone brightly.

Think about how local decisions are made in your neighbourhood. Urban local bodies have elected representatives. These representatives speak for citizens and their interests. Members of village and urban local bodies are elected. In villages, community members also make decisions together.

In a village, people often know one another and help each other. They work together in the fields and celebrate festivals together. Back in the city, your voice remains just as important. Every voice matters in democracy, even when city democracy seems more complicated. Speak up and take part in your community. You can help your neighbours, too.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Living Together in Cities and Villages
activities.body: City life is busy, crowded and noisy. People there often rush. People in cities may be independent. They may not know their neighbours. But cities can show strong community spirit. In heavy rain, a house fell down. Dozens of people came together. They cleared away the broken pieces. They checked for people stuck inside. Democracy gives everyone a voice. Elected local representatives speak for citizens.
keyPoints: Cities are busy, crowded and noisy.
Communities can help people in hard times.
Everyone's voice matters in democracy.
activities.explanation: People live differently in cities and villages. They can still share responsibility.

activities.prompt: In a busy city, how can every citizen have a voice?
steps: Busy, crowded city life can make democracy seem complicated.
Urban local bodies have elected representatives, so citizens can be heard.
These representatives are elected members, so citizens can choose them.
Therefore every citizen’s voice matters, even in a complicated city.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What Is City Life Like?
activities.prompt: Which description fits city life?
options: Busy and crowded, with many tall buildings
Quiet and empty, with very few people
Always slow, with nobody rushing around
Filled with people who always know their neighbours
activities.explanation: Cities are busy and crowded, with many tall buildings and people rushing around.

activities.title: Village Life Together
activities.prompt: Match each village activity with its matching action.
activities.explanation: Villagers work together, celebrate together, and make decisions together.

activities.title: Helping After the House Fell
activities.prompt: A house fell down in heavy rain. What did city people do?
options: They waited for someone else to clear the broken bricks
They left without checking if anyone was hurt
They came together to clear bricks and find people stuck inside
They only talked about it with their neighbours
activities.explanation: Many people came together, cleared the bricks, and checked that nobody was stuck inside.

activities.title: Every Voice Matters
activities.prompt: Everyone's voice matters in democracy. Even in cities, democracy can seem more ______.
activities.hint: Democracy in a city can seem hard to understand.
activities.explanation: Democracy may seem complicated in a city. But everyone's voice still matters.

activities.title: A Community Helps
activities.prompt: Put the events in the correct order.
items: They clear rubble and check for trapped people
activities.explanation: Heavy rains came first, then the collapse, and then people worked together to help.

activities.title: Who Speaks for Citizens?
activities.prompt: City leaders are chosen by vote. What do they do?
options: They speak only for buildings
They speak for citizens and their needs
They take away every citizen's voice
They decide citizens need not take part
activities.explanation: City leaders chosen by vote speak for citizens and their needs.

activities.prompt: After heavy rain, a house collapsed in a city. Many residents did not know each other well. Why did they still help?
options: They felt shared responsibility for people in their community.
They all knew each other well before the house fell.
Only elected representatives were allowed to clear the rubble.
Helping neighbours was a special duty for city officials.

why.They all knew each other well before the: This mistake thinks helping requires knowing every neighbour beforehand.
why.Only elected representatives were allowe: This mistake thinks elected representatives should do all the work.
why.Helping neighbours was a special duty fo: This mistake treats helping as an official duty rather than citizen responsibility.

activities.explanation: This is right because helping after a collapse shows shared community responsibility.

activities.prompt: Village communities make decisions together. Cities have elected representatives. How do citizens choose members of both local bodies?
options: Citizens in both places choose local body members through elections.
Only city residents vote, while villages choose members without elections.
Village members are chosen by city representatives, not by citizens.
Both places appoint all local members without any citizen choice.

why.Only city residents vote, while villages: This mistake confuses making decisions together with having no elections.
why.Village members are chosen by city repre: This mistake reverses the choice of representatives and the citizens who choose them.
why.Both places appoint all local members wi: This mistake ignores the elections held for local body members.

activities.explanation: This is right because members of both village and urban local bodies are elected.

activities.prompt: A simple map shows many tall buildings and very crowded roads. What kind of place does this most likely show?
options: A busy and crowded city with many tall buildings.
A quiet village where people rarely leave their homes.
A countryside area with few roads and no buildings.
A noisy village where everyone works in nearby fields.

why.A quiet village where people rarely leav: This mistake ignores the tall buildings and crowded roads on the map.
why.A countryside area with few roads and no: This mistake contradicts the many buildings and crowded roads on the map.
why.A noisy village where everyone works in: This mistake mixes village work in fields with the city shown on the map.

activities.explanation: This is right because the map shows features of a busy, crowded city.

activities.prompt: A city has many neighbourhoods and needs local decisions. Citizens want their interests represented. How should its local body be formed?
options: By electing representatives to speak for citizens and their interests.
By choosing only people from the busiest part of the city.
By letting neighbours decide every issue without any elections.
By giving all decisions to people who do not live there.

why.By choosing only people from the busiest: This mistake ignores the interests and voices of citizens in other neighbourhoods.
why.By letting neighbours decide every issue: This mistake ignores the elections held for urban local body members.
why.By giving all decisions to people who do: This mistake removes citizens from the choosing and representing process.

activities.explanation: This is right because urban local bodies elect representatives for citizens’ interests.

activities.prompt: Dozens of people gathered after a house collapsed. They cleared rubble and checked for trapped people. What does this show about their actions?
options: They worked together to care for their community after the collapse.
They only came because they knew every person inside.
They were electing representatives for the local body.
They gathered because city life is always noisy and crowded.

why.They only came because they knew every p: This mistake wrongly assumes people need to know everyone before helping.
why.They were electing representatives for t: This mistake confuses helping after a collapse with choosing local representatives.
why.They gathered because city life is alway: This mistake gives an everyday city feature as the reason for their help.

activities.explanation: This is right because their shared work showed community spirit and responsibility.

activities.prompt: A city meeting feels busy and complicated. One resident has an important concern. What should happen to that resident’s voice?
options: It should be heard because every voice matters in democracy.
It should wait because only representatives have proper voices.
It should be ignored because residents may not know neighbours.
It should count only if other residents approve it first.

why.It should wait because only representati: This mistake wrongly gives only representatives the right to be heard.
why.It should be ignored because residents m: This mistake wrongly thinks not knowing neighbours cancels a citizen’s voice.
why.It should count only if other residents: This mistake makes one citizen’s voice depend on other citizens’ approval.

activities.explanation: This is right because everyone’s voice matters in democracy, even in a city.

activities.context: Residents in a city have different needs and want a say in decisions affecting urban life. They approach the city government and ask to be included in decision-making. The government agrees that citizens should have a meaningful role. Their request reflects an approach in which power is shared, allowing people to take part rather than remain outside public decisions.
activities.prompt: If the city follows the approach in the case, what should happen next?
options: Residents should gain a role in decisions affecting city life.
Residents should receive information only after decisions are final.
The Union Government should make every urban decision without residents.
Citizen participation should end because urban governance is complex.

why.Residents should receive information onl: Listening after decisions are final does not share decision-making power.
why.The Union Government should make every u: The Union Government is at the top, but urban decisions are not taken only by it.
why.Citizen participation should end because: Complexity does not remove the need for participation.

activities.explanation: Good governance aims to empower citizens to take part.

activities.context: Residents in a city have different needs and want a say in decisions affecting urban life. They approach the city government and ask to be included in decision-making. The government agrees that citizens should have a meaningful role. Their request reflects an approach in which power is shared, allowing people to take part rather than remain outside public decisions.
activities.prompt: What would happen if the city stopped sharing power with residents?
options: Participatory democracy would weaken because citizens could not share decisions.
Participatory democracy would strengthen because decisions would become faster.
Urban governance would become simpler because diversity would disappear.
Rural governance would replace urban governance in the pyramid.

why.Participatory democracy would strengthen: Removing participation weakens this idea rather than strengthening it.
why.Urban governance would become simpler be: Greater complexity does not make urban diversity disappear.
why.Rural governance would replace urban gov: Rural and urban governance remain different parts of the pyramid.

activities.explanation: Sharing power in decision-making is the central idea of participatory democracy.

activities.context: A town is divided into wards. In one ward, residents notice a blocked drain and a leaking water pipe. The ward committee has noticed both problems. In another part of the town, residents are concerned about single-use plastics. The committee also learns that ward work is organised differently in another State. Residents believe that their local community should have a direct say in managing these matters.
activities.prompt: After noticing the blocked drain, what should the ward committee do next?
options: Send the problem to the authorities.
Organise a health camp about it.
Run a campaign against single-use plastics instead.
Watch for more problems before reporting this one.

Health camps are activities, but they do not report the drain.
why.Run a campaign against single-use plasti: A plastics campaign would address a different issue.
why.Watch for more problems before reporting: Waiting would leave the known problem unreported.

activities.explanation: A blocked drain is a problem that ward committees report.

activities.context: A town is divided into wards. In one ward, residents notice a blocked drain and a leaking water pipe. The ward committee has noticed both problems. In another part of the town, residents are concerned about single-use plastics. The committee also learns that ward work is organised differently in another State. options: Ward functioning can vary from one State to another.

Ward committees help local communities and report problems.
why.Only one State can organise ward activit: More than one State can organise ward activities.

activities.explanation: The way wards function differs between States.

activities.context: Residents of an area noticed that waste was being mixed and a water pipe was leaking near the street. activities.prompt: The residents find that their waste has been mixed together. What should they do next?
options: Separate the waste correctly and follow the segregation instructions.
Leave all the waste mixed until collection time.
Move the mixed waste to another area without sorting it.
Leave the sorting entirely to the local body.

why.Leave all the waste mixed until collecti: Mixed waste does not help the collection process.
why.Move the mixed waste to another area wit: Moving waste elsewhere does not correct the separation problem.
why.Leave the sorting entirely to the local: Citizens also have a duty to separate waste correctly.

activities.context: Residents of an area noticed that waste was being mixed and a water pipe was leaking near the street. Urban local bodies will need to perform fewer functions.
Citizens will no longer need to report local problems.
Garbage collection will become more difficult for the local body.

why.Urban local bodies will need to perform: The range of local-body functions does not depend on one citizen action.
why.Citizens will no longer need to report l: Reporting problems remains a useful citizen duty.
why.Garbage collection will become more diff: Careful waste separation makes garbage collection easier.

activities.explanation: Performing duties helps local bodies work efficiently.

activities.context: At a civic-history display, a student learns that the Greater Chennai Corporation was formerly the Madras Corporation, established on 29 September 1688 and India’s oldest municipal institution. Use the present-day Chennai title and leave out the institution’s earlier name.
Use Bombay Municipal Corporation as the earlier title because the panel discusses another municipal corporation.
Keep the earlier Madras title as the main label because Greater Mumbai is the only body with a changed name.

why.Use the present-day Chennai title and le: Removing the earlier name would hide part of the institution’s history.
why.Use Bombay Municipal Corporation as the: Bombay Municipal Corporation was the earlier title associated with Greater Mumbai.
why.Keep the earlier Madras title as the mai: Greater Chennai Corporation also has a present-day title different from its earlier name.

activities.explanation: The display should show both the current and former identities.

activities.context: At a civic-history display, a student learns that the Greater Chennai Corporation was formerly the Madras Corporation, established on 29 September 1688 and India’s oldest municipal institution. The East India Company issued its charter in the previous year, covering Fort St. George and nearby territories. A panel mentions Greater Mumbai’s earlier title, the Bombay Municipal Corporation, created in 1865.

The earlier charter alone would still have marked the proper start of municipal administration.
The later renaming would have marked the proper start instead.
The creation of the Bombay body would have marked Chennai’s proper start.

why.The earlier charter alone would still ha: The earlier charter alone did not provide municipal taxing power.
why.The later renaming would have marked the: A later change in the corporation’s name was not the stated starting point.
why.The creation of the Bombay body would ha: The Bombay body’s creation was unrelated to Chennai’s municipal administration.

activities.explanation: Municipal administration properly began when the city gained taxing power.

activities.prompt: Explain why the creation of the Madras Corporation and the proper beginning of municipal administration were different events.
activities.answer: The Madras Corporation was created on 29 September 1688 under a charter issued by the East India Company a year earlier. Municipal administration properly began later, when Parliament’s 1792 Act gave power to levy municipal taxes. Therefore, the corporation’s creation and the proper beginning of municipal administration were different events.
points: The corporation was created on 29 September 1688.
Its charter was issued by the East India Company a year earlier.
The 1792 Act gave the city power to levy municipal taxes.
Proper municipal administration began when taxing power was granted.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between a Municipal Corporation and a Municipal Council.
activities.answer: A Municipal Corporation is the highest urban body in cities with more than 10 lakh residents, such as Chennai and Indore. It is also called Mahanagar Nigam. A Municipal Council is the highest body in cities with 1–10 lakh residents and is also called Nagar Palika.
points: A Municipal Corporation serves cities with more than 10 lakhs.
Chennai and Indore have Municipal Corporations.
Municipal Corporation is also called Mahanagar Nigam.
Municipal Council is also called Nagar Paliki.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: If city residents knew their neighbours as well as many villagers do, what would probably happen when another emergency occurs?

They would rely more on elected representatives to do all the helping.
They would become less likely to take part in local decisions.
They would usually ignore the needs of people around them.

why.They would rely more on elected represen: Representatives represent interests but do not replace neighbours helping.
why.They would become less likely to take pa: Knowing neighbours can support, rather than weaken, collective decisions.
why.They would usually ignore the needs of p: This is opposite to the mutual help common in villages.

Although city life is busy, noisy, and often makes residents seem independent, the emergency brought out their community spirit. Only people who joined the rubble-clearing work
All citizens affected by local decisions

why.Only people who joined the rubble-cleari: Helpers are not the only citizens whose interests matter.
why.Only people who work together in village: Village field workers are not the deciding group for an urban local body.

activities.prompt: Explain why a village community may respond to a crisis differently from a city community.
activities.answer: Village residents often know one another and help each other. They also work together and make decisions together. These ties can make community action easier. City residents are often more independent and may not know their neighbours, but the collapsed-house case shows that they can still come together in an emergency.
points: Village residents often know one another.
They work and make decisions together.
City residents may be more independent.
City residents can still show community spirit.

chapters.title: The Value of Work
chapters.summary: In this chapter: the work around us; economic and non-economic activities; types of economic activities; payments and value addition.

lessons.title: The Work Around Us

activities.prompt: What work surrounds you at home and in your neighbourhood?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Work
activities.body:
You begin your tour when Geeta Aunty returns home from work. She is wearing her uniform. You soon learn that she is a pilot in the Indian Air Force. Her job is one of the works around you.

At Kabir’s home, you meet his grandfather. He has retired from the Border Security Force. Now, he tends the vegetable garden and runs errands for the home. You see two tasks that now fill his daily life.

At Anu’s home, you meet her parents. They sell uniforms and other ready-made garments. Anu’s mother is usually home when the children return from school. She contributes to a voluntary group that teaches stitching. Her contribution is another kind of work around you.

You then meet Rohan, a software engineer. At weekends, he volunteers to teach computer skills. Free Geography classes are also provided for children in the neighbourhood. You finish your tour with a clear view of work around you.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Work Around Us
activities.body: People around us have different jobs. Geeta Aunty is a pilot in the Indian Air Force. Kabir's grandfather left the Border Security Force. Now he takes care of a vegetable garden. He also does small jobs for his home. Anu's parents sell uniforms and ready-made clothes. Anu's mother teaches sewing in a volunteer group. Rohan is a software engineer. On weekends, he teaches computer skills. Free Geography classes are given to children nearby.
keyPoints: People have different kinds of work.
Some people help their family and neighbours.
Some work is teaching and helping others.
activities.explanation: This lesson shows many kinds of work around us.

activities.prompt: Anu’s mother is usually home when children return. Can we say she has no work?
steps: Anu’s mother is usually home, but her parents sell uniforms and ready-made garments.
So being home does not mean there is no family work.
She contributes to a group that teaches stitching, so her work also helps others.
Therefore, she is not free from work just because she is usually home.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Who is a pilot in the Indian Air Force?
options: Geeta Aunty
Anu’s mother
Rohan
Kabir’s grandfather
activities.explanation: Geeta Aunty is the pilot in the Indian Air Force.

activities.prompt: Geeta Aunty works as a ______ in the Indian Air Force.
activities.hint: She flies an aircraft.
activities.explanation: the lesson says Geeta Aunty is a pilot.

activities.prompt: What does Anu’s mother contribute to?
options: A voluntary group that teaches stitching
A group that teaches computer skills
A group that provides free Geography classes
A shop selling uniforms and garments
activities.explanation: Anu’s mother contributes to a voluntary group that teaches stitching.

activities.prompt: Match each person with the work mentioned.
pairs: pilot in the Indian Air Force
activities.explanation: Each person or family has a different kind of work.

activities.prompt: What does Kabir’s grandfather do now?
options: He teaches computer skills at weekends.
He tends a vegetable garden and runs home errands.
He sells uniforms and ready-made garments.
He provides free Geography classes.
activities.explanation: After retirement, he tends the garden and runs home errands.

activities.prompt: Which statement correctly describes two forms of learning support?
options: Rohan teaches computer skills, and free Geography classes are provided.
Anu’s mother teaches Geography, and Rohan sells uniforms.
Kabir’s grandfather teaches stitching, and Geeta runs Geography classes.
Anu’s parents teach computer skills, and Kabir sells garments.
activities.explanation: Rohan teaches computer skills, while free Geography classes are also provided.

activities.prompt: Anu’s mother is usually home when children return. A child says she has no work. What is the best evidence against this?
options: She wears a uniform when the children return.
She stays near the school gate every afternoon.
She buys vegetables for the family after lunch.
She helps sell uniforms with her husband.

why.She wears a uniform when the children re: A uniform alone does not show that she sells uniforms.
why.She stays near the school gate every aft: Staying near the school does not show family or group work.
why.She buys vegetables for the family after: Buying vegetables is a home duty, not evidence of selling uniforms.

activities.explanation: Her family sells uniforms and ready-made garments, so she has family work.

activities.prompt: Kabir’s grandfather retired from the Border Security Force. He now tends a garden and runs errands. What changed?
options: He stopped doing every kind of work.
He only tends the garden and does no errands.
His work changed from service to home tasks.
His errands now take the place of his garden.

Retirement ended one job, but it did not end all work.
why.He only tends the garden and does no err: The fact says that he also runs errands for the home.
why.His errands now take the place of his ga: He still tends the garden, so errands did not replace it.

activities.explanation: He retired from service and now tends a garden and runs errands.

activities.prompt: A weekend notice says Rohan teaches computer skills. He is a software engineer. What differs?
options: Weekend teaching is extra to his software engineering work.
Both roles are the same because both involve computers.
Weekend teaching means he stopped being a software engineer.
He teaches computer skills only on weekdays.

why.Both roles are the same because both inv: Using computers does not make teaching and engineering the same job.
why.Weekend teaching means he stopped being: Volunteering at weekends does not end his job as an engineer.
why.He teaches computer skills only on weekd: The fact says he teaches computer skills at weekends, not weekdays.

activities.explanation: Rohan’s job is software engineering, while weekend teaching is volunteering.

activities.prompt: Anu’s mother is usually home. Geeta Aunty returns home as a pilot. Why do their days look different?
options: One has no work; the other works only at home.
One helps with family trade; the other serves as a pilot.
Both do the same work in different clothes.
One tends a garden; the other teaches stitching.

why.One has no work; the other works only at: This mistakes home duties for no work and ignores Geeta Aunty’s pilot work.
why.Both do the same work in different cloth: Different roles and places do not make their work the same.
why.One tends a garden; the other teaches st: This gives Geeta Aunty Kabir’s grandfather’s garden duty.

activities.explanation: Anu’s mother helps with the family trade, while Geeta Aunty serves as a pilot.

lessons.title: Economic and Non-Economic Activities

activities.prompt: Which activities are economic, and which are non-economic?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Market Tour
activities.body:
Imagine that you are visiting a market. People exchange goods and services around you. A market is where these exchanges happen. You can exchange goods for other goods. Services can be exchanged for other services.

Watch the people working. Economic activities involve money or payment in money’s worth. Money’s worth is the monetary value a person places on an object. A fee is payment for professional advice or services. You pay this fee for such help.

Geeta Aunty receives a salary for serving the country. Her work is an economic activity because she is paid. Rohan receives a salary for working for a software company. His paid work is economic too.

However, not every activity brings payment. Activities are divided into economic and non-economic activities. Non-economic activities do not generate income or wealth. You see Rohan volunteering during the weekend. His weekend volunteering is a non-economic activity.

You also care for your grandparents. Youth doing this is non-economic. At the market, you saw money and exchanges. You also saw volunteering without income. Now you can tell the kinds apart.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Understanding Economic Activities
activities.body: There are two kinds of activities: economic and non-economic. Economic activities involve money, or payment in money's worth. Money's worth means the amount of money a person thinks an object is worth. A market is a place where people trade goods (things you buy) and services. Goods and services can also be swapped for other goods and services. A fee is money paid for expert advice or services. Non-economic activities do not earn money or wealth.
keyPoints: Economic activities involve money or things worth money.
Non-economic activities do not earn money or wealth.
A market is a place where people trade goods and services.
activities.explanation: Payments show economic activities. Activities without earnings are non-economic.

activities.prompt: A child receives advice and pays a professional a fee. Is this activity economic?
steps: The child receives professional advice from a professional.
The child pays a fee, which is payment for advice.
Payment means money or money’s worth is involved.
Therefore, the activity is economic because payment is received.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Spotting an Economic Activity
activities.prompt: Which statement about economic activities is correct?
options: They do not involve money or payment.
They involve money or payment in money’s worth.
They always involve a fee.
activities.explanation: Economic activities involve money or payment in money’s worth.

activities.title: Rohan’s Paid Work
activities.prompt: Rohan receives a ______ for working for a software company.
activities.hint: This is payment for his work.
activities.explanation: The fact says Rohan receives a salary for this work.

activities.title: Match Each Idea
activities.prompt: Match each word with its correct meaning.
pairs: involve money or payment in money’s worth
a place where people exchange goods and services
payment for professional advice or services
do not generate income or wealth
activities.explanation: Each pair matches an idea with its meaning from the lesson.

activities.title: Linking People and Activities
activities.prompt: Which choice correctly links a person and an economic activity?
options: Rohan receives a fee for weekend volunteering.
Rohan receives a salary for weekend volunteering.
Geeta Aunty receives a salary for serving the country.
activities.explanation: Geeta Aunty receives a salary, so serving the country is economic.

activities.title: Payment for Expert Help
activities.prompt: A payment for advice or help from an expert is called a ______.
activities.hint: People pay this money to experts.
activities.explanation: A fee is money paid for advice or services.

activities.title: Classifying Rohan’s Activities
activities.prompt: Put these ideas in order. Use them to classify (sort) Rohan’s activities.
items: Economic activities give money or things worth money.
Rohan gets a salary for work at a software company.
Rohan’s weekend volunteering (unpaid help) is a non-economic activity.
activities.explanation: Rohan’s salary (pay for work) shows economic work. His weekend volunteering is non-economic.

activities.prompt: A child needs advice and pays a professional a fee. What happens in this activity?
options: The child receives advice in return for payment.
The child receives advice, but the professional earns no income.
The child pays, but no professional service is received.
The child works for the professional in exchange for advice.

why.The child receives advice, but the profe: This confuses a useful service with a reason to earn no income.
why.The child pays, but no professional serv: This wrongly assumes payment happens without any service.
why.The child works for the professional in: This reverses who receives advice and who provides it.

activities.explanation: A fee is payment for professional advice or services.

activities.prompt: One person gives vegetables, and another gives housework in return. Why is this an economic exchange?
options: The goods and services are exchanged for each other.
The vegetables have value, but services cannot be exchanged.
The vegetables are exchanged, but the service is ignored.
Money must change hands for this to be an exchange.

why.The vegetables have value, but services: This wrongly believes that only goods can be exchanged.
why.The vegetables are exchanged, but the se: This overlooks the service given in return.
why.Money must change hands for this to be a: This wrongly thinks money must always change hands.

activities.explanation: Goods and services can be exchanged for other goods and services.

activities.prompt: Rohan receives a salary for working for a software company. His weekend volunteering is non-economic. Which comparison is correct?
options: His paid work involves income, but his weekend volunteering does not.
Both activities earn income because both help other people.
His weekend volunteering earns income, but his paid work does not.
Neither activity involves money, payment, or income.

why.Both activities earn income because both: This wrongly assumes that helping people always creates income.
why.His weekend volunteering earns income, b: This reverses the paid and unpaid activities.
why.Neither activity involves money, payment: This ignores the salary received for his paid work.

activities.explanation: His salary creates income, while his weekend volunteering does not.

activities.prompt: A youth cares for grandparents without receiving income or wealth. How should this activity be classified?
options: Non-economic, because it generates neither income nor wealth.
Economic, because caring for family takes useful work.
Economic, because the grandparents provide money’s worth.
Non-economic, because all family care happens in markets.

why.Economic, because caring for family take: This confuses useful work with income or wealth.
why.Economic, because the grandparents provi: This wrongly treats family care as payment in money’s worth.
why.Non-economic, because all family care ha: This wrongly assumes that all family care happens in markets.

activities.explanation: Non-economic activities do not generate income or wealth.

activities.prompt: Geeta Aunty receives a salary for serving the country. Why is her activity economic?
options: Her salary shows that money is involved.
Her service to the country means no payment is needed.
Her salary shows that she works without any income.
Her activity is economic only if it happens in a market.

why.Her service to the country means no paym: This wrongly thinks public service removes the need for payment.
why.Her salary shows that she works without: This confuses receiving a salary with having no income.
why.Her activity is economic only if it happ: This wrongly treats a market as a requirement for economic activity.

activities.explanation: Her salary is money received for her work.

lessons.title: Types of Economic Activities

activities.prompt: What might you discover about work and payment on a village tour?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Village Workers and Their Pay
activities.body:
You arrive near Kavya’s village, where a highway is being built. Technicians operate excavators and bulldozers at the site. The travel time is expected to fall from five hours to two hours.

You meet Kavya’s uncle, a technician who operates a bulldozer. He receives a monthly salary for his services.

Then you visit Kavya’s aunt at the village post office. She receives a monthly salary for her work. She also conducts online classes for students preparing for school exams. For these classes, she charges a weekly fee.

Later, you watch Sahil, a farm labourer, use a tractor to till land. He earns a daily wage for his work. His pay arrives in two forms. He receives part in cash and the rest in mangoes.

You compare the workers and their rewards. The technician and the post-office worker receive a monthly salary. Sahil earns a daily wage. Kavya’s aunt charges a weekly fee for classes. The mangoes given to Sahil are payment in kind. You see that payment can take different forms.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Different Work and Payment
activities.body: A highway is being built near Kavya’s village. Technicians operate excavators and bulldozers there. Kavya’s uncle operates a bulldozer and receives a monthly salary. His aunt works at the village post office. She conducts online classes and charges a weekly fee. Sahil tills land using a tractor. He earns a daily wage, partly in cash and partly in mangoes. Payment in kind means paying with goods instead of money.
keyPoints: People do different kinds of work.
Workers receive payment in different ways.
Mangoes are payment in kind.
activities.explanation: These examples show how work and payment can differ.

activities.prompt: How can road building give paid work and faster travel?
steps: A highway brings excavators and bulldozers, so road building is secondary work.
Kavya’s uncle earns monthly by operating a bulldozer, so this work pays.
The new route may be shorter, so travel could become faster.
Thus, travel may fall from five hours to two hours.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

lessons.title: Payments and Value Addition

activities.prompt: How can you discover the value someone adds while making an object?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Rajesh Adds Value
activities.body:
Imagine that you visit a nearby market and meet Rajesh, a carpenter. He buys wood there to make furniture. You see him pay ₹600 for the wood used in furniture. This payment shows an economic activity because money is involved. Such activities have value in terms of money.

Next, you watch Rajesh use special tools and other materials. His skill, time and effort help him turn the wood into furniture. This change creates a new form, so it is called value addition. Economic activities add value at every stage of a process.

When the chair is ready, Rajesh takes it to the market. He sells each chair there for ₹1,000. You compare this price with the ₹600 paid for wood. The remaining ₹400 represents the value added to the chair. This remaining value comes from Rajesh's skill, time and effort.

Buying the wood and selling the chair are economic activities because they involve payment. You can now explain Rajesh's work as value addition. You also learn that payment in kind means non-cash payment received for work.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: How Rajesh Adds Value
activities.body: Rajesh is a carpenter. He buys wood for ₹600. He uses tools and other materials to build furniture. He sells each chair for ₹1,000. The extra ₹400 is value added. It comes from his skill, time and effort. Buying and selling are economic activities. They involve payment. Value addition means changing something into a new form. Payment in kind is payment for work, but not in cash.
keyPoints: Rajesh turns wood into furniture.
The value added to each chair is ₹400.
Payment in kind is payment that is not cash.
activities.explanation: Rajesh changes wood into furniture. This adds value.

activities.prompt: Rajesh buys wood for ₹600 and sells a chair for ₹1,000. Where does the extra ₹400 come from?
steps: Rajesh pays ₹600 because he needs wood to make furniture.
His tools, skill, time and effort turn the wood into a chair.
He sells the chair for ₹1,000 because buyers pay for the finished furniture.
The remaining ₹400 is the value he adds while changing the wood.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What Does Rajesh Buy?
activities.prompt: What does Rajesh buy from the nearby market?
options: Wood
Chairs
Tools
Payment in kind
activities.explanation: Rajesh buys wood from a nearby market for making furniture.

activities.title: The Cost of Wood
activities.prompt: Rajesh pays ₹______ for the wood used to make furniture.
activities.hint: Think about the amount Rajesh pays for wood.

activities.title: Rajesh’s Work

activities.title: Rajesh’s Work in Order

activities.explanation: Rajesh buys wood, uses tools and materials, builds furniture and sells the chair.

activities.title: Payment Without Cash
activities.prompt: Payment in kind is ______ payment received for work.
activities.hint: Think about payment that does not use money.
activities.explanation: Payment in kind means non-cash payment received for work.

activities.prompt: Rajesh buys wood for ₹600 and sells a chair for ₹1,000. What explains the extra ₹400?
options: His skill, time and effort add value to the wood.
Buying the wood alone adds all the extra value.
Selling the chair removes value from the wood.
Payment for wood adds value before Rajesh does any work.

why.Buying the wood alone adds all the extra: This mistake thinks the purchase alone creates all value.
why.Selling the chair removes value from the: This mistake thinks selling destroys the value that was added.
why.Payment for wood adds value before Rajes: This mistake confuses paying for wood with adding value while making furniture.

activities.explanation: This is right because the extra value comes from his skill, time and effort.

activities.prompt: Payment in kind means non-cash payment received for work. If food is received after working, which conclusion is fair?
options: The food is payment in kind because it was received for work.
The food is only payment if it is sold for money.
The food is payment in kind only before the work starts.
The food is payment in kind only when special tools are used.

why.The food is only payment if it is sold f: This mistake wrongly thinks payment in kind must first become money.
why.The food is payment in kind only before: This mistake wrongly thinks payment must come before the work.
why.The food is payment in kind only when sp: This mistake wrongly thinks special tools are needed for payment in kind.

activities.explanation: This is right because payment in kind can be non-cash payment for work.

activities.prompt: Compare buying Rajesh's wood with selling his finished chair. What happens to value at these steps?
options: Value is added at both steps because payment is involved.
Value is added only when the wood becomes furniture.
Value is added only when Rajesh buys wood from the market.
Value disappears whenever payment for the goods changes hands.

why.Value is added only when the wood become: This mistake thinks value appears only after furniture is finished.
why.Value is added only when Rajesh buys woo: This mistake thinks value appears only at the buying stage.
why.Value disappears whenever payment for th: This mistake thinks payment takes value away from each stage.

activities.explanation: This is right because economic activities add value at every stage.

activities.prompt: Rajesh paid ₹600 for wood and sells each chair for ₹1,000. Why does making the chair matter?
options: Turning wood into furniture adds value and leaves ₹400.
Turning wood into furniture removes value and leaves ₹400.
Buying the wood adds the same value as making the chair.
Selling the chair matters only because the market is nearby.

why.Turning wood into furniture removes valu: This mistake wrongly treats making furniture as removing value.
why.Buying the wood adds the same value as m: This mistake ignores the value added while making furniture.
why.Selling the chair matters only because t: This mistake wrongly links added value to the market's location.

activities.explanation: This is right because making furniture adds value and leaves ₹400.

activities.prompt: A market record shows ₹600 paid for wood. It also shows ₹1,000 received for a chair. What does this source show?
options: The difference of ₹400 is the value added.
The wood and the chair each cost ₹1,000.
The payment for the chair is less than the wood payment.
The record shows no value was added to the wood.

This mistake gives both wood and chair the same cost.
why.The payment for the chair is less than t: This mistake reverses which payment is larger.
why.The record shows no value was added to t: This mistake ignores the difference shown by the record.

activities.explanation: This is right because ₹1,000 minus ₹600 leaves ₹400 as value added.

lessons.title: The Importance of Non-Economic Activities

activities.prompt: What makes non-economic activities valuable in our lives?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Caring for Others
activities.body:
You begin at home, where parents cook food for the family. You watch this care happen through their hands. Such cooking is a non-economic activity. It may not involve money.

Next, you help children with schoolwork. You see them receive guidance with their lessons. You also see grandparents cared for. These caring activities are non-economic activities.

Then you join family members helping to renovate the house. Everyone shares the work. This work is another non-economic activity.

Your tour now reaches a temple, a gurudwara, a mosque and a church. Here, sevā is seen. It contributes to society without expecting anything in return. A temple distributes prasād to its devotees.

At a gurudwara, a community kitchen serves food free to every visitor. You also find a langar at the Golden Temple. Finally, you remember why these activities matter. These activities may not involve money. Yet the value they create is important in our lives.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Activities That Help Us
activities.body: Non-economic activities help people and communities without needing money. Examples include cooking for your family and helping children with schoolwork. Caring for grandparents and renovating your house are also examples. Their value is important in our lives. Sevā is seen in temples, gurudwaras, mosques and churches. It contributes to society without expecting anything in return.
keyPoints: They may not involve money.
They create important value.
Sevā serves society.
activities.explanation: These activities make life better for families and communities.

activities.prompt: A girl helps her brother with homework. No money changes hands. Why can her help still matter?
steps: Helping with schoolwork is non-economic because it is family support without payment.
This help creates value because the child gets needed schoolwork support.
This value matters because non-economic activities are important in our lives.
Therefore, unpaid homework help can still be important.

activities.prompt: Which statement about non-economic activities is correct?
options: Non-economic activities must involve money.

activities.hint: It shows that involving money is not always needed.
activities.explanation: The facts say they may not involve money.

activities.explanation: This helps children with learning and is listed as a non-economic activity.

options: It creates value for the family without money.

why.It creates money for the family through: This mistake treats family cooking as paid work.
why.It matters only when the family buys foo: This mistake thinks value depends on buying food.
why.It matters only when visitors receive th: This mistake wrongly makes visitors part of family cooking.

activities.explanation: Family cooking is non-economic and creates value.

activities.prompt: A family cares for grandparents every day. No payment is given. Why can this care still be important?
options: It creates value for the family without money.

why.It creates money for the family through: This mistake assumes family care should bring outside money.
why.It matters only when grandparents help w: This mistake mixes grandparent care with house renovation.
why.It matters only when visitors receive fr: This mistake mixes grandparent care with serving visitors.

activities.explanation: Caring for grandparents is non-economic and creates value.

activities.prompt: A map marks a langar at the Golden Temple. A source says gurudwara kitchens serve every visitor free food. What do these facts suggest together?
options: The Golden Temple is linked with community food service.

why.The Golden Temple has a paid restaurant: Nothing in the facts says the Golden Temple has a paid restaurant.

options: They both give something to people who visit.

lessons.title: The Strength of Community Participation

activities.prompt: What happens when a whole community works together?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Working Together for Cleanliness
activities.body:
You begin a walk through your neighbourhood with a broom. Today, you join the Swachh Bharat Abhiyan, which works to keep our surroundings clean. It depends on the collective efforts of all Indian citizens. You are already showing this spirit.

At home, you keep your home and surroundings clean. On the street, you meet others cleaning streets and roads together. You also help clean parks and other public places. In community areas, people work side by side.

As you continue, you see how these efforts can make a clean home. They can also make your neighbourhood, society and nation clean. The lesson is simple: cleanliness grows when everyone contributes. You have seen why individual care and teamwork must go together.

Now you enter a festival where the community gathers. Van Mahotsav, celebrated as the festival of forests, brings everyone together. You join others in tree plantation drives. The festival creates awareness about the value of trees.

During festivals, people organise many activities. They decorate the place and share the food they cook. You leave ready to join your community's cleaning efforts.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Working Together for a Clean India
activities.body: People work together to keep their area clean. Swachh Bharat Abhiyan needs all Indian citizens to work together. People also clean their homes. Everyone does their own part. People clean streets, roads, parks and other public places. Together, they can keep the home, neighbourhood, society and nation clean. Van Mahotsav brings people together to plant trees. It also teaches why trees matter.
keyPoints: Every citizen helps keep the area clean.
People clean shared places together.
Van Mahotsav helps people plant trees.
activities.explanation: When people work together, they make communities cleaner.

activities.prompt: Our street needs cleaning, but each family cleans only its own home. How can we clean our neighbourhood?
steps: Shared streets need community care because they are used by everyone.
Neighbours should clean streets and roads together because collective effort covers common spaces.
They should clean parks and other public places too because these are shared places.
Together, these actions can make our home, neighbourhood, society and nation clean because everyone contributes.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Whose work does the Swachh Bharat Abhiyan need?
options: Only children
All Indian citizens
Only city officials
Only people living in cities
activities.explanation: The abhiyan needs the work of all Indian citizens.

activities.prompt: Each person keeps their home and surroundings clean ______.
activities.hint: This means each person does their own part.
activities.explanation: Each person helps. They keep their home and surroundings clean.

activities.prompt: The Swachh Bharat Abhiyan needs all Indian citizens to work together.
activities.explanation: It needs all Indian citizens to work together.

activities.prompt: Match each community effort with its main idea.
activities.explanation: The abhiyan cleans surroundings. Van Mahotsav celebrates forests. Tree drives unite the community, and festivals bring organised activities.

activities.prompt: What does Van Mahotsav bring people together to do?
options: Keep food stalls open

options: Cleaning a street, cleaning a park, planting trees
Cleaning a home, planting one tree, avoiding neighbours

Cleaning roads, waiting alone, leaving parks dirty
activities.explanation: People clean streets, parks and public places together. They also join tree plantation drives.

activities.prompt: A street has rubbish. Families clean their homes, then neighbours clean the street together. What result is most likely?
options: Only the family homes will become clean.
The whole neighbourhood will become cleaner.
The street will stay dirty for ever.
Public parks will become dirtier.

This treats individual home cleaning as enough for shared spaces.
This wrongly assumes that working together will not improve the street.
This confuses the result of shared cleaning with a worsening result.

activities.explanation: This is right because collective cleaning can make the neighbourhood clean.

activities.prompt: At one time, one person sweeps a road. Later, neighbours sweep it together. What changes most clearly?
options: The cleaning becomes a shared community effort.
The road is cleaned by only one person.
Home cleaning becomes less important.
Public places need no cleaning.

This ignores the neighbours who later join the cleaning.
This wrongly suggests that shared cleaning reduces home cleaning.
This wrongly assumes that public places do not need cleaning.

activities.explanation: This is right because people have come together to clean the road.

activities.prompt: Van Mahotsav is the festival of forests. People join tree plantation drives. What is the main reason for joining?
options: To work together for trees and forest awareness.
To keep every street clean alone.
To decorate places and share cooked food.
To stay away from community activities.

This confuses forest participation with solitary home cleaning.
why.To decorate places and share cooked food: This describes festival activities rather than tree plantation drives.
This misunderstands a community activity as something people avoid.

activities.explanation: This is right because tree planting and awareness about trees' value happen together.

activities.prompt: During festivals, people organise activities and share food. At Van Mahotsav, people plant trees. What connects both events?
options: Both bring people together for shared action.
Both ask people to work alone at home.
Both aim only to decorate the same place.
Both stop people from joining together.

This wrongly treats shared activities as solitary work.
why.Both aim only to decorate the same place: This ignores the tree planting and festival activities.
This misunderstands both events as ways to avoid community work.

activities.explanation: This is right because community participation joins people in both events.

activities.prompt: A community report lists street cleaning, park cleaning, and tree planting. What does the report suggest?
options: People join together to care for shared places.
People care only for their own private rooms.
People meet only to eat and decorate.
People organise no work for the community.

why.People care only for their own private r: This confuses community work with work limited to private homes.
This ignores the cleaning and tree planting listed in the report.
why.People organise no work for the communit: This wrongly treats the listed activities as a lack of organised work.

activities.explanation: This is right because the listed work shows people caring for shared places together.

activities.prompt: The Swachh Bharat Abhiyan depends on collective efforts. A colony wants to follow it. What should happen first?
options: Every citizen should join in cleaning shared spaces.
One citizen should clean all the public places.
Families should keep cleaning only inside homes.
Neighbours should wait for the nation to act alone.

why.One citizen should clean all the public: This wrongly puts the whole task on only one citizen.
why.Families should keep cleaning only insid: This ignores the need to clean streets, parks and other shared places.
why.Neighbours should wait for the nation to: This misunderstands collective action as waiting for others to act alone.

activities.explanation: This is right because the Abhiyan depends on the collective efforts of all citizens.

activities.context: The neighbourhood children notice the work done by adults around them. Geeta Aunty comes home in her uniform; she is a pilot in the Indian Air Force. Kabir’s grandfather, retired from the Border Security Force, tends the vegetable garden and runs errands. Kabir’s grandfather tends the garden and runs errands after retirement.
Anu’s parents sell garments, and her mother helps a stitching group.

activities.context: Geeta Aunty receives a salary for serving the country. Rohan receives a salary for working for a software company, so both are carrying out economic activities. activities.context: Geeta Aunty receives a salary for serving the country. Rohan receives a salary for working for a software company, so both are carrying out economic activities. On the weekend, Rohan volunteers and does not receive income, so this is a non-economic activity. He also takes care of his grandparents. chapters.title: Economic Activities Around Us
chapters.summary: In this chapter: the primary sector; the secondary sector; the tertiary sector; the story of the anand milk cooperative.

lessons.title: The Primary Sector

activities.prompt: Which jobs begin with nature’s help?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Primary Activities
activities.body:
Imagine you are visiting places where useful things begin. You soon notice that each place works closely with nature. These are known as primary activities, or primary sector economic activities.

First, you visit a farm. You watch grains and vegetables grow in the fields. Farmers do primary work because they grow food using natural resources. You also see poultry farms, where workers collect eggs. Getting eggs from poultry farms is also primary work.

Next, you travel to a forest. You see workers collecting wood from trees. Collecting wood from forests is a primary activity. The wood is a raw material taken directly from nature.

After this, you enter a mine and watch coal being extracted. Extracting coal from mines is a primary activity. Later, you visit fisheries, where workers take fish from the water. Taking fish from fisheries is a primary activity. Finally, you think about farming, fishing and forestry. These are examples of primary activities that depend directly on nature to produce goods.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: What is the primary sector?
activities.body: Primary activities depend directly on nature to make goods. This means people take raw materials straight from nature. These activities are also called the primary sector. Farming, fishing and forestry are examples. They include growing grains and vegetables, taking fish, collecting wood, and getting eggs.
keyPoints: Primary activities depend directly on nature.
They take raw materials straight from nature.
Farming, fishing and forestry are examples.
activities.explanation: The primary sector connects nature, raw materials and goods.

activities.prompt: Growing grains and collecting wood seem different. Why are both primary work?
steps: Growing grains is primary work because it depends directly on nature.
Collecting wood is also primary because it takes raw materials from nature.
Both belong to the primary sector because both use nature directly.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Choose a primary activity
activities.prompt: Which activity is primary work?

Making goods from goods
Using materials after nature is no longer involved
Producing goods without raw materials

activities.explanation: Primary activities depend directly on nature, so this statement is false.

activities.explanation: Farming takes raw materials directly from nature to produce goods.

options: It takes raw materials directly from nature.

activities.explanation: The primary sector involves taking raw materials directly from nature.

activities.explanation: This shows that nature directly provides the grains.

why.Both get their raw materials only from p: This wrongly thinks nature's raw materials come only from poultry farms.

activities.explanation: Both workers take raw materials straight from nature.

why.This is fishing work because wood comes: This confuses wood with fish from fisheries.
why.This is poultry work because the wood co: This confuses wood with eggs from poultry farms.

activities.explanation: The wood comes directly from nature, so the work is primary.

options: Their work is primary because eggs come directly from nature.
Their work is not primary because eggs need no farm.

Their work is not primary because poultry farms do not depend on nature.

why.Their work is not primary because eggs n: This wrongly treats poultry farm products as separate from nature.
why.Their work is primary only if the eggs a: This wrongly thinks primary work depends on selling eggs.
why.Their work is not primary because poultr: This wrongly claims poultry farms do not depend on nature.

activities.explanation: Getting eggs directly from nature makes this primary work.

why.Because the worker does not take raw mat: This wrongly denies the direct use of nature.
why.Because the worker grows vegetables rath: This confuses forestry work with farming work.
why.Because the worker takes eggs from poult: This confuses collecting wood with getting eggs.

activities.explanation: The worker takes wood directly from nature as a raw material.

options: Growing vegetables and mining coal are both primary work.
Growing vegetables is primary, but mining coal is not.
Mining coal is primary, but growing vegetables is not.
Neither activity is primary because both take raw materials.

why.Growing vegetables is primary, but minin: This wrongly thinks only farming work is primary.
why.Mining coal is primary, but growing vege: This wrongly thinks only mining work is primary.
why.Neither activity is primary because both: This wrongly believes taking raw materials prevents primary work.

activities.explanation: Both growing vegetables and mining coal depend directly on nature.

lessons.title: The Secondary Sector

activities.prompt: What can grains, wood and cotton become after some clever work?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Secondary Work
activities.body:
You visit places where houses, roads and other structures are built. These activities belong to the secondary sector. You also provide water, electricity and gas. These are secondary activities too. Your tour shows many kinds of work.

Next, you enter factories and production units. Here, goods are manufactured and processed. You watch mills turn grains from farms into flour. The grains become flour.

Then, you follow wood from forests. You see it changed into furniture and paper. Wood from forests can become these products. This is another example of secondary work.

Later, you find cotton being used to make clothes. Workers turn cotton into clothing. You understand why factories and production units matter. They make and process goods. You know secondary activities build structures, provide services and transform materials into products.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: What Is the Secondary Sector?
activities.body: The secondary sector includes work that makes things and provides services. Builders construct houses, roads and other structures. Providers supply water, electricity and gas. Factories and production units manufacture and process goods. Mills turn farm grains into flour. Forest wood can become furniture and paper. Cotton is used to make clothes.
keyPoints: Secondary work includes construction and supplying services.
Factories and production units manufacture and process goods.
Raw materials become useful products such as flour, furniture, paper and clothes.
activities.explanation: The secondary sector makes goods and provides services.

activities.prompt: A town needs a new house and water. Why do both jobs belong together?
steps: Building a house is secondary work because houses are structures.
Providing water is secondary work because it is grouped with electricity and gas.
Both jobs are secondary activities, so they belong in the secondary sector.
The same sector therefore includes construction and providing services.

activities.prompt: Match each material or work to its result.

activities.explanation: Mills turn grains from farms into flour, so this is the correct order.

activities.prompt: Why are mills part of the secondary sector?
options: They build houses, roads and other buildings.
They provide water, electricity and gas.
They manufacture and process goods.

activities.explanation: Factories manufacture (make) goods. A mill does this by turning grain into flour.

activities.prompt: A maker wants to make paper. Which material can be changed to make it?

Wood from forests

why.Turn grains into flour and make paper: These jobs do not meet the town's road and water needs.
why.Process cotton into clothes and build ho: These jobs do not meet the town's road and water needs.

activities.prompt: Workers build houses while another team provides electricity. What do these jobs have in common?

This confuses all secondary work with factory production.
This confuses secondary work with processing farm crops.

activities.explanation: Building structures and providing electricity belong to the secondary sector.

lessons.title: The Tertiary Sector

activities.prompt: What could you discover about different kinds of work?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Services
activities.body:
You begin a tour of the tertiary sector. You meet a fruit and vegetable vendor. The vendor sells farm produce to households.

Next, you meet a technician. The technician repairs and services electronic items, such as mobile phones and televisions. You also meet a mechanic, who repairs vehicles such as cars and tractors.

Further along, you meet an electrician. The electrician makes sure electricity is supplied regularly. You pause and learn about this important service.

After that, you try a mobile and internet service. These services belong to the tertiary sector. You then visit a hotel and a restaurant. Software development and services in these places are tertiary activities.

Before you finish, you put the tour together. The tertiary sector includes all these service activities. It is also called the service sector. You leave with a clearer picture of the work around you.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Services in the Tertiary Sector
activities.body: The tertiary sector is also called the service sector. Technicians repair and service electronic items. These include mobile phones and televisions. Mechanics repair vehicles. These include cars and tractors. Electricians make sure electricity comes regularly. Mobile and internet services are part of this sector. Fruit and vegetable sellers sell farm crops to homes. Making software is a tertiary activity. So are services in hotels and restaurants.
keyPoints: The tertiary sector is also called the service sector.
Technicians, mechanics and electricians give services.
Mobile, internet, hotel and restaurant services are tertiary activities.
activities.explanation: This sector has many useful services for homes and other places.

activities.prompt: A family buys fruit and vegetables from a vendor. Is this activity part of the tertiary sector, and why?
steps: The vendor sells farm produce to households, so this is service work.
Service work belongs to the tertiary sector, also called the service sector.
Therefore, the vendor's sale is a tertiary activity.

Only the stall, because only selling is a service.

why.Only the garage, because only repairing: This wrongly thinks only repairing vehicles is a service.

Vendor for fruit, technician for car, electrician for phone.

why.Technician for fruit, electrician for ca: This mixes up produce, vehicle, and phone services.
why.Electrician for fruit, mechanic for car,: This mixes up produce, vehicle, and phone services.
why.Vendor for fruit, technician for car, el: This mixes up produce, vehicle, and phone services.

activities.explanation: This is right because the vendor, mechanic, and mobile service match each need.

activities.prompt: An electrician cannot do the work that keeps electricity supplied. What could happen next, and why?
options: Electricity might not be supplied regularly.
Cars and tractors might not get repaired.
Farm produce might not reach households.
Mobile phones might not receive internet services.

why.Cars and tractors might not get repaired: This wrongly connects electricity work with vehicle repairs.
This wrongly connects electricity work with produce selling.
why.Mobile phones might not receive internet: This wrongly connects electricity work with mobile services.

activities.explanation: This is right because electricians make sure electricity is supplied regularly.

lessons.title: The Story of the Anand Milk Cooperative

activities.prompt: What happens when farmers choose to work together?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Anand Milk Cooperative
activities.body:
You meet Anand farmers. They milk their cows and sell milk to a nearby dairy.
Together, they approached Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel for advice.

As you follow their story, Patel advises them to form a cooperative.
This choice can make them independent and free them from relying on middlemen.
As a group, they take charge of collecting, processing and distributing milk.

You learn that AMUL was set up in 1946 CE.
You visit the factory that farmers set up in Anand.
You see the farmers sharing every task.
Sharing all the tasks helps them raise their income slowly.

During your tour, you see how milk production is a primary activity.
This is because milk comes directly from livestock.
You watch milk become powder, ghee, cheese and butter.
Turning milk into products is secondary work.

Finally, you follow AMUL products through transport, trade and retail.
These are tertiary activities.
You now see how shared work brought independence and slowly higher income.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Farmers Build Together
activities.body: Farmers near Anand sold milk to a dairy nearby. The farmers went to Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel together. Patel told them to form a cooperative. He also told them to be independent. A cooperative means farmers work together as a group. Independent means they do not need middlemen, or people in between. The group collected milk, processed it and sent it out. They built a factory in Anand. AMUL started in 1946 CE. Sharing work helped their income grow slowly.
keyPoints: A cooperative is farmers working together as a group.
AMUL started in 1946 CE.
Sharing work helped farmers raise their income slowly.
activities.explanation: Working together helped farmers slowly raise their income.

activities.prompt: Why should nearby farmers join a milk cooperative instead of working alone?
steps: Working alone can leave farmers relying on middlemen.
Together, they can collect, process and distribute milk.
This shared work frees them from middlemen and helps them become independent.
Sharing all tasks helps their income rise slowly.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Patel tells the farmers to form a cooperative. It helps them become ______.
activities.hint: This means they do not need middlemen.
activities.explanation: Patel's advice helped the farmers work together. They became independent.

activities.prompt: Match each activity with its type of work.
pairs: Transporting, trading and retailing AMUL products
activities.explanation: Milk production is primary work. Making milk products is secondary work. Moving, trading and retailing are tertiary activities.

activities.prompt: What did the cooperative help the farmers stop doing?
options: Sharing all their work
Using middlemen
Collecting their milk
Processing their milk
activities.explanation: The cooperative helped the farmers stop using middlemen.

activities.prompt: Put the farmers' group tasks in order.
activities.explanation: The farmers first collected milk, then processed it and distributed it.

activities.prompt: Why is milk production a primary activity?
options: Milk comes straight from animals.
Milk is made into butter.
AMUL products go to shops.
Milk products are bought and sold.
activities.explanation: Milk comes straight from animals, so milk production is a primary activity.

activities.prompt: The cooperative frees farmers from middlemen. What effect can this have?
options: The farmers can become more independent.
The farmers can become more dependent.
The farmers can stop sharing tasks.
The farmers can stop raising income.

This reverses the meaning of independence.
This wrongly assumes that shared work would end.
This forgets that shared tasks helped income rise slowly.

activities.explanation: Patel wanted farmers to become independent through a cooperative.

activities.prompt: Before the cooperative, farmers sold milk to a nearby dairy. After it, what changed?
options: They handled collecting, processing and distribution together.
They kept selling only to nearby dairies.
They stopped sharing the milk work.
They gave up processing the milk.

why.They kept selling only to nearby dairies: This keeps the earlier nearby-dairy selling pattern.
This wrongly assumes that the farmers stopped sharing work.
This forgets that the farmers took charge of processing.

activities.explanation: The farmers took charge of collecting, processing and distributing milk together.

activities.prompt: Farmers in Anand approached Sardar Patel together. Why did acting together matter?
options: They could form a cooperative and become independent.
They could sell milk without using any dairy.
They could stop making milk products.
They could keep control of the middlemen.

why.They could sell milk without using any d: Patel advised a cooperative, not avoiding all dairies.
The farmers still needed to process and distribute milk.
why.They could keep control of the middlemen: The cooperative freed farmers from middlemen, not the other way round.

activities.explanation: A group could form the cooperative that Patel advised.
