lessons.title: How the Three Sectors Work Together

activities.prompt: How does a book travel from raw materials to your hands?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Book’s Journey
activities.body:
Join a book-making tour and watch three sectors work together. You begin with natural raw materials, ready to become useful finished goods.

At each stage, you see why teamwork matters. Every step of making books depends on all three sectors working together.

During the tour, you look at how raw materials are turned into things people can use. Workers help carry out this work. Finished products are made for people to use or consume.

After you finish reading, think about the paper around you. Used paper can be recycled to make new paper. This gives materials another useful journey.

Recycling one tonne of paper saves 17 trees. It also saves space in places where waste is dumped. As you complete the tour, you see how recycling supports the whole process.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Working Together
activities.body: The three sectors work together at every step of making books. They help turn raw materials from nature into finished goods. Used paper can be recycled to make new paper. Recycling one tonne of paper saves 17 trees. It also saves space where waste is dumped.
keyPoints: All three sectors work together at every step of making books.
They turn raw materials from nature into finished goods.
Recycling paper saves trees and space at waste dumps.
activities.explanation: The sectors work together. Recycling helps save trees and space.

activities.prompt: Schools need books and old paper. How can three sectors help?
steps: Raw materials become finished goods, because people need products to use.
All three sectors work together, because every book-making stage depends on them.
Used paper becomes new paper, because recycling gives old paper another use.
Recycling saves trees and dump space, so reuse helps the whole process.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: A Shared Goal
activities.prompt: Which sentence shows the shared goal of the three sectors?
options: They keep every stage of work separate.
They turn natural raw materials into finished goods.
They make raw materials less useful.
They stop finished goods from being made.
activities.explanation: Good choice! The sectors help turn raw materials into useful finished goods.

activities.title: Useful Connections
activities.prompt: Match each starting point with its result.
pairs: Space saved where waste is dumped
activities.explanation: Great matching! These pairs show what the sectors and recycling achieve.

activities.title: Paper Steps
activities.prompt: Put these paper steps in the correct order.
activities.explanation: Used paper is recycled, and this helps make new paper.

activities.title: Benefits of Recycling
activities.prompt: Which benefit comes from recycling paper?
options: It saves 17 trees and makes more dumping space.
It saves dumping space but uses more trees.
It changes used paper into natural raw materials.
It stops books from being made.
activities.explanation: Yes! Recycling one tonne saves 17 trees and saves dumping space.

activities.title: A Careful Plan
activities.prompt: A book-making team has used paper. Which plan follows the facts?
options: Choose one sector and let it work alone.
Recycle used paper but ignore the three sectors.
Let all three sectors work and recycle used paper.
Make books without using any paper.
activities.explanation: Great plan! All three sectors work together, and used paper can be recycled.

activities.prompt: A town recycles used paper. Which two benefits can follow?
options: It saves trees and space in waste dumps.
It saves trees and increases space in waste dumps.
It saves raw materials and stops people using books.
It saves dump space and uses more new paper.

why.It saves trees and increases space in wa: This mistake reverses recycling's effect on dump space.
why.It saves raw materials and stops people: This mistake thinks recycling reduces the use of books.
why.It saves dump space and uses more new pa: This mistake reverses recycling's effect on paper use.

activities.explanation: Recycling saves both trees and space in waste dumps.

activities.prompt: A school recycles one tonne of paper. Why can this save trees?
options: Recycled paper can replace the need for new paper.
Used paper is kept in dumps, so new paper is not needed.
Recycled paper needs more trees than unused paper.
New books are made only from fresh raw materials.

why.Used paper is kept in dumps, so new pape: This mistake thinks dumping used paper reduces the need for new paper.
why.Recycled paper needs more trees than unu: This mistake treats recycled paper as needing more trees.
why.New books are made only from fresh raw m: This mistake thinks new books cannot use recycled paper.

activities.explanation: Recycling one tonne saves 17 trees and makes new paper.

activities.prompt: One school recycles used paper, but another dumps it. What difference can follow?
options: The recycling school saves trees and space at dumps.
The recycling school fills its dump with more paper.
The dumping school saves more trees than the recycling school.
Both schools save trees because both handle used paper.

why.The recycling school fills its dump with: This mistake reverses recycling's effect on dump space.
why.The dumping school saves more trees than: This mistake gives dumping the benefit that belongs to recycling.
why.Both schools save trees because both han: This mistake assumes any handling of paper saves trees.

activities.explanation: Recycling saves trees and space in waste dumps.

activities.context: A farmer grows grains and vegetables on farms. Workers extract coal from mines. Another worker collects wood from forests, while a fisher takes fish from fisheries. A poultry farm also provides eggs. Together, these activities show how people take raw materials directly from nature to produce goods, so they form part of the primary sector economic activities.
activities.prompt: If the worker who collects wood from forests cannot work, what would happen next to the activity shown in the case?
options: Wood collection would be reduced for that day.
Growing grains and vegetables would also stop.
Taking fish from fisheries would change into mining work.
Getting eggs from poultry farms would become the mine's work.

why.Growing grains and vegetables would also: Farming is a separate activity and would not stop.
why.Taking fish from fisheries would change: Fishing would not turn into mining.
why.Getting eggs from poultry farms would be: Poultry work and mining remain separate.

activities.explanation: Correct: the missing worker would reduce wood collection.

activities.context: A farmer grows grains and vegetables on farms. Workers extract coal from mines. Another worker collects wood from forests, while a fisher takes fish from fisheries. A poultry farm also provides eggs. Together, these activities show how people take raw materials directly from nature to produce goods, so they form part of the primary sector economic activities.
activities.prompt: If the poultry farm changes from getting eggs to growing grains and vegetables, which result should follow?
options: The changed work would still be in the primary sector.
The changed work would leave the primary sector because it no longer provides eggs.
The changed work would become mining work.
The changed work would become forestry work.

why.The changed work would leave the primary: Getting eggs is not the only kind of primary work.
why.The changed work would become mining wor: Growing crops does not turn farming into mining.
why.The changed work would become forestry w: Growing crops does not turn farming into forestry.

activities.explanation: Correct: growing grains and vegetables is primary work.

activities.prompt: Explain why the activities described in the case are all primary activities.
activities.answer: The activities are primary because each one takes raw materials directly from nature to produce goods. Farming grows grains and vegetables, mining extracts coal, and forestry collects wood. Fisheries take fish, while poultry farms provide eggs. Therefore, all the work described is part of the primary sector economic activities.
points: Each activity depends directly on nature.
Raw materials are taken directly from nature.
Farming, mining, forestry, fishing and poultry work are included.
The activities belong to the primary sector.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A town needs new houses and roads, and its homes need water, electricity and gas. A factory receives cotton and makes clothes, while a mill turns grain from farms into flour. Workers also take wood from forests and change it into furniture and paper. The town is considering more structures and services, so people want to know which work belongs in the secondary sector and how production changes materials.
activities.prompt: If cotton arrives at a factory, what is it used to make?
options: Clothes
Flour
Furniture and paper
Roads

why.Flour: Flour is made from grain from farms.
why.Furniture and paper: Furniture and paper can be made from wood from forests.
why.Roads: Roads are structures that belong to the secondary sector.

activities.explanation: Cotton is used to make clothes.

activities.context: A town needs new houses and roads, and its homes need water, electricity and gas. A factory receives cotton and makes clothes, while a mill turns grain from farms into flour. Workers also take wood from forests and change it into furniture and paper. The town is considering more structures and services, so people want to know which work belongs in the secondary sector and how production changes materials.
activities.prompt: Which statement best describes what happens when wood from forests is changed into furniture and paper?
options: It is secondary-sector production because the wood is processed into goods.
It is secondary-sector work because the wood comes from a forest.
It is secondary-sector production because furniture and paper are structures.
It is not secondary-sector work because the material is changed.

why.It is secondary-sector work because the: A forest is the source of the wood, but the processing is what makes this secondary work.
why.It is secondary-sector production becaus: Furniture and paper are goods, not the structures listed with houses and roads.
why.It is not secondary-sector work because: Changing materials into goods is a key part of secondary-sector work.

activities.explanation: Changing wood into goods is manufacturing and processing in the secondary sector.

activities.prompt: Explain how the examples of mills, forest wood and cotton show that secondary activities can change materials into goods.
activities.answer: Secondary activities include work that changes materials into goods. A mill turns grain from farms into flour, cotton is used to make clothes, and wood from forests becomes furniture and paper. These examples show processing and manufacturing, so they belong to the secondary sector.
points: Mills turn farm grain into flour.
Cotton is used to make clothes.
Forest wood becomes furniture and paper.
These activities manufacture or process goods.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A household buys fruit and vegetables from a vendor. Later, a technician services a mobile phone and a mechanic repairs a car. An electrician checks that electricity continues to be supplied regularly. The household also uses mobile and internet services. Software is developed and used in a hotel and a restaurant. All these activities belong to the tertiary sector, also called the service sector.
activities.prompt: A tractor needs to be repaired. Who should carry out the repair?
options: The mechanic, because this person repairs vehicles such as tractors.
The electrician, because this person makes sure electricity is supplied regularly.
The technician, because this person repairs and services electronic items.
The vendor, because this person sells farm produce to households.

why.The electrician, because this person mak: Regular electricity supply is the electrician's responsibility.
why.The technician, because this person repa: Technicians work with electronic items rather than vehicles.
why.The vendor, because this person sells fa: Vendors sell farm produce rather than repair vehicles.

activities.explanation: A mechanic repairs vehicles, and a tractor is a vehicle.

activities.context: A household buys fruit and vegetables from a vendor. Later, a technician services a mobile phone and a mechanic repairs a car. An electrician checks that electricity continues to be supplied regularly. The household also uses mobile and internet services. Software is developed and used in a hotel and a restaurant. All these activities belong to the tertiary sector, also called the service sector.
activities.prompt: Which explanation correctly identifies why the hotel and restaurant software work is tertiary?
options: It is software development and service work in hotels and restaurants.
It is the selling of farm produce to households.
It is the repair of electronic items such as mobile phones and televisions.
It is the repair of vehicles such as cars and tractors.

why.It is the selling of farm produce to hou: Selling farm produce to households is the work of fruit and vegetable vendors.
why.It is the repair of electronic items suc: Repairing electronic items is the work of technicians.
why.It is the repair of vehicles such as car: Repairing vehicles is the work of mechanics.

activities.explanation: Software development and services in hotels and restaurants are tertiary activities.

activities.prompt: Explain why the activities described in the case are all part of the tertiary sector.
activities.answer: These activities all provide services. The vendor supplies farm produce to households; technicians service electronics; mechanics repair vehicles; and electricians ensure regular electricity. Mobile and internet services, along with software services in hotels and restaurants, are also tertiary activities.
points: Vendors supply farm produce to households.
Technicians and mechanics provide repair and servicing services.
Electricians make sure electricity is supplied regularly.
Mobile, internet, and hotel or restaurant software services are tertiary activities.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Farmers in Anand district sold their milk to a nearby dairy and approached Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel together. Following his advice, they formed a cooperative, took charge of collecting, processing and distributing milk, and set up AMUL in 1946 CE. They also established a factory in Anand. By sharing the work, they slowly raised their income and became independent instead of relying on middlemen.
activities.prompt: Suppose the farmers had ignored Sardar Patel’s advice and continued selling as individual sellers. What would most likely have happened?
options: They would have remained dependent on middlemen instead of gaining independence together.
They would have become independent because they shared every task.
They would have raised their income slowly by distributing milk separately.
They would have set up a factory in Anand while continuing to rely on middlemen.

why.They would have become independent becau: Option 1 is wrong because independence came through forming a cooperative and acting together.
why.They would have raised their income slow: Option 2 is wrong because income rose slowly when all the farmers shared the tasks.
why.They would have set up a factory in Anan: Option 3 is wrong because building a factory alone would not remove their dependence on middlemen.

activities.explanation: Option 0 is correct because the cooperative was advised as a way to avoid dependence on middlemen.

activities.context: Farmers in Anand district sold their milk to a nearby dairy and approached Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel together. Following his advice, they formed a cooperative, took charge of collecting, processing and distributing milk, and set up AMUL in 1946 CE. They also established a factory in Anand. By sharing the work, they slowly raised their income and became independent instead of relying on middlemen.
activities.prompt: Why was setting up a factory in Anand important for the farmers’ cooperative?
options: It would remove the need to process milk at all.
It would help the farmers handle milk processing and distribution as a group.
It would make milk production a tertiary activity.
It would allow the farmers to stop sharing the work.

why.It would remove the need to process milk: Option 1 is correct because the cooperative took charge of processing and distributing milk.
why.It would make milk production a tertiary: Option 3 is wrong because transforming milk into products is secondary work.
why.It would allow the farmers to stop shari: Option 4 is wrong because sharing all the tasks helped the farmers work together and raise their income.

activities.explanation: Option 2 is wrong because milk production directly from livestock is a primary activity.

activities.prompt: Why did the farmers in Anand district form a cooperative?
activities.answer: Farmers in Anand district approached Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel together. He advised them to form a cooperative so that they could become independent and avoid relying on middlemen. As a group, they took charge of collecting, processing and distributing milk, and this sharing of tasks helped their income rise slowly.
points: The farmers approached Sardar Patel together.
He advised them to form a cooperative.
The cooperative helped them avoid reliance on middlemen.
Sharing all tasks helped their income rise slowly.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A book-making activity begins with natural raw materials and turns them into finished books for people to use or consume. Every stage depends on all three sectors working together, so no single sector can complete the whole process alone. After books have been used, their paper is collected. Instead of leaving that paper in waste-dumping places, the activity sends it for recycling, and the recycled paper can be used to make new paper.
activities.prompt: If the activity stopped recycling the used paper, what would be one likely result?
options: Waste-dumping places would have less space saved.
Waste-dumping places would need more room.
More trees would be saved.
The used paper could become new paper.

why.Waste-dumping places would have less spa: This reverses the effect because recycling saves space in waste-dumping places.
Recycling saves trees, so stopping it would not save more trees.
Making new paper from used paper requires recycling.

activities.explanation: Without recycling, this space-saving effect would be lost.

activities.context: A book-making activity begins with natural raw materials and turns them into finished books for people to use or consume. Every stage depends on all three sectors working together, so no single sector can complete the whole process alone. After books have been used, their paper is collected. Instead of leaving that paper in waste-dumping places, the activity sends it for recycling, and the recycled paper can be used to make new paper.
activities.prompt: After the used books are collected, what should the activity do next?
options: The sheets should enter the recycling process and later become new paper.
The sheets should be dumped with other waste.
The sheets should be used as finished products for people.
The sheets should be stored without being recycled.

why.The sheets should be dumped with other w: Dumping it would lose the benefits of recycling.
why.The sheets should be used as finished pr: The next step is recycling rather than treating the sheets as finished products.
why.The sheets should be stored without bein: Storing it without recycling would miss the stated benefits.

activities.explanation: Used paper can be recycled to make new paper.

activities.prompt: Explain why all three sectors must work together when making books.
activities.answer: Making books is a connected process. Natural raw materials must be turned into finished goods, and the final products are for people to use or consume. Every stage depends on all three sectors working together, so if one sector does not help, the whole process cannot move forward successfully.
points: Natural raw materials are turned into finished goods.
Finished products are made for people to use or consume.
Every stage depends on all three sectors.
The sectors must work together to complete the process.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Economic Activities Around Us

activities.prompt: Cotton is used to make clothes. Which sector does this work belong to?
options: Primary sector
Secondary sector
Tertiary sector
Primary and tertiary sectors
activities.explanation: Making clothes changes raw cotton into a finished product. This is secondary work.

activities.prompt: Mobile and internet services belong to the primary sector.
activities.explanation: Good try. Mobile and internet services belong to the tertiary or service sector.

activities.prompt: Match each activity with the correct economic sector.
activities.explanation: Well done. Farming uses nature directly, factories process goods, and technicians provide services.

activities.prompt: Changing wood into furniture and paper is ______ work.
activities.hint: This sector changes raw materials into finished goods.
activities.explanation: Exactly. Changing forest wood into furniture and paper is secondary work.

activities.prompt: Why is catching fish a primary activity?
options: Because it depends on nature
Because factories process it
Because it repairs electronic items
Because it supplies electricity
activities.explanation: Yes. Fishing takes fish straight from nature, so it is a primary activity.

activities.prompt: Put the milk journey in the correct order.
activities.explanation: Great ordering. Collecting is primary work, processing is secondary, and retailing is tertiary.

activities.prompt: Sharing all cooperative tasks raised the farmers' income quickly.
activities.explanation: Good try. Sharing all the tasks helped the farmers raise their income slowly.

activities.prompt: AMUL was set up in ______ CE.
activities.hint: Use the year given in the chapter.
activities.explanation: Correct. AMUL was set up in 1946 CE.

activities.prompt: What happens when one tonne of paper is recycled?
options: It saves 17 trees
It makes waste dumping spaces larger
It stops all paper making
It uses more forest wood
activities.explanation: Yes. Recycling one tonne of paper saves 17 trees and saves waste dumping space.

activities.prompt: Match each raw material with a product made from it.
activities.explanation: Excellent. These materials are changed into useful products through secondary work.
